b1-w1-module-q1-1:
From 07 - Introduction to Ethics. The lecture separates morals from ethics: morals are personal, intuitive and subjective, while ethics is the objective, external intellectual framework within which decision-making takes place. That is what “rational and deliberative decision-making” describes, and it matches the ethical deliberation sequence (dilemma → rational deliberation → judgement).

  • A (intuitive, hard to challenge) describes morals, the social-intuitionist gut call.
  • C (a judgment of how things should be) is the personal moral view, not the framework used to reach a decision.
  • D (a social contract with retribution when broken) describes law, not ethics.
b1-w1-module-q12-12:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. The WHO list in the lecture answers each option directly.

  • A true: refugees face barriers accessing care (legal status, language, discrimination, not understanding the system).
  • C true: PTSD is more prevalent among refugees and asylum seekers than in the host population.
  • D true: breakdown of the health system in the country of origin is one of the WHO's ten points, and it is why chronic conditions go untreated.
  • B false: refugees are healthy in general - they have to be well enough to make the journey, and infectious disease is low.
b1-w1-module-q14-14:
From 09 - History of Medicine. The lecture names imperturbability or equanimity as William Osler's most famous piece of advice to physicians; Osler emphasized the doctor-patient relationship, bedside manner and bedside teaching.

  • Hippocrates rejected religious and magical healing and made the practitioner a diagnostician and therapist.
  • Galen set Hippocratic medicine within an anatomy and physiology framework and added the four temperaments.
  • Robert Koch is one of the champions of germ theory, with Pasteur and Lister.
b1-w1-module-q15-15:
From 09 - History of Medicine. Humoral theory (blood, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm) dominated until modern medical research in the 19th century, when germ theory challenged it: microorganisms (“wee beasties”) cause disease, championed by Pasteur, Lister and Koch, and leading to the biomedical model (identify the organism, develop a lab test, find a chemotherapeutic agent).

  • C (supernatural) and D (astrology) describe the religious/magical era that Hippocrates replaced - they came before humoral theory, not after it.
  • A (miasma) is not presented in the lecture as the successor; germ theory is the one named as displacing humoral theory.
b1-w1-module-q16-16:
From 09 - History of Medicine. The lecture's one-line summary of Galen is exactly option B: he took clinical Hippocratic medicine and set it within a wider anatomy and physiology framework, arguing humoral theory must be supplemented by practical experience (and adding the four temperaments).

  • A overstates it: the lecture says he investigated anatomy and physiology, not that he was the first to dissect a human body.
  • C (diet and exercise regimen) is not his contribution in the lecture.
  • D (circulation of blood through heart and lungs) is not attributed to Galen anywhere in the lecture; his framework remained humoral.

b1-w1-module-q19-19.html:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. The epidemiological transition is a long-term shift in the pattern of mortality and morbidity as countries develop, so all three statements hold.

  • A true: the transition is defined by changing causes of death and a shift in the age pattern of mortality from younger to older ages - mortality is what drives it.
  • B true: the lecture states it is closely associated with a demographic and socioeconomic transition.
  • C true: the three basic models are classical (Western), accelerated (e.g., Japan) and contemporary (developing countries).

flags.title: Option A is only partly covered
flags.html: 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health supports B and C word for word; the phrase “mortality is a fundamental factor in population dynamics” is not in the note, and A is inferred from the note's definition of the transition.

b1-w1-module-q20-20.html:
The demographic transition describes a population moving from high birth and death rates to low ones. Mortality falls first, then fertility declines; with fewer births and longer lives the age structure shifts upward, so population aging is its signature. 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health mentions the demographic transition only as travelling alongside the epidemiological one, with mortality shifting from younger to older ages.

  • A and C keyed: declining fertility and an aging population are the two features of the transition.
  • B fails: increasing fertility runs the wrong way - the transition ends in low fertility.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w1-module-q21-21:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health (levels-of-prevention table in 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1). Tertiary prevention reduces complications and disability in existing symptomatic or advanced disease - e.g., anticoagulating atrial fibrillation to prevent stroke.

  • A fails: primordial prevention (health promotion) targets the whole population specifically to prevent risk factors from arising.
  • B fails: primary prevention targets people with one or more risk factors to stop disease developing; identifying high-risk individuals is the high-risk strategy, a separate axis.
  • C fails: secondary prevention targets people with early, limited disease (screening), not the general population.
b1-w1-module-q22-22:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. The population strategy asks “why did this happen and could it have been prevented?” and seeks to control the determinants of disease incidence - the causes of incidence rather than the causes of cases.

  • A fails: its whole mechanism is to lower the mean or shift the distribution of risk factors.
  • B fails: this is the prevention paradox - large benefit to the community but a small benefit to each individual.
  • D fails because C is correct.
b1-w1-module-q23-23:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. The high-risk (individual) strategy seeks to identify high-risk, susceptible individuals and offer them individual protection - e.g., flagging systolic BP over 140. It truncates the risk distribution and addresses the causes of cases.

  • B fails: the lecture lists “might reduce mortality (e.g., screening for cancer)” as an advantage.
  • C fails: the traditional public health approach is the population strategy; the high-risk strategy is the clinical, individual approach.
  • D fails because A is correct.
b1-w1-module-q24-24:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. A risk factor is an individual characteristic or behaviour that increases the likelihood of a negative health outcome, so all three statements hold.

  • A true: the lecture sorts them into non-modifiable (genetic), socioeconomic/environmental (hard to change) and modifiable (lifestyle/behavioural).
  • B true: genetic, behavioural (smoking, alcohol, diet, activity) and socioeconomic factors all appear.
  • C true: a factor can only raise the likelihood of an outcome that has not yet happened - the chronic disease continuum runs upstream determinants → risk factors → risk conditions → disease.

b1-w1-module-q25-25.html:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. Multimorbidity is the co-occurrence of two or more chronic conditions in one person, with no one disease necessarily more central - a holistic, patient-centred framing. Co-morbidity is the opposite framing: an index disease holds priority over the others, a specialist, disease-centred approach.

  • B is right: coexistence of multiple diseases in an individual is the definition.
  • C is wrong: one disease being central is what defines co-morbidity, not multimorbidity.
  • A (synonymous with comorbidity) is contradicted by the lecture, which draws the distinction explicitly.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key includes A (“synonymous with comorbidity”), but 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health defines multimorbidity (no disease more central, patient-centred) and co-morbidity (an index disease holds priority, disease-centred) as different things, and 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 repeats the distinction. On the lecture, only B is true.

b1-w1-module-q26-26:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. The lecture states that risk factors and protective factors might have synergistic relationships and tend to cluster together, and are therefore difficult to isolate.

  • A true: they cluster, including with socioeconomic and environmental factors.
  • B true: synergy is named directly.
  • C false: clustering and synergy are exactly why their discrete effects are hard to isolate - randomized trials of risk factors are not possible, only preventive trials.

b1-w1-module-q27-27.html:
From 03 - Social Pediatrics (Week 4, Health Canada determinants) and 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. Social determinants (income, education, employment, housing, race and racism, access to care) shape physical and mental health and drive health disparities everywhere - the lecture's point is that upstream causes produce downstream differences in outcome.

  • A fails: producing major disparities is what makes them a public health priority.
  • C fails: they operate in every country, not only low-income ones.
  • D: in the epidemiology lecture genetics is a separate, non-modifiable risk factor, which is the framing the key uses.

flags.title: Option D may also be true
flags.html: Health Canada's list of social determinants in 03 - Social Pediatrics (Week 4) includes “biology and genetic endowment”, so on that lecture D is also a determinant. The key (B only) follows the epidemiology lecture's split of genetic from social factors.

b1-w1-module-q3-3:
From 07 - Introduction to Ethics. In the paternalistic model the physician decides what is best and presents only what will secure consent, promoting the patient's well-being over their choice. Here the physician tells Joe he needs a feeding tube and when it will happen - no options, no exploration of his values, no discussion.

  • Informative would lay out all the options and risks and let Joe choose.
  • Interpretive would help Joe elucidate his own values (important in ALS, where goals of care vary) and match an intervention to them.
  • Deliberative would engage him in dialogue about which health-related values are most worth pursuing.
b1-w1-module-q4-4:
From 07 - Introduction to Ethics. Principlism is the pluralistic theory: autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice are equally ranked, in no particular order, and may conflict, so they must be balanced case by case.

  • Utilitarianism is monistic - one supreme principle (maximize utility), nothing to balance.
  • Pragmatism rejects any universal principle and looks for a practical “third way”.
  • Narrative ethics works through story and personal identity rather than principles.
b1-w1-module-q5-5:
From 07 - Introduction to Ethics. Anti-theorists hold that ethical theories distort moral understanding, and instead emphasize cultural embeddedness, particularities and the untidiness of our moral lives - casuistry, narrative ethics, pragmatism and virtue ethics all start from the messy particular case.

  • B (duties set by maxims) is deontology, a classical monistic theory.
  • C (principles structuring decisions) is principlism, a classical pluralistic theory.
  • D (public policy) is the home ground of utilitarianism - triage, formularies, QALYs.
b1-w1-module-q6-6:
From 07 - Introduction to Ethics. Utilitarianism judges an action by its consequences and aims to maximize good outcomes; the lecture lists policy (transplant, triage) and public health (pandemic directives) as its home in medicine. Allocating scarce ICU beds in a pandemic is a triage protocol for the most benefit to the most people.

  • Casuistry reasons from an analogous past case, which a new pandemic protocol may not have.
  • Deontology centres duty to the individual patient regardless of consequences - it cannot rank patients by benefit.
  • Communitarianism stresses community relationships and identity, not a benefit-maximizing allocation rule.

b1-w1-module-q7-7.html:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. Reading the terms in stem order as i = Cultural Safety, ii = Culture, iii = Cultural Competence, the lecture's definitions give:

  • A = ii (Culture): the knowledge, beliefs and values shared by members of a society.
  • B = iii (Cultural Competence): the ability to understand and interact effectively with people of other cultures.
  • C = i (Cultural Safety): fostering an environment that is spiritually, socially and emotionally safe - first defined by a Maori nurse, and based on self-determination and decolonization.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes the three terms are i, ii, iii in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w1-module-q8-8: From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. Implicit bias is an association outside conscious knowledge that leads to negative assumptions about a person on the basis of an irrelevant characteristic such as gender or race. Offering a different set of contraceptive options to women because they are from BIPOC communities is a clinical decision shaped by race rather than by the patient's needs or preferences - the textbook pattern, and one the clinician may not be aware of (measurable with the implicit association test). It also treats patients unequally in the wrong sense: equity means responding to a person's actual differences, not to a group label.
b1-w1-module-q9-9:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. The lecture defines implicit bias as negative assumptions made on the basis of any irrelevant characteristic, giving gender and race as examples - it is not restricted to marginalized groups.

  • LGBTQ+ (sexual orientation, gender identity), women and men (gender), BIPOC (race), youth and the elderly (age) are all irrelevant characteristics that can trigger biased assumptions.
  • Including men is the discriminating point: a majority or dominant group can still be the target of an implicit or explicit bias, so every option is correct.

b1-w1-new-q11-11.html:
From 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health. In the delayed degenerative disease stage CVD and cancer are the leading causes of death; prevention delays onset and treatment prolongs survival, life expectancy reaches about 70+, and age-related disease such as Alzheimer's rises (high-income countries).

  • A fails: pestilence and famine is malnutrition and infection, with CVD only 5-10% of deaths.
  • B fails: in receding pandemics people do live long enough (to about 50) to experience chronic disease.
  • C: the lecture describes this stage as chronic disease overtaking infection with CVD at under 50% of deaths - see the flag.

flags.title: Option C also matches the lecture
flags.html: 06 - Introduction to Epidemiology & Population Health gives the degenerative and man-made disease stage as chronic conditions overtaking infection with CVD at “< 50%” of deaths, and 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 says the same. That is what option C states, so on the notes C is not clearly false. D is the stage the notes describe unambiguously.

b1-w1-new-q16-16:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees.

  • A true: the lecture organizes refugee health issues into pre-migration (trauma, violence), migration (dangerous journey, camps, family separation) and post-migration stages.
  • B true: post-migration issues include securing housing and financial stability and difficult access to services.
  • D true: children without parents or a guardian are especially vulnerable (a WHO point).
  • C false: mental health (PTSD, repeated losses) and chronic disease (untreated through health-system breakdown or a long journey) are two of the WHO's five areas of refugee health.

b1-w1-new-q17-17.html: From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. The lecture's cultural competence continuum places forced assimilation and subjugation (cultural destructiveness) and racism (cultural incapacity) at its lowest stages, and grounds cultural safety in self-determination and decolonization - a concept first defined because of poor health outcomes in the colonized Maori people. Colonization is the historical system and racism the ongoing practice that sustains it, so they act together on Indigenous health, which is why decolonizing care is offered as the remedy.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note addresses Indigenous health in Canada directly; the reasoning extends the cultural safety and decolonization material in 10 - Cultural Competence. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w1-new-q2-2:
From 01 - Introduction to MCC Clinical Presentations. A symptom is what the patient perceives as not normal and complains of; a sign is objective evidence the practitioner observes or elicits on examination. A severe rash is both: the patient notices it and comes in because of it, and the clinician can see and describe it.

  • A or B alone is incomplete - each captures only one side of the finding.
  • D fails: a diagnosis identifies the underlying illness (burn, poisoning); “rash” is a finding that still needs a differential.
b1-w1-new-q3-3:
From 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach. The patient-centred method splits context in two. Proximal context is generally modifiable and directly influences illness: family, education, employment, social supports, financial security. Distal context is non-modifiable and acts indirectly: culture, community, faith/beliefs, ecosystem, society.

  • A (faith/beliefs), C (culture) and D (society) are all distal.
  • E fails because it pairs a distal factor (faith) with employment.

b1-w1-new-q6-6.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization (Week 2), which holds the imaging material. The question asks for the false statement. The lecture's density table runs air (black) → water (charcoal) → soft tissue (grey) → bone (white) → metal (white with beam hardening), so bone appearing grey is false.

  • A true: radiographs separate structures by tissue opacity (silhouetting), which follows density.
  • B true: MRI weighting (T1 for fat, T2 for fluid, proton density for cartilage and tendon) distinguishes soft tissues x-ray cannot.
  • C true: ultrasound uses high-frequency sound in real time; the Doppler detail is not in the note but is standard.

b1-w2-meds2024-q12-12:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. In the lecture's sequence, after the peak at about +45 mV the V.G. K+ channels, which are slower than the Na+ channels, keep opening while the V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated; K+ rushes out and the membrane repolarizes from +45 back toward -70 mV.

  • Depolarization is driven by rapid Na+ channel opening and Na+ influx.
  • Hyperpolarization is the undershoot while K+ channels close slowly and K+ keeps leaving.
  • Resting membrane potential is set by K+ leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump, with V.G. channels in their resting configuration.

b1-w2-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 02 - Genetics (Week 3), with prions from 16 - How Viruses Work. A dominant negative effect is a mutant protein that disrupts the normal protein from the other allele, usually by interacting with it - “better to have no neighbour than a bad one”.

  • i fits: the lecture's own example is severe osteogenesis imperfecta, where the mutated alpha chain is incorporated and ruins orderly collagen coiling.
  • iii fits by the same logic: a prion is a misfolded protein that transmits its misfolded shape onto normal copies of the same protein.
  • ii fails: the CFTR defect in cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive loss of function - carriers are fine because the normal copy is a backup, so nothing is poisoning it.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the three scenarios are i (collagen), ii (CFTR), iii (prions) in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-meds2024-q3-3:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The question asks for the incorrect statement. The lecture's table has skeletal and cardiac muscle as striated; only smooth muscle is not, so C is wrong.

  • A correct: cardiac and smooth muscle each have a single central nucleus (skeletal is a multinucleated syncytium with peripheral nuclei).
  • B correct: skeletal is voluntary; cardiac and smooth are involuntary.
  • D correct: T-tubules are in skeletal (triads) and cardiac (wider, at the Z line, diads); smooth muscle uses caveolae instead.
  • E correct: intercalated discs (gap junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes) are unique to cardiac muscle.
b1-w2-meds2024-q4-4:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, which stay stationary; in the sliding filament model the thin filaments slide over them, so filament lengths do not change and the A band stays constant.

  • H zone shortens: it is the thick-filament-only centre, which narrows as thin filaments slide in.
  • I band shortens: it is the thin-filament-only region, which narrows as the Z lines are pulled toward the M line.
  • U band is not a sarcomere structure (the bands are A, I, H, with Z and M lines).
b1-w2-meds2024-q6-6:
From 07 - Nerves. Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons in the central nervous system, one cell covering many axons (40-50 internodal segments); the lecture names CNS demyelination as multiple sclerosis, and because oligodendrocytes do not proliferate there is no repair.

  • C fails: myelinated PNS axons are wrapped by Schwann cells, one cell per segment of one axon - these are spared in MS.
  • A and B fail: unmyelinated axons have no myelin for an attack on myelinating cells to remove.
b1-w2-module-q1-1:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The lecture lists four classes of macromolecule: carbohydrates (energy, glycogen/starch structure), lipids (energy storage, membranes, signalling), proteins (structure, enzymes, hormones, transport) and nucleic acids (the genetic blueprint).

  • D fails: fatty acids are micromolecules - the building blocks of lipids, not a class of their own.
  • E fails: hormones are a function performed by members of other classes - peptide hormones such as insulin are proteins, steroid hormones are lipids.

b1-w2-module-q19-19.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. Numbering the terms in stem order (I White fat, II Dense irregular, III Loose, IV Embryonic, V Dense regular, VI Brown fat):

  • A - V: dense regular CT is packed with type I collagen, only fibroblasts in rows, little room for anything else.
  • B - IV: embryonic CT is mesenchyme - pluripotent cells that give rise to fibroblasts, adipocytes, osteoblasts and more.
  • C - II: dense irregular CT forms most organ capsules and the reticular dermis.
  • D - VI: brown fat (multilocular, mitochondria-rich) is abundant in newborns for energy and thermoregulation.
  • E - I: white adipose tissue is described in the overview as highly cellular (unilocular adipocytes).
  • F - III: loose CT lies under epithelia and carries vessels and nerves.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes the six terms are I-VI in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-module-q2-2:
From 01 - Biochemistry. Simple sugars are the cell's nutrients and provide energy when metabolized; polysaccharides (glycogen, starch) store that sugar or form structural components. Energy is the headline function.

  • A (build bone) is a mineral and connective-tissue job, not a carbohydrate one.
  • C (digest lactose) is what an enzyme (lactase) does; lactose is itself a carbohydrate, the substrate rather than the digester.
  • D (produce enzymes) belongs to proteins: the lecture lists enzymes among protein functions.
b1-w2-module-q21-21:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. Elastic cartilage is type II collagen plus elastin, and it sits where tissue must stretch and recoil (epiglottis, larynx, pinna of the ear, auditory tube). The lecture places the same elastin in loose connective tissue, the walls of blood vessels such as the aorta, and the vocal cords. It is one fibre type, made the same way by fibroblasts (proelastin, fibrillin and MAGP co-assembling and cross-linking), so the statement is true.

  • B fails: there is no separate “cartilage elastin”; what differs between tissues is how much elastin there is, not what kind.
b1-w2-module-q23-23:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. Chondrocytes divide within cartilage to form isogenous groups, and those groups sit in lacunae; the matrix inside a lacuna is territorial, the matrix between lacunae interterritorial. So the statement is false.

  • Canaliculi belong to bone: they are the channels through which osteocytes contact one another, with gap junctions passing nutrients cell to cell.
  • Cartilage is avascular and has no such network, which is why it relies on diffusion and regenerates poorly.
  • A trap to avoid: osteoclasts sit in Howship's lacunae, a different use of the word.

b1-w2-module-q25-25.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. Each description names one bone structure from the lecture.

  • A secretes osteoid = osteoblasts (secrete bone matrix on demand, start mineralization with alkaline phosphatase).
  • B processes from osteocytes = canaliculi, where gap junctions pass nutrients.
  • C multinucleated, digests mineralized bone = osteoclasts (fused monocytes/macrophages, up to 30 nuclei, in Howship's lacunae).
  • D lateral conduits to Haversian canals = Volkmann's canals, connecting osteons horizontally.
  • E fully differentiated, embedded in bone = osteocytes, derived from osteoblasts.
  • F collagen from the periosteum = Sharpey's fibres, projecting into the outer lamellae.

“Matrix” is a distractor that matches nothing.

flags.title: The term numbering is off by one
flags.html: The stem lists seven terms, but the key's Roman numerals only work if “Matrix” is left out of the count (I Canaliculi, II Osteoclasts, III Volkmann's, IV Sharpey's, V Osteoblasts, VI Osteocytes). Read literally with Matrix as II, the key would give nonsense such as osteoid-secreting Sharpey's fibres. The matches above are the ones the key intends.

b1-w2-module-q3-3:
From 01 - Biochemistry. Micromolecules are the small units combined to build macromolecules, plus the small “others” the cell needs.

  • Micromolecules: nucleobases (B; the lecture lists nucleotides as the essential unit), fatty acids (E), minerals (F) and vitamins (H), the last two among the lecture's “others” with metabolites, cofactors, metals and water.
  • Macromolecules: the four the lecture opens with - carbohydrates (A, polysaccharides of hundreds of sugars), proteins (C, chains of amino acids), nucleic acids (D) and lipids (G).

The trap is fatty acid vs lipid: the fatty acid is the simplest building block, and the lipid is the class it builds.
b1-w2-module-q36-36:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The nucleus is one of the lecture's three discriminators between muscle types, so the statement is false.

  • Skeletal: a multinucleated syncytium - myoblasts fuse during development into one long cell, with the nuclei pushed to the periphery.
  • Cardiac: a single, centrally located nucleus in short branching fibres joined by intercalated discs.
  • Smooth: a single central nucleus in a spindle-shaped cell, often wavy or corkscrew-like when contracted.

Striation splits them differently (skeletal and cardiac striated, smooth not), which is why the two features are worth keeping apart.
b1-w2-module-q4-4:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The lecture contrasts the two nucleic acids on strandedness, stability and bases.

  • DNA: double stranded (C), sturdy and relatively stable (A), and uses thymine (D).
  • RNA: single stranded (F), degraded quickly (E), and uses uracil (B) in place of thymine. It is RNA that is translated into protein (G), read in three-letter codons.

The lecture puts that stability gap to work in sample prep: an enzyme that quickly breaks down the weaker RNA leaves the more stable DNA behind.
b1-w2-module-q40-40:
From 02 - Physiology (Homeostasis). Total body water splits 2/3 intracellular, 1/3 extracellular, and the ECF splits again 3/4 interstitial, 1/4 plasma.

  • I (3/4 of ECF) = interstitial fluid (C); III (1/4 of ECF) = plasma (D).
  • II (1/3 of TBW) = ECF (A); IV (2/3 of TBW) = ICF (B).
  • V (rich in potassium) = ICF: K+ is the main intracellular ion (about 150 vs 5 mmol/L outside), while Na+, Cl- and Ca2+ dominate outside.
  • VI (the internal environment) = ECF, the fluid bathing the cells that homeostasis holds constant.

The fractions nest: a fraction of the ECF is never a fraction of total body water.

b1-w2-module-q5-5.html:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The lecture assigns these features as follows.

  • Proteins: primary-to-quaternary structure (A: sequence, helix/sheet, 3D fold, multi-protein complex) and enzymes (D), which head the list of protein functions.
  • Lipids: energy storage (C, fatty acids stored as triglycerols), fatty acids (E, the simplest lipid) and cholesterol (F, a membrane component and steroid-hormone precursor).
  • Nucleotides (B) are neither. They are the building blocks of nucleic acids; proteins are built from 20 or 21 amino acids.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key puts B (nucleotides) under proteins. 01 - Biochemistry says proteins are made of amino acids and lists nucleotides as the unit of nucleic acids, so on the lecture nucleotides belong to neither column. The option may have been garbled from “amino acids”.

b1-w2-module-q52-52:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. The four modes are named for the distance the signal travels and the route it takes.

  • A nearby target = paracrine (IV): messengers act over short distances so neighbours coordinate locally.
  • B own cell = autocrine (I): the ligand binds receptors on the cell that released it, which the lecture links to cancer and metastasis.
  • C long-distance target = long-distance signalling (II), i.e. endocrine: hormones carried to target cells in the bloodstream.
  • D direct contact = cell-cell contact signalling (III): gap junctions, or surface proteins binding and changing conformation.

b1-w2-module-q53-53.html:
From 07 - Nerves. Each description names one cell or event from the lecture's glial-cell and nerve-regeneration notes.

  • A phagocytes activated by CNS injury = microglia (III): migratory, and they turn phagocytic when the CNS is damaged.
  • B bridging axons and blood vessels = astrocytes (II): a scaffold between capillaries, fibres and neurons that maintains the blood-brain barrier.
  • C loss of CNS myelin = multiple sclerosis (VI), demyelination of oligodendrocyte myelin.
  • D PNS myelin = Schwann cells (IV); oligodendrocytes do the CNS.
  • E outgrowths after an axon is cut = axonal sprouts (I), grown from the proximal stump through cords of Schwann cells.
  • F gaps in the myelin = nodes of Ranvier (V), which allow saltatory conduction.

flags.title: Typo in the options
flags.html: Option B reads “CAN”, which means CNS. The stem's opening words (“type of cellular communication”) also do not fit these items, which are glial cells and nerve structures.

b1-w2-module-q57-57:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. Depolarization moves the membrane potential toward zero or positive and hyperpolarization moves it more negative, so what matters is whether the charge crossing is net positive in or positive out.

  • Depolarization (A): Ca2+ entry (I) and Na+ entry (IV) both bring positive charge in. Their equilibrium potentials (about +135 and +60 mV) sit far above -70 mV.
  • Hyperpolarization (B): Cl- entry (II) brings negative charge in, and K+ exit (III) takes positive charge out. This is the K+ efflux behind repolarization and the undershoot after an action potential.

A common slip: an ion leaving has the opposite effect of the same ion entering.
b1-w2-module-q6-6:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The lecture states it outright: the main function of enzymes is to lower activation energy. They speed up a reaction that could happen on its own but otherwise happens very slowly or not at all.

  • A (synthesize) and B (decompose) describe particular reactions an enzyme may catalyse, not what makes something an enzyme. It does either by lowering the barrier.
  • D (slow product formation) is backwards. The lecture ties slow product formation to low substrate concentration; enzymes speed products up, which is why raising substrate helps when little enzyme is made.

b1-w2-module-q60-60.html:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. The action potential is all-or-none: once the graded depolarization reaches threshold (about -55 mV), voltage-gated Na+ channels open and the spike always runs to about +45 mV. Inactivated Na+ channels then create the refractory period, which keeps it one-way.

  • Action potential (B): I (all-or-none) and II (refractory period).
  • Graded potential (A): III (amplitude depends on stimulus strength), IV (no threshold) and V (can be summed). It is the variable depolarization that has to build up to threshold before a spike fires.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives A (graded) = I, II and B (action potential) = III, IV, V, which swaps the two. 08 - Cellular Communication calls the action potential all-or-none, gives it absolute and relative refractory periods, and triggers it at a threshold, so I and II belong to B and III-V to A.

b1-w2-module-q69-69.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. Each plane is named for how it divides the body.

  • Coronal: anterior/posterior halves, a slice running left to right, so the image shows the body face-on.
  • Sagittal: left/right halves, a front-to-back slice, so the image shows the body in profile. Through the midline it is the median sagittal plane; anywhere else, parasagittal.
  • Transverse (axial): superior/inferior halves, the CT-style cross-section, read as if standing at the patient's feet looking toward the head.

The key pairs Coronal with image III, Sagittal with I and Transverse with II.

flags.title: The image did not survive extraction
flags.html: The three images this question refers to were not banked, and the key line is garbled (“The correct answer is A. – III; B – I; C – II”), keying option A alone although it is a three-way match. The keyed mapping could not be checked against the picture; the explanation defines each term from the lecture instead.

b1-w2-module-q7-7:
From 03 - Histology and Tissue Types. Each dye has the opposite charge of what it stains.

  • Hematoxylin is the basic stain (A), and it stains acids blue (C): DNA, so nuclei come out blue.
  • Eosin is the acidic stain (B), and it stains bases pink (D): cytoplasmic proteins.

The trap is putting “acidic” and “stains acids” together. H&E is the principal stain in histology because it is quick and cheap and still shows a great deal of microscopic anatomy.
b1-w2-module-q70-70:
From 09 - Anatomy. Every pair is read in the anatomical position.

  • 1 heart / diaphragm: superior (A), toward the head. 7 pelvis / skull: inferior (E).
  • 2 ankle / knee: distal (F), further from the trunk. 6 shoulder / elbow: proximal (C), toward the trunk.
  • 3 thumb / index finger: lateral (D). With the palms forward, the thumb is furthest from the midline.
  • 4 spinal cord / umbilicus: posterior (G), dorsal.
  • 5 heart / lung: medial (H), nearer the midline.
  • 8 muscles / skin: deep (B), further in from the surface.

Proximal/distal apply to the limbs; superior/inferior to the axial body.

b1-w2-module-q71-71.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. The lecture's four laterality terms:

  • 1 liver and heart = contralateral (D): on opposite sides, the liver on the right and the heart mostly left of the midline.
  • 2 femurs = bilateral (B): a paired right and left structure.
  • 3 spleen = unilateral (C): a single organ on one side (the left).
  • 4 liver and right kidney = ipsilateral (A): both on the right.

Unilateral and bilateral describe one structure; ipsilateral and contralateral compare two.

flags.title: The image did not survive extraction
flags.html: The full-body MRI this question refers to was not banked. The keyed mapping could not be checked against the picture; the explanation defines each term from the lecture instead.

b1-w2-module-q72-72.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. Each movement term from the lecture, applied to the key:

  • 1 left shoulder = abducted (C): the arm moved away from the midline.
  • 2 left ankle = plantarflexed (E): the toes pointed (dorsiflexion brings them toward the shin).
  • 3 right knee = flexed (B): the joint angle decreased.
  • 4 left knee = extended (D): the angle increased, the leg straight.
  • 5 right forearm = pronated (A): the palm faces backward and the radius crosses the ulna.

flags.title: The image did not survive extraction
flags.html: The yogi skeleton with its coloured joints was not banked, and option A reads “Protonated” where it means pronated. The keyed mapping could not be checked against the picture; the explanation defines each term from the lecture instead.

b1-w2-module-q73-73.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. The key reads A = sternal angle, B = midclavicular line, C = anterior median line and D = costal margin. The landmarks:

  • Sternal angle: the prominence of the sternum where the 2nd ribs insert, the key landmark for counting ribs.
  • Costal margin: the lower edge of the ribs, along the anterior attachment of the diaphragm, dividing thorax from abdomen.
  • Anterior median line: the vertical line down the middle of the sternum.
  • Midclavicular line: the vertical line through the midpoint of each clavicle.

flags.title: The labelled image and options are missing
flags.html: This question has no options: it identified labels A-D on a figure that was not banked, so the key cannot be checked against the picture. 09 - Anatomy covers the sternal angle and costal margin; the two vertical lines are described from general anatomy, not from the note.

b1-w2-module-q74-74.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. The key reads A = anterior axillary fold, B = axillary fossa, C = arm, D = cubital fossa and E = forearm. The regions:

  • Arm (brachium): shoulder to elbow.
  • Forearm (antebrachium): elbow to wrist.
  • Cubital fossa: the inner (anterior) elbow, where blood pressure is measured.
  • Axillary fossa: the armpit hollow beneath the shoulder joint.
  • Anterior axillary fold: the front wall of the armpit, the skin fold over the lower border of pectoralis major.

flags.title: The labelled image and options are missing
flags.html: This question has no options: it identified labels A-E on a figure that was not banked, so the key cannot be checked against the picture. 09 - Anatomy covers the arm, forearm and cubital fossa; the axillary fold and fossa are described from general anatomy, not from the note.

b1-w2-module-q75-75.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. The key reads A = inguinal ligament, B = thigh, C = popliteal fossa and D = leg. The regions:

  • Thigh: hip to knee.
  • Leg: knee to ankle. In anatomy, “leg” never means the whole lower limb.
  • Popliteal fossa: the hollow behind (posterior to) the knee.
  • Inguinal ligament: runs from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic bone, marking the abdomen's boundary with the thigh.

flags.title: The labelled image and options are missing
flags.html: This question has no options: it identified labels A-D on a figure that was not banked, so the key cannot be checked against the picture.

b1-w2-module-q76-76.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. In the anatomical position the palms face forward and the feet stand together, and “medial” means nearest the midline.

  • D big toe: on the medial side of the foot, and with the feet together the two big toes nearly touch at the midline.
  • B thumb: with the palms forward, the thumb is the most lateral digit.
  • A capitate: a carpal bone in the middle of the wrist, far lateral to the trunk.
  • C humerus: out in the arm, lateral to the trunk.
  • E femur: it angles in toward the knee, but its upper end sits out at the hip, so the shaft as a whole lies well lateral to the big toe.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 09 - Anatomy defines the anatomical position (palms forward, feet flat, toes forward) but does not rank these structures; the comparison is reasoned from that definition.

b1-w2-module-q77-77:
From 09 - Anatomy. On a limb, position is described along its length: proximal is toward the trunk and distal toward the extremities. The fingers lie further from the trunk than the elbow, so they are distal to it.

  • A medial is about closeness to the midline; with the palms forward, most fingers are no more medial than the elbow.
  • B anterior compares front and back, not position along a limb.
  • D superficial compares depth from the skin.
  • E superior is wrong: in the anatomical position the arms hang down, so the fingers sit below the elbow.
b1-w2-module-q78-78:
From 09 - Anatomy. The anatomical position is standing with the head facing forward, feet flat, toes facing forward, and palms facing forward. Palms facing backward (B) is not the anatomical position. It is pronation, which the lecture defines as palms back with the radius and ulna crossed. The anatomical position keeps them parallel (supinated).

  • A standing upright, C toes forward and D feet together are all part of the definition.
  • E elbows extended is consistent with it: the arms hang straight at the sides.

Lying face up in the same posture is supine; face down is prone.
b1-w2-module-q84-84:
From 09 - Anatomy. The lecture defines superficial as toward the first layer of skin, and deep as toward the inside of the body, so “shallow, close to the surface” is superficial.

  • A deep is the exact opposite of superficial, on the same depth axis.
  • B distal and C proximal are on a different axis: position along a limb, away from or toward the trunk. Neither says anything about depth.
b1-w2-module-q86-86:
From 09 - Anatomy. The lecture defines inferior as away from the head, i.e. below another structure in the anatomical position. Superior (B) is its opposite, toward the head.

  • A proximal and C distal describe position along a limb relative to the trunk, not up or down. The hand is distal to the elbow, and it is also inferior only because the arms hang down.

Superior/inferior are the terms for the axial body; proximal/distal are for the limbs.
b1-w2-module-q87-87:
From 09 - Anatomy. Contralateral means on the opposite side of the body. The liver and the heart, for example, lie on opposite sides.

  • C ipsilateral is its pair, the same side, as with the liver and the right kidney. That is the definition the key line quotes, and it describes the distractor.
  • A bilateral describes paired right and left structures, such as the femurs.
  • B unilateral describes something on one side only, such as the spleen.

Unilateral and bilateral describe one structure; ipsilateral and contralateral compare two.
b1-w2-module-q91-91:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The lecture splits lymphoid organs by job. The primary lymphoid organs, the thymus and red bone marrow, produce lymphocytes. The secondary lymphoid organs store them.

  • A appendix, C tonsils (palatine) and D spleen are all secondary lymphoid organs, as are the aggregated lymphoid nodules. Lymphocytes live and meet antigen there, but are not produced there.

Red bone marrow is the only primary organ offered.

b1-w2-module-q96-96.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The musculoskeletal system supports the body, allows motion and protects the vital organs. Its table divides the jobs among the parts.

  • A cartilage = smooth articulating surfaces (III): articular hyaline cartilage gives a smooth surface for joint movement.
  • B bones = structure and protection (I).
  • C ligaments = bone to bone (V).
  • D joints = enable movement between bones (VI).
  • E tendons = muscle to bone (IV). Tendons and ligaments are both dense regular connective tissue, type I collagen in rows (06 - Connective Tissue).
  • F muscles = produce movement at joints (II).

Tendon vs ligament is the classic trap: tendon joins muscle to bone, ligament joins bone to bone.

b1-w2-module-q97-97:
From 04 - Introduction to the Nervous System. Sort each item on two axes: sensory (afferent) or motor (efferent), then body wall (somatic) or viscera (visceral/autonomic).

  • A stomach ache = visceral sensory: pain from a viscus, carried by visceral afferents, which is why it feels diffuse and achy and is often referred.
  • B pain from skin = somatosensory: somatic afferents bring sensation from the body wall (skin, skeletal muscle, joints) in through the dorsal root.
  • C efferent to a gland = autonomic motor: the ANS acts on viscera, glands, smooth and cardiac muscle.
  • D efferent to gluteus maximus = somatic motor: impulses to skeletal muscle leave through the ventral root.
b1-w2-module-q98-98:
From 10 - Body System Organization. Each function comes straight from the lecture's system table.

  • A endocrine = regulates via hormones (VI).
  • B musculoskeletal = produces movement (VIII).
  • C digestive = absorbs nutrients into blood (IV).
  • D nervous = responds to external and internal stimuli (I): sensory input, integration, motor output.
  • E reproductive = produces gametes (II).
  • F lymphatic = collects excess tissue fluid (III), returning leaked fluid to the blood.
  • G urinary = filters waste from blood (V).
  • H cardiovascular = transports oxygen (IX), with nutrients and hormones.
  • I respiratory = exchanges blood gases (VII).

Watch the pair: lungs exchange gas, and the cardiovascular system carries it.
b1-w2-new-q10-10:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. The four bone cells form a lineage plus one outsider.

  • A marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells = osteoprogenitor cells (III), in the periosteum and endosteum, which differentiate into osteoblasts during repair.
  • B actively secrete matrix = osteoblasts (II), which also start mineralization with alkaline phosphatase.
  • C interconnected network that maintains calcification = osteocytes (IV): osteoblasts walled into matrix, linked by canaliculi, and mechanosensory.
  • D multinucleated cells that resorb matrix = osteoclasts (I), the outsider, fused from blood monocytes/macrophages rather than the mesenchymal line.

b1-w2-new-q13-13.html:
From 07 - Nerves. The lecture defines Nissl bodies as stacks of endoplasmic reticulum: rough ER studded with ribosomes, in the neuron's cell body (perikaryon). The heavy protein synthesis they carry out supplies the long axon. The answer the lecture supports is C.

  • B (groups of Golgi bodies) is not what Nissl bodies are. The lecture's only Golgi point is that the Golgi apparatus is not found in axons.
  • A (mitochondria) and D (peroxisomes) are other organelles, not the basophilic clumps that make up Nissl substance.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is B (groups of Golgi bodies), but 07 - Nerves states “Nissl bodies = stacks of endoplasmic reticulum”, which is option C.

b1-w2-new-q16-16.html:
From 02 - Physiology (Homeostasis). The note's discriminator: a negative feedback loop counteracts the stimulus and is homeostatic, while a positive loop reinforces the stimulus and needs an external event to stop it.

  • C (childbirth): contractions push the fetus against the cervix, which drives stronger contractions; the loop only ends with delivery.
  • E (blood clotting): each activated factor recruits more, amplifying the clot until the vessel is sealed.
  • A, B, D (temperature, blood sugar, osmolality) are the note's own examples of monitored variables held in an acceptable range: a deviation triggers a correction that shuts itself off, which is negative feedback.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 02 - Physiology (Homeostasis) defines positive and negative feedback but does not name childbirth or clotting as examples; those two are reasoned from the definition. Verify before relying on it.

b1-w2-new-q18-18:
From 02 - Osmosis. Tonicity is a solution's ability to cause water movement. A hypotonic solution (about 200 mOsm/kg against the cell's ~300) has less solute outside than inside, so water is drawn into the cell by osmosis and it swells (the note's mnemonic: the ‘O’ in hypOtonic means the cell expands).

  • A (no change) describes an isotonic solution, where there is no net water movement.
  • B (shrink) describes a hypertonic solution, which pulls water out of the cell.
b1-w2-new-q19-19:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. The note's sequence: a graded depolarization reaches threshold (about −55 mV); voltage-gated Na+ channels open and the membrane depolarizes rapidly to about +45 mV; Na+ channels inactivate and K+ rushes out, repolarizing it toward −70 mV; the slow K+ channels stay open too long, so it hyperpolarizes (undershoot) before the Na+/K+ pump restores rest.

  • A puts repolarization before depolarization; there is nothing to repolarize from yet.
  • C starts with repolarization and ends with depolarization, the reverse of the cycle.
  • D swaps the last two: the undershoot follows repolarization, it does not precede it.
b1-w2-new-q2-2:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The note states that the main function of enzymes is to lower activation energy. They do not supply it, so A is the false statement.

  • B is true word for word: enzymes facilitate a reaction that could happen on its own but does not, or happens very slowly.
  • C is true: a catalyst speeds a reaction without changing what goes in or what comes out.
  • D is true on the note: higher substrate concentration means faster product formation, which is why a disease with little (or poorly binding) enzyme can be treated by raising the substrate to make use of the enzyme that is present.
b1-w2-new-q23-23:
From 09 - Anatomy. The note pairs dorsiflexion (bringing the toes toward the shin) with plantar flexion (pointing the toes), so pointing the toes down is plantarflexion.

  • A (depression) moves the scapulae (shoulders) away from the ears.
  • B (pronation) is a forearm movement: palms face backward with the radius and ulna crossed.
  • D (flexion) is the general term for decreasing a joint angle; at the ankle the specific terms are dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, so it is not the best answer.

b1-w2-new-q25-25.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The note's endocrine row lists the adrenals as regulating metabolism, the immune system, blood pressure and the stress response, and gives blood calcium to the parathyroids (and the thyroid). So D is the false pairing.

  • A is true: the pancreas is listed for blood sugar.
  • B is true: the gonads are listed for the reproductive organs and secondary sex characteristics.
  • C is true: the pineal gland is listed for circadian rhythms.

b1-w2-new-q27-27.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The note's CT entry: x-ray based thin axial slices, more expensive than plain radiography, with a much larger dose of ionizing radiation, and not recommended in pregnancy. That makes A true.

  • B fails on “unlike an MRI”: 09 - Anatomy says all axial scans are read as if standing at the patient's feet looking toward the head, and that convention applies to axial MRI as well.
  • C is the reverse: CT gives a much larger radiation dose than a radiograph (MRI and ultrasound use none).
  • D contradicts the note, which says CT is not recommended for pregnant women.

b1-w2-new-q7-7.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. Taking the terms as I loose, II dense irregular, III reticular, IV dense regular (the order the stem lists them), the keyed mapping matches the note's table exactly.

  • A – II: dense irregular CT is found in most organ capsules and the reticular layer of the dermis; its type I and III collagen is woven into a mat, making it resilient and protective.
  • B – IV: dense regular CT (tendons, ligaments, joint capsules) has fibroblasts and type I collagen in rows, for high stress resistance.
  • C – III: reticular CT (type III collagen from reticular cells) supports the hematopoietic tissues: marrow, lymph nodes, spleen.
  • D – I: loose CT sits under epithelia, carries vessels and nerves, and has poorly organized fibres.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes the four tissues are I-IV in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-new-q8-8.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. With I = white and II = brown adipose tissue:

  • White (C, D, G, H): the adult energy store and insulator; unilocular (one lipid vacuole per cell), which pushes the nucleus to the periphery; the cells can grow about 4× before dividing, and once divided are hard to clear.
  • Brown (A, B, E, F): abundant in newborns (2-5% of body weight) for thermoregulation; multilocular (many small droplets), so the nucleus stays central; packed with mitochondria, which is what makes it a heat generator.

The discriminator is locularity: one droplet displaces the nucleus, many droplets leave it central.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes I = white and II = brown adipose tissue, the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-new-q9-9.html:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. With I hyaline, II elastic, III fibrocartilage, the key matches the note's cartilage table.

  • A – II: elastic cartilage (type II collagen plus elastin) is where shape must spring back: epiglottis, larynx, pinna and auditory canal.
  • B – III: fibrocartilage (types I and II collagen, chondrocytes in parallel rows) resists compression: intervertebral discs, menisci, the jaw, tendon insertions.
  • C – I: hyaline, the most common type (type II collagen, isogenous groups), forms the growth plates, ventral rib ends and the walls of the respiratory tree.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes I = hyaline, II = elastic, III = fibrocartilage, the order the stem lists them.

b1-w2-sa-q13-13:
From 06 - Connective Tissue. The note describes the osteoclast as formed by the fusion of peripheral blood monocytes/macrophages, multinucleated (up to 30 nuclei), secreting acid and metalloproteinases that resorb bone in Howship's lacunae. Every element of C is there.

  • A describes the osteoblast, which becomes an osteocyte once enclosed in matrix.
  • B describes the osteoprogenitor cell, which differentiates into bone-depositing osteoblasts.
  • D mixes the osteoclast's nuclei with the osteocyte's location; osteocytes are single cells in lacunae derived from osteoblasts.
  • E has the right function but the wrong origin: osteoclasts come from the monocyte line, not from osteoblasts.
b1-w2-sa-q21-21:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The note says proteins are made of 20 or 21 amino acids, and lists amino acids among the essential micromolecules that combine to form macromolecules.

  • B (monosaccharides) build carbohydrates such as glycogen and starch.
  • C (nucleotides) build the nucleic acids DNA and RNA.
  • D (peptides) are short chains of amino acids, already assembled; they are a stage of protein structure, not the basic unit.
  • E (fatty acids) are the simplest lipids, stored as triglycerides.
b1-w2-sa-q22-22:
From 01 - Biochemistry. The note calls nucleic acids the “blueprint” for how to build a cell: DNA and RNA carry the genetic code in three-letter codons, and it is the nucleic acid that is isolated and sequenced (whole genome, exome or targeted panel) to read genetic information.

  • A (lipids) store energy, form membranes and act in signalling.
  • C (carbohydrates) provide energy and structural polysaccharides.
  • D (proteins) are the product the code specifies; analysing them shows what is expressed, not the inherited sequence itself.
b1-w3-module-q10-10:
From 02 - Genetics. The note lists fragile X among the triplet repeat disorders: a CGG expansion causing transcriptional silencing and loss of function, and one of its examples of anticipation.

  • B (mosaicism) is a de novo mutation present in only some tissues (somatic or gonadal).
  • C (epigenetic) covers parent-of-origin effects such as Prader-Willi/Angelman imprinting and uniparental disomy.
  • D (mitochondrial) is maternally inherited mtDNA disease with heteroplasmy and a threshold effect.
b1-w3-module-q11-11:
From 02 - Genetics. Read the pedigree for who transmits. The affected mother (2) has all four children affected, sons and daughters alike. Her affected daughters (5, 9) again pass it to every child, while her affected sons (3, 7) have no affected children. Transmission only through the mother, to all offspring, is the note's mitochondrial signature: all mitochondria come from the egg, so all of an affected mother's children inherit them.

  • A (AD) would give about half of each sibship affected and would pass through affected fathers too.
  • B (AR) would not appear in every generation with every child affected.
  • C (X-linked) fails because affected fathers pass an X to every daughter, yet 3's and 7's daughters are unaffected, and X-linked disease would not affect every daughter of an affected mother.
b1-w3-module-q12-12:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. The note splits preconception counselling into primary prevention (review personal and family history, and act before pregnancy to reduce risk, chiefly folic acid 0.8-1 mg/day from 3 months before conception through the first trimester to cut neural tube defects) and secondary prevention (prenatal screening and diagnosis).

  • B, C, D (anatomy ultrasound, NT scan, dating ultrasound) are all imaging done during the pregnancy to detect or date what is already there, which is screening (secondary), not prevention of the problem arising.
b1-w3-module-q14-14:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. The note's organising idea: screening tests estimate risk; only the invasive tests diagnose. Amniocentesis (15-20 weeks, samples amniotic fluid, about 1/200 miscarriage risk) is invasive and diagnostic, as is CVS.

  • A (NIPT) analyses placenta-derived cell-free DNA in maternal blood; it is a screen for T13, T18, T21 and sex chromosomes.
  • B (eFTS) combines NT with bloodwork to give a risk estimate against a 1:350 cut-off.
  • C (NT scan) flags increased risk when NT is 3.5 mm or more; it cannot confirm anything.

b1-w3-module-q15-15.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. The note's carrier-screening list is organised by ancestry, and for Middle Eastern couples it names hemoglobinopathies and thalassemias, screened by red cell size and hemoglobin electrophoresis.

  • A (Tay-Sachs) is the screen for Ashkenazi Jewish (1/30) and French Canadian (1/14) couples.
  • D (cystic fibrosis) is offered to European couples, usually with a personal or family history or clinical features.
  • B (familial Mediterranean fever) does not appear on the note's list at all.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 05 - Genetic Screening does not mention familial Mediterranean fever; B is ruled out only because the lecture's screening list for Middle Eastern couples names thalassemias and hemoglobinopathies instead.

b1-w3-module-q16-16:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. Ontario newborn screening covers mostly autosomal recessive metabolic diseases plus endocrine diseases, sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, SCID, spinal muscular atrophy, critical congenital heart disease and congenital hearing loss. Myotonic dystrophy is not on it; 02 - Genetics files it with the CTG triplet repeat disorders, not with the newborn-screened conditions.

  • A (SCID) is on the list by name.
  • B (congenital hypothyroidism) falls under the endocrine diseases screened.
  • D (sickle cell) is on the list by name.
b1-w3-module-q2-2:
From 01 - Child Development. The lecture frames development through the biopsychosocial model, and its sociological factors include finances, community support, access to services and early intervention, and education, childcare and preschool. Limited income, poor access to fresh food and a single wait-listed preschool are exactly those.

  • A (biological) covers nutrition assessment as a health measure, immunization, and acute or chronic illness in the child.
  • B (psychological) covers nurturing and attachment, stimulation and enrichment, and family mental health.
  • D, E (cultural, legal) are not arms of the biopsychosocial model the lecture uses.
b1-w3-module-q3-3:
From 02 - Genetics. The note defines anticipation in almost these words: as a disorder passes to the next generation, symptoms appear at an earlier age (and more severely) each time. It is the hallmark of triplet repeat disorders such as fragile X and Huntington disease, where the repeat expands.

  • A (penetrance) is the fraction of carriers who show the phenotype.
  • B (genetic heterogeneity) is different variants (allelic) or different genes (locus) producing the phenotype.
  • D (pleiotropy) is one variant causing effects in multiple organs.
b1-w3-module-q4-4:
From 02 - Genetics. Locus heterogeneity is mutations in different genes, at different loci, causing the same phenotype. Two collagen genes (COL1A1 and COL1A2) each producing osteogenesis imperfecta fits that definition.

  • B (allelic heterogeneity) is different variants within the same gene, as in beta thalassemia and the beta-globin gene.
  • C (imprinting) is parent-of-origin expression maintained by methylation.
  • D (incomplete penetrance) is a carrier of the mutation not showing the disease; it says nothing about how many genes are involved.

b1-w3-module-q5-5.html:
From 02 - Genetics. Taking the definitions as I-V in stem order, the key matches the note's dominant-inheritance terms:

  • A – I (dominant negative): the mutant protein interferes with the normal one from the other allele, as the mutant alpha chain does in severe osteogenesis imperfecta.
  • B – II (haploinsufficiency): one working allele is not enough, as with ELN in Williams syndrome.
  • C – V (gain of function): increased activity of the normal product, as in achondroplasia.
  • D – IV (pleiotropy): one gene, many organs, as with collagen in OI affecting bone, eyes, ears and joints.
  • E – III (penetrance): the proportion of carriers who show clinical signs.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes the five definitions are I-V in the order the stem lists them.

b1-w3-module-q6-6:
From 02 - Genetics. Most people with an autosomal dominant disorder are heterozygous. Each child gets one of the affected parent's two alleles, so each pregnancy carries a 1 in 2 (50%) chance, regardless of sex.

  • A (1%) is the note's figure for recurrence after an apparently de novo mutation, from gonadal mosaicism.
  • B (25%) is the risk of an affected child when both parents are carriers of a recessive condition.
  • D (75%) would need both parents affected (heterozygous) with a dominant condition.
b1-w3-module-q7-7:
From 02 - Genetics. A heterozygote for a recessive condition has one normal and one variant allele, and the note puts it plainly: a carrier is fine because they have a “backup” copy. They are healthy carriers, and the note adds that penetrance does not apply to recessive disorders.

  • A (mildly symptomatic) is the note's caveat for female carriers of X-linked conditions (skewed X inactivation), not autosomal recessive ones.
  • C (healthy non-carriers) fails because they do carry the variant allele.
  • D (affected) requires two variant alleles: a homozygote or a compound heterozygote.

b1-w3-module-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Genetics. Taking the descriptions as I-III in stem order:

  • A – I (compound heterozygote): two different variants on the two alleles of the same gene, the note's “trans” arrangement, which leaves no good copy and so causes recessive disease.
  • B – III (homozygote): two alleles of the same gene carrying the same variant; affected.
  • C – II (obligate heterozygotes): an affected person with an autosomal recessive disorder can only pass on a variant allele, so every child must be at least a carrier, whether or not they are tested.

flags.title: Numbering lost from the stem
flags.html: The roman numerals in this question were stripped when it was transcribed; the mapping assumes the three descriptions are I-III in the order the stem lists them.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 02 - Genetics defines homozygotes and the cis/trans arrangement but does not use the term “obligate heterozygote”; that pairing is reasoned from the note's recessive inheritance rules.

b1-w3-module-q9-9:
From 02 - Genetics. An affected father passes his Y to every son and his X to every daughter. The note gives the numbers: affected males cannot transmit the condition to their sons (0% affected sons) and 100% of daughters are carriers. No male-to-male transmission is the X-linked signature.

  • B, D (50% or 100% affected sons) would need the son to receive his father's X, which he never does.
  • C (50% carrier sons) fails twice: sons get no X from their father, and a male with one X is hemizygous, so he is either affected or unaffected, never a carrier.
b1-w3-new-q16-16: From 09 - Nutrition. The lecture's list of barriers to healthy food choices contains each of A-D almost word for word: financial uncertainty and the cost of healthy foods, lack of time, the need to ration food within the family, and a lack of nutrition knowledge and skills. It also adds distance from healthy food and a lack of transportation. Since every option is on the list, E (all of the above) is the only complete answer.
b1-w3-new-q18-18:
From 10 - Infant Nutrition. The lecture's special formulas are exactly these four, so E is right, while noting that most infants never need one and switching does not help colic:

  • Lactose-free: a cow's milk based formula without lactose.
  • Hydrolyzed whey: lower osmolality, may improve gastric emptying.
  • Soy: for vegetarian families, lactase deficiency and galactosemia.
  • Protein hydrolysate: for infants who cannot digest, or are allergic to, intact protein, or with fat malabsorption; more expensive.
b1-w3-new-q7-7:
From 02 - Genetics. Affected individuals are almost all male, and the pattern follows the X. The affected mother (1) has both sons affected and her daughters (4, 6) unaffected, which fits carrier daughters. Carrier daughter 4 with an unaffected partner has one affected son (9), and all her daughters are unaffected: the note's “female carriers to sons”. Affected son 7 married to an affected woman (8) has all children affected, as expected when the mother has two variant X's.

  • A (AD) fails because unaffected 4 has an affected son (a skipped generation).
  • B (AR) would need unrelated partners 2 and 3 both to be carriers, and would not favour males.
  • D (new dominant) fails because the grandmother is already affected, so nothing arose de novo.

The figure is printed mirror-reversed, so the numbers read backwards.
b1-w3-ra-q1-1:
From 02 - Genetics. The mother had ADPKD, an autosomal dominant condition, and the note gives the rule: a 1 in 2 (50%) chance that each child inherits the trait, males and females equally. Her hypertension and abdominal distension raise suspicion, but the question asks only for the inheritance-based prior risk.

  • A (1%) is the gonadal-mosaicism recurrence risk after a de novo mutation, but here the mother is affected.
  • B (25%) applies to autosomal recessive inheritance from two carrier parents.
  • D (75%) would need both parents affected.
b1-w3-ra-q4-4:
From 02 - Genetics. The note names Duchenne muscular dystrophy as its example of X-linked inheritance: males are affected almost exclusively because they are hemizygous, and the variant passes from female carriers to sons. That is exactly this family, a carrier mother with an affected son.

  • B (AD) would make the carrier mother affected herself.
  • C (mitochondrial) would give disease to all her children regardless of sex, and involves mtDNA, not a nuclear gene like DMD.
  • D (AR) would need the father to be a carrier too, and would not favour sons.
b1-w3-ra-q5-5:
From 02 - Genetics. A carrier mother has one normal and one DMD-variant X, and each child receives one of them at random. So each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant. The note's breakdown by sex: 50% of sons affected and 50% of daughters carriers.

  • A fails because daughters also get their father's normal X, so they are at most carriers (unless skewed X inactivation), not all affected.
  • B overstates it: half of daughters are carriers, not all. “All daughters carriers” is the rule for an affected father.
  • C overstates it: half of sons, not all.

b1-w3-sa-q5-5.html:
From 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing. The lecture's organising idea: a karyotype shows chromosome structure, including balanced rearrangements, while a microarray shows gene content, that is, gains and losses. A balanced translocation such as t(11;22) moves material without adding or removing any (06 - Chromosomal Anomalies: “no missing information, but the information is shuffled”), so a microarray sees a normal dosage. It needs a karyotype.

  • A (Turner, 45,X) is a whole-chromosome loss, an obvious dosage change.
  • B (15q11.2 deletion) and E (500 kb DMD duplication) are submicroscopic copy-number changes, the imbalances microarray exists to find.
  • D (mosaic trisomy 21) is extra chromosome 21 material in a proportion of cells, still a gain in content.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing does not address mosaicism; that microarray can detect mosaic trisomy (at a reasonable mosaic level) is reasoned from its detecting gains in content.

b1-w4-module-q1-1:
From 06 - Adolescent Development. The Tanner scale is built on external sex characteristics, and pubic hair has its own Tanner I-V sequence for both males and females, so B holds for boys and girls alike.

  • A fails: the first sign is breast budding in girls and testicular enlargement in boys; pubic hair follows.
  • C fails: girls increase fat with each pubertal stage, but boys lose fat in early adolescence.
  • D fails: emotion and reward seeking are limbic; the prefrontal cortex carries executive function (planning, impulse control).
  • E reverses it: the prefrontal cortex matures later than the limbic regions, the note's explanation for adolescent risk taking.
b1-w4-module-q13-13:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. A live attenuated vaccine still replicates, so the immune response is similar to natural infection and gives longer-lasting and broader immunity than a non-live vaccine can.

  • B (killed/inactivated) is safe and stable because it cannot replicate, but that is exactly why its response is weaker and mostly humoral: it needs adjuvants, a primary series, and booster doses as antibody titres fall.

The trade-off to remember: live vaccines buy durability at the price of being contraindicated in the immunocompromised, pregnant women and neonates.

b1-w4-module-q15-15.html:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. A bone marrow transplant recipient is immunocompromised. For varicella the note gives him one option: post-exposure varicella immunoglobulin within 96 hours, the passive protection used for the immunocompromised, pregnant women and neonates of non-immune mothers. The window is short, so the mother should contact his doctor now (C, D).

  • A fails: sharing a classroom with an infectious case is an exposure; varicella does not need physical contact to spread.
  • B fails: varicella vaccine is live attenuated, contraindicated in the immunocompromised.
  • E fails: checking immunity spends the 96-hour window, and a transplant recipient's prior immunity cannot be relied on; IG is indicated regardless.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 09 - Introduction to Vaccines does not define what counts as a varicella exposure or discuss immunity testing after transplant; the reasoning for A and E is from general principles.

b1-w4-module-q16-16:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. The twin is immunocompetent but has no immunity, so he gets post-exposure varicella vaccine within 3-5 days, the note's PEP for immunocompetent people aged 1 year or more. A second dose is also how injectable live vaccines catch the few who did not respond to the first.

  • A fails: varicella IG is reserved for those who cannot be vaccinated – immunocompromised, pregnant women, neonates of non-immune mothers.
  • C fails: being healthy does not protect him; testing shows he is susceptible and has been exposed.
  • D fails: IG is unnecessary in a healthy host, and passive antibody may interfere with the active response to the vaccine.
b1-w4-module-q2-2:
From 06 - Adolescent Development. The note states it directly: in adolescents, self-harm is often a response to feeling invalidated by the environment, and self-harm and suicidality are symptoms of distress and maladaptive coping (E). That is why validation is the key to de-escalation.

  • A overstates: early attachment and ACEs are one risk factor among several (heritability, pubertal differences, substance use, parenting mismatch), not the cause of most concerns.
  • B swaps the two: internalizers respond to the soothing effect on the fear system; externalizers to the activating effect on the reward system.
  • C names the wrong stage: the adolescent stage is identity vs. role confusion; autonomy vs. shame and doubt belongs to toddlerhood.
  • D contradicts the note: gender dysphoria not addressed appropriately increases psychiatric comorbidity.
b1-w4-module-q20-20:
From 04 - School Age. At 4 Sam is preoperational. Classifying objects using more than one quality (number and value) is a concrete-operational skill (7-11 years), and the note's own example is that the older child “would choose 1 loonie over 5 pennies”. Sam attends only to how many coins there are (D).

  • A: reversibility is also concrete-operational, but it is about seeing the opposite perspective, not weighing two attributes of the coins.
  • B: causality is not at stake in picking coins.
  • C: semi-logical thinking produces misconceptions about causes (“my parents divorced because I was bad”), not this choice.
  • E: the choice is predictable from his stage, not random.
b1-w4-module-q3-3:
From 06 - Adolescent Development. Transition of care is one of the note's four considerations in adolescent illness: moving from paediatric to adult care is hard unless planned, so overlap services and do a “warm hand over” (C).

  • A fails: interview adolescents without parents after explaining confidentiality, encouraging collaboration where possible and safe.
  • B fails: non-adherence is often a youth asserting independence when they feel little control, or a regimen disrupting their life; it is not a refusal of treatment.
  • D fails: HEADSS is a confidential interview done without parents present.
  • E fails: peers and self-image shape how adolescents manage illness; visible illness can make fitting in hard.
b1-w4-module-q4-4:
From 08 - Immune System. The note's definitions: innate immunity looks for general evidence of infection or injury (PAMPs, DAMPs via pattern recognition receptors); adaptive immunity identifies very specific targets through antigen-specific TCRs and BCRs (B).

  • A fails on “exclusively”: NK cells are lymphoid yet innate.
  • C misplaces the delay: adaptive responses take days because rare specific clones must be selected and expanded, not because receptor binding is slow; “always” also overstates.
  • D fails: adaptive depends on innate – dendritic cells use PAMPs to decide which antigens to collect and show to T cells.
  • E fails: innate cells present antigen (dendritic cells) and carry out adaptive effector functions (macrophages phagocytosing antibody-coated targets).

b1-w4-module-q5-5.html:
From 08 - Immune System. T cells cannot see antigen on their own. A dendritic cell decides what to collect using PAMPs sensed by its pattern recognition receptors, then presents peptide on MHC to T cells; the innate signal is what licenses an adaptive response to that antigen (C).

  • A fails: adaptive immunity “must learn how or if to respond”; non-self alone is not sufficient.
  • B fails: PRRs are not antigen-specific; they detect general patterns. Specificity comes from TCRs and BCRs.
  • D fails: immunoglobulin domains are structural parts of TCRs and antibodies, not a rule for which molecules trigger which arm.
  • E fails: cytokines lack the antigen-specific signal; the TCR must bind peptide:MHC.

flags.title: Partly beyond the note
flags.html: 08 - Immune System describes dendritic cells choosing antigens by PAMPs and presenting them to T cells, but does not name costimulation; that part of option C is general immunology.

b1-w4-module-q6-6:
From 08 - Immune System. The pairings are fixed: CD8 with MHC class I (nearly all nucleated cells, endogenous pathway, cytosolic and intracellular-pathogen peptides) and CD4 with MHC class II (immune cells such as dendritic cells and macrophages, exogenous pathway). Only C states this correctly, killing virally infected cells being the CD8 role. Despite “choose all”, the key is a single option.

  • A and B swap the co-receptors.
  • D starts right but CD4 cells are helpers that drive inflammation through cytokines; killing is CD8 (and NK) work.
  • E fails: TCRs are MHC-restricted, and CD4 binds class II only.
b1-w4-module-q7-7:
From 08 - Immune System. MHC and antigen processing decide what T cells can “see”, so there is major pressure to keep HLA diverse to prevent immune blind spots. Each person carries a different combination from a huge pool of alleles, so each person's T cells are shown different peptides (B).

  • A fails: a person's handful of HLA products cannot present every peptide; that limit is why population diversity matters.
  • C fails: antibodies (BCRs) bind antigen directly; only TCRs are MHC-restricted.
  • D fails: HLA is simply the human name for the MHC, which other species have too.
  • E fails: the MHC is still the major determinant of tissue compatibility, important in stem cell transplantation, and HLA type shapes disease susceptibility.

b1-w4-module-q8-8.html:
From 08 - Immune System and 01 - Common Childhood Behaviors. Available immediately means innate: macrophages and neutrophils recognizing targets through PRRs, here the lipid and carbohydrate components of bacterial walls, which are PAMPs (D).

  • A fails: NK cells recognize cell stress in host cells and induce their apoptosis; they do not kill bacteria through PRRs.
  • B is adaptive: phagocytosis via Fc receptors needs antibody, which exists only after B-cell activation (opsonization).
  • C is adaptive twice over, and CD8 cells see MHC class I, not II.
  • E fails: neutrophils have no BCR; the BCR belongs to B cells.

b1-w4-module-q9-9.html:
From 01 - Common Childhood Behaviors (innate vs adaptive table) and 08 - Immune System.
