The adaptive column of the note's table lists exactly B, C and D: phagocytosis of antibody-bound targets via Fc receptors (opsonization), CD4 T cells maintaining inflammation with cytokines after seeing antigen on MHC II, and CD8 T cells killing with perforin/granzyme after seeing antigen on MHC I.

  • A fails: NK cells do not recognize specific antigen on MHC I; that is the CD8 T cell. NK cells join the adaptive response only through antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity.
  • E fails: tissue-resident cells making cytokines after Toll-like receptor recognition of viral RNA is the innate inflammation row, a PRR response.

b1-w4-new-q16-16:
From 04 - School Age. Piaget's stages in the note's order: sensorimotor (0-2) – learning through activity, object permanence; preoperational (2-7) – symbolic representation and play; concrete operational (7-11) – conservation, reversibility, classifying by more than one quality; formal operational (12+) – abstract and hypothetical reasoning (C).

  • A and D start with preoperational, but object permanence and sensorimotor learning come first.
  • B puts formal before concrete; logical thought about concrete objects precedes abstract thought.
b1-w4-new-q7-7:
From 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability. The note's six steps for giving the news of a disability are: introduce self, sit down if parents are agreeable, give a warning phrase, get to the point quickly, allow parents time to absorb the information, and be comfortable with silence and remain present. All four options are on that list.

“Get to the point quickly” is the one students hesitate over. It sits alongside the warning phrase, not against empathy: once warned, parents are served by directness rather than a long lead-in. Around the conversation, the informing interview has a familiar provider, both parents present, a timely diagnosis, and follow-up time to review.
b1-w4-sa-q11-11:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. The note's live attenuated viral vaccines are measles, oral polio, rotavirus, varicella and yellow fever, and live vaccines are contraindicated in the immunocompromised, pregnant women and neonates because they can cause vaccine-strain disease (C). Every other option is non-live:

  • A (Hib) is a conjugate subunit vaccine.
  • B (pneumococcal polysaccharide) is a polysaccharide subunit vaccine (poorly immunogenic under 2 years).
  • D (hepatitis B) is a protein subunit vaccine.
  • E (hepatitis A) is an inactivated whole-cell vaccine.

b1-w4-sa-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Adolescent Development. Every listed option is a recognised consequence of restrictive dieting, so “all of the above” (E):

  • A – energy restriction suppresses the reproductive axis, giving menstrual irregularity or amenorrhea.
  • B – undernutrition causes poor concentration, irritability and fatigue.
  • C – restriction drives a restrict-binge cycle.
  • D – dieting is a leading risk factor for developing an eating disorder.

The note's approach reflects this seriousness: ask how long the teen has been changing their eating to influence shape or weight, take lying and standing vitals, an ECG, and a broad panel of bloodwork.

flags.title: Mostly beyond the note
flags.html: 06 - Adolescent Development gives only the screening question and the work-up for disordered eating; the listed consequences of dieting are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

b1-w1-module-q10-10.html:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. True. The note lists why cultural competence matters: culture is a determinant of health, and cultural competence is patient-centred, increases detection of culture-specific diseases, lowers risks for patients, and reduces disparities in care.

The link to the patient-centred clinical method is the distal context: culture, community and faith shape how a patient views disease, treatment and expectations. Understanding that context is part of understanding the whole person.

review.t: Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees

b1-w1-module-q11-11.html:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees. False. Ignoring differences and treating everyone the same is cultural blindness, stage 3 of 6 on the continuum, and it meets only the dominant group's needs. Cultural competence (stage 5) is defined by recognising individual and cultural differences.

The note's equality-versus-equity contrast makes the same point: treating people equally ignores their differences, while treating them equitably recognises, responds to and respects those differences.

review.t: Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees

b1-w1-module-q13-13.html:
Related: 09 - History of Medicine. Fildes' The Doctor shows a physician keeping vigil at a sick child's bedside in a humble cottage, with almost nothing he can do but be present. Its appeal was its portrayal of the values of the ideal physician: compassion, attentiveness and dedication (B). The same ideal runs through the note's account of Osler, who stressed the doctor-patient relationship and bedside manner.

  • A: it carried no government public-health message.
  • C: it was a conventional Victorian genre painting, not a technical innovation.
  • D: it shows the absence of technology; the doctor has only his presence to offer.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w1-module-q17-17.html:
From 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach. An unexplained palpable neck mass needs a diagnosis, and the note's biopsy table gives fine needle aspiration (cells) for a palpable lesion. Choosing Wisely also says to consider the least invasive test first, which FNA is (C).

  • A and D are more invasive: surgical removal (excisional) and incisional biopsy come after a less invasive sample.
  • B: MRI characterises the mass but gives no tissue diagnosis, and the note calls it the most expensive, slowest modality.
  • E: an unexplained mass in an adult cannot be ignored because it is painless; neoplasm stays on the differential.

review.t: Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach

b1-w1-module-q18-18.html:
From 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach. The note separates two lists. ADLs are basic self-care: feeding, dressing, bathing, walking; deficits suggest a need for home care or a nursing facility. IADLs are the tasks of living independently: cooking, cleaning, transportation, laundry, managing finances.

  • B (transportation) is the IADL, so it is the exception.
  • A (feeding), C (bathing) and D (dressing) are all core ADLs.

A way to hold it: ADLs are what you do for your body; IADLs are what you do to run a household.

review.t: Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach

b1-w1-module-q2-2.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Ethics. Ethical deliberation is the path from a moral dilemma through rational deliberation to a judgement. It is needed only where values genuinely conflict. In C, offering valve surgery to an older patient with comorbidities means weighing beneficence against non-maleficence, the patient's values and quality of life (singing in the choir), and autonomy in a shared decision.

  • A and D carry no ethical conflict: equivalent kits, or stairs versus elevator, are practical preferences.
  • B has a clear duty: a young post-operative patient in arrest with no known contrary wishes gets CPR; there is no dilemma to deliberate.

b1-w1-module-q28-28.html:
From 03 - Social Pediatrics. The note says the social determinants of health have a profound impact on physical and mental health, emotional well-being, epigenetics and health behaviours, which is why they drive systemic health disparities (C).

  • A fails: their impact is profound, not small.
  • B fails: Health Canada's list (income, education, employment, childhood experiences, gender, culture, race and racism, and more) applies to everyone; Indigenous populations are one group they affect heavily.
  • D fails: clinicians act on them, and the note's downstream interventions are exactly service-level work to increase equitable access to health and social services.

b1-w1-new-q18-18.html:
All four are colonial policies and practices whose effects on Indigenous health persist, so E.

  • A: the Indian Act (1876) imposed federal control over First Nations identity, governance and land, and is still in force.
  • B: forced relocation of Inuit communities (the High Arctic relocations of the 1950s) broke ties to land and livelihood.
  • C: the residential school system removed children from families and culture, with abuse and intergenerational trauma.
  • D: child welfare, past (the Sixties Scoop) and present (overrepresentation of Indigenous children in care), continues that separation.

The course's cultural safety material ties this together: cultural safety rests on self-determination and de-colonization.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w1-new-q8-8.html:
Chronic stress keeps the arousal system (sympathetic and HPA axis) switched on. That sustained activation is itself a source of long-term biological damage (A), and chronic cortisol exposure promotes appetite, central fat deposition and weight gain (C). So the key is D, “A and C”, and it rules out B.

The bank's reason for excluding B is that ADH is not produced during stress. That is questionable (see the flag). A safer reading is that B is wrong as a blanket “high levels of ADH and cortisol” claim, so E (“all of the above”) falls with it.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

flags.title: The bank's rationale is doubtful
flags.html: The source key says ADH is not produced during stress. In standard physiology, vasopressin (ADH) is co-secreted with CRH during stress and potentiates ACTH release, so stress can raise ADH. The keyed letter (D) may still reflect the course's intent, but do not learn “stress does not release ADH” from this question. No vault note covers it.

b1-wb-fom-q8.html:
From 02 - Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach. VITAMIN C&D classifies by cause, and the cause here is a motorcycle striking him: the T of VITAMIN, traumatic/toxic (C). The bruising and internal bleeding are the result, not the category.

  • A (vascular) is the tempting distractor, since bleeding involves vessels, but vascular means a primary vessel problem such as an aneurysm or infarct, not a vessel torn by impact.
  • B, D, E: nothing infectious, autoimmune or metabolic is suggested.
  • F, G, H, I: no medical intervention, tumour, congenital lesion or degeneration explains an acute injury after a collision.

review.t: Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach

b1-wb-fom-q86.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (Block 2) and 02 - Imaging in Cardiovascular Disease (PoM 1). The Framingham risk score estimates 10-year cardiovascular disease risk from age, sex, smoking status, total cholesterol, HDL and systolic BP (D). It drives lipid management: under 10% lifestyle and re-estimate in 5 years, 10-19% add a moderate-potency statin, 20% or more a high-potency statin.

  • A: osteoporosis risk is estimated with other tools (such as FRAX).
  • B: diabetes risk has its own calculators; diabetes is an input to CV risk, not Framingham's output.
  • C: it is a clinical CVD risk tool, not an actuarial life-expectancy table.

b1-w2-meds2024-q10-10.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The sequence in the note: Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin C, causing a conformational change that frees tropomyosin from the myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin then binds actin and makes its power stroke. So calcium-bound troponin lets tropomyosin come away from actin (C).

  • A reverses the effect: calcium-bound troponin permits actin-myosin binding.
  • B names the wrong calcium-binding protein: calcium binds troponin, not tropomyosin.
  • D: calcium does not bind the actin-myosin complex; the power stroke is the myosin head's conformational change.
  • E: calcium does not act through myosin here, and the effect is to move tropomyosin away from actin, not bind it on.

b1-w2-meds2024-q11-11.html:
From 08 - Cellular Communication. The note's modes of cell signalling are autocrine (a cell signals itself), paracrine (short-distance messengers), cell-cell contact (mediators through gap junctions), synaptic (neurotransmitter release) and endocrine (hormones carried in the bloodstream).

  • A (synaptic), B (gap junctions), C (endocrine) and D (paracrine) are all on that list.
  • E (“uterine”) names an organ, not a signalling mode, so it is the exception. The uterus's own cells communicate through the modes above; visceral smooth muscle there uses gap junctions.

b1-w2-module-q101-101.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization (MRI). Look at the fluid. The note: T1-weighted (short TE and TR) gives a mostly grey/black image in which fluid is dark; T2-weighted (long TE and TR) shows fluid and pathologic tissue with a bright signal.

  • In the left image the ventricles and sulci (CSF) are dark and white matter is paler than grey matter: T1, image A.
  • In the right image the CSF is bright white: T2, image B.

Rule of thumb: water is white on T2, so if the ventricles glow, it is T2.

flags.title: Image labels assumed
flags.html: The figure carries no A/B labels; this explanation assumes A is the left image and B the right, matching the order in the stem. On that reading the key (A) agrees with the note.

b1-w2-module-q26-26.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. True. Skeletal muscle has three nested connective tissue layers, and the note places endomysium between individual muscle fibres, wrapping each one.

  • Epimysium surrounds the entire muscle.
  • Perimysium surrounds bundles of fibres (fascicles).
  • Endomysium surrounds each fibre (cell).

Memory hook: epi = upon (the outside of the whole muscle), peri = around (the bundle), endo = within (each fibre).

b1-w2-module-q27-27.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. False: a muscle fibre is a muscle cell. In skeletal muscle, precursor cells fuse during development into a multinucleated syncytium, so one long fibre, spanning the length of the muscle with its nuclei pushed to the periphery, is a single cell. The note's own anatomy list says fascicles “contain individual muscle fibers (cells)”.

The trap is the word “fibre”, which suggests a strand made of many cells, or confusion with myofibrils and filaments, which are structures inside the cell.

b1-w2-module-q30-30.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. False. The note's comparison of the three muscle types:

  • Skeletal: striated, voluntary, multinucleated with peripheral nuclei.
  • Cardiac: striated but involuntary, single central nucleus, branching fibres joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions.
  • Smooth: not striated, involuntary, spindle-shaped.

The trap is striation: cardiac muscle looks like skeletal muscle under the microscope, but striation reflects sarcomere organisation, not voluntary control.

b1-w2-module-q35-35.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. The lecture's location row is the discriminator: cardiac muscle is found exclusively in the heart, while skeletal muscle attaches to bone and smooth muscle lines vessels, soft tissues and the respiratory and GI tracts. Skeletal and smooth muscle can sit side by side (e.g. along the GI tract), but cardiac muscle never joins them outside the heart, so no tissue or organ other than the heart can intermix all three. The statement is therefore false.

  • Skeletal: striated, voluntary, multinucleated with peripheral nuclei.
  • Cardiac: striated, involuntary, single central nucleus, intercalated disks.
  • Smooth: not striated, involuntary, spindle-shaped.

b1-w2-module-q66-66.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. The lecture defines the three positions against each other:

  • Anatomical position: standing, feet flat with toes forward, head forward, palms facing forward.
  • Supine: lying down in anatomical position, i.e. on the back, face and palms up.
  • Prone: lying on the stomach, face down.

So the supine skeleton is the one lying horizontally, face up. The upright skeleton is anatomical position, and the face-down one is prone. Mnemonic: you can carry soup (supine/supination) when you lie face up.

flags.title: Figure lost from the question
flags.html: The four skeleton images (A-D) did not survive transcription, so the explanation gives the rule for picking the supine one, not which letter shows it.

b1-w2-module-q68-68.html:
From 09 - Anatomy. Right and left are always the patient's own sides, described from anatomical position, never the viewer's. A figure shown facing you therefore has the patient's right on the viewer's left. The lecture uses the same convention for scans: axial images are read as if standing at the patient's feet looking toward the head, which again puts the patient's right on the left of the screen.

  • Left = II, the side on the viewer's right.
  • Right = I, the side on the viewer's left.

The trap is labelling the figure from your own point of view, which swaps the two.

flags.title: Figure lost from the question
flags.html: The labelled image was stripped in transcription. The explanation assumes a front-facing figure with I on the viewer's left and II on the viewer's right, which is what the key implies.

b1-w2-module-q92-92.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The lecture divides the abdomen into four quadrants through the midline and the waist (RUQ, LUQ, RLQ, LLQ). The key is consistent with I = RUQ, II = LUQ, III = RLQ:

  • Liver (B) and gallbladder (E) = I, right upper quadrant: the gallbladder sits under the liver.
  • Stomach (A) and spleen (D) = II, left upper quadrant.
  • Appendix (C) = III, right lower quadrant, off the caecum.

09 - Anatomy adds that the liver, stomach and spleen all lie beneath the ribcage, which is why the upper quadrants hold them. No structure maps to IV (LLQ).

flags.title: Figure lost from the question
flags.html: The quadrant diagram was stripped in transcription; the I-IV labels are inferred from the key, and the organ positions are standard anatomy rather than stated organ by organ in the note.

b1-w2-module-q93-93.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The urinary system table lists the organs in the order urine travels, which is also top to bottom on a diagram:

  • Kidneys (B) = I: filter the blood; highest structures, in the upper posterior abdomen.
  • Ureters (A) = II: transport urine from each kidney down to the bladder.
  • Bladder (C) = III: stores and expels urine, lowest, in the pelvis.

The urethra, which drains urine from the bladder, is the fourth organ in the table but is not asked here.

flags.title: Figure and options lost from the question
flags.html: The labelled image and option letters were stripped in transcription. The explanation assumes A, B, C are ureter, kidneys, bladder in the order the stem lists them, and that I-III run superior to inferior.

b1-w2-module-q94-94.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The reproductive row of the systems table gives each structure's job, which is how to place it on a sagittal pelvis:

  • Female: ovary (gametes and hormones, III), cervix (VI) leading down into the vagina (II), and the female urethra (IV) anterior to the vagina.
  • Male: testis (sperm and hormones, I), ductus deferens (transports sperm up from the epididymis, VII), prostate (prostatic seminal fluid, just below the bladder, VIII), and the male urethra (V) running through prostate and penis.

The keyed mapping is A-III, B-VIII, C-V, D-II, E-I, F-VI, G-IV, H-VII with the structures in stem order.

flags.title: Figure and options lost from the question
flags.html: The labelled diagram and option letters were stripped in transcription. The explanation assumes A-H are the eight structures in the order the stem lists them; the numeral positions cannot be checked without the image.

b1-w2-new-q22-22.html:
From 05 - Muscle Tissue. Excitation-contraction coupling runs electrical → chemical → mechanical:

  • The action potential spreads down the T-tubules (inward folds of the sarcolemma).
  • This makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release Ca2+ from its terminal cisternae (the triad).
  • Ca2+ binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites.
  • Only then can myosin bind actin and perform the power stroke, so actin slides over myosin and the I band and H zone shorten.

A puts myosin binding before calcium-troponin binding, impossible while tropomyosin blocks the sites. B and D release calcium before the voltage reaches the SR, reversing cause and effect.

b1-w2-new-q26-26.html:
From 07 - Nerves and 10 - Body System Organization. Sensory neurons are pseudo-unipolar or bipolar cells that carry impulses from receptors to the CNS: they are the afferent fibres, so D is true. Motor neurons are the efferent limb.

  • A false: the peripheral nervous system has 12 pairs of cranial nerves.
  • B false: there are 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
  • C false: voluntary movement is skeletal muscle under somatic motor control; the sympathetic system is part of the autonomic, involuntary division.

b1-w2-new-q28-28.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. The lecture's radiograph rules answer every option. A structure needs a minimum of 2 radiographs at 90° to one another (e.g. AP/PA plus lateral), because one 2D view suffers from summation, where overlapping structures mimic an abnormality. Four is not the minimum, so C is the false statement.

  • A true: plain films use ionizing radiation, but CT is the modality the lecture singles out for a much larger dose.
  • B true: a radiograph is a 2D projection, unlike CT's slices.
  • D true: air is least dense and appears black; bone and metal appear white.

b1-w2-new-q3-3.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization. Each level of blinding hides allocation from one more party (stem order: I open label, II single, III double, IV triple):

  • Open label (I) = all parties aware → B.
  • Single blind (II) = the patient or the clinician is unaware → D.
  • Double blind (III) = both patient and investigator unaware → A.
  • Triple blind (IV) = patient, investigator and the analysts unaware → C.

12 - Evidence-Based Medicine adds why it matters: blinding reduces performance and detection bias, and is critical when the outcome is subjective, less so when it is objective.

b1-wb-fom-q78.html:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration (Week 5). All venous blood leaving the GI tract enters the portal system, draining through the portal vein to the liver before it reaches the systemic veins: absorbed nutrients → portal system → liver → caval system → IVC → right atrium.

  • C hepatic veins come after the liver, carrying blood out of it into the IVC.
  • A IVC is later still: it receives the hepatic veins.
  • D SVC drains the head, neck and upper limbs, not the gut.

The first-pass route through the liver is why the order matters.

b1-w3-module-q1-1.html:
From 01 - Child Development. The lecture's brain-development section says the brain grows most rapidly during prenatal life, then keeps increasing in size and complexity through the first 3 years (~100 billion neurons at birth, ~15,000 synapses per neuron by age 3). Plasticity is greatest when the brain is being built fastest, so it peaks before birth and then declines.

  • At birth, preschool, school age, adolescence (A, B, C, E): plasticity is still high in early childhood, which is why 08 - Developmental Milestones says early intervention works best started as early as possible, but each later period is less plastic than the one before.

After birth, pruning removes unused connections and sculpting strengthens used ones, narrowing what can still change.

flags.title: Only partly covered
flags.html: 01 - Child Development puts the fastest brain growth in the prenatal period and 08 - Developmental Milestones ties early intervention to plasticity, but neither note states outright that plasticity is highest prenatally.

b1-w3-module-q13-13.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. NIPT (cell-free placental DNA, after 9 weeks) is indicated, and in Ontario funded, only for a previous trisomy, maternal age 40+, NT > 3.5 mm, or a positive eFTS. The 21-year-old with an abnormal NT scan meets one, so C.

  • A a 35-year-old is below the 40+ age threshold.
  • B Noonan syndrome is a single-gene disorder; NIPT screens for T13, T18, T21 and sex chromosomes, and a prior Noonan baby is not an indication.
  • D 3+ miscarriages should prompt parental karyotyping for a balanced translocation (06 - Chromosomal Anomalies), not NIPT.

PoM 2's 16 - Genetic Screening for Pregnancy in Canada lists the same OHIP indications.

b1-w3-module-q17-17.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. The lecture states that newborn screening is done on the baby within 24 hours of birth, which is the keyed answer. The panel (30 disorders in Ontario, most autosomal recessive metabolic diseases) is chosen by the Wilson and Jungner criteria: a serious disease with an asymptomatic stage, which is why the sample is taken so early, before symptoms appear.

  • 12 hours (A) is earlier than the lecture's timing.
  • 48 and 72 hours (C, D) are later than it: most babies have gone home by then, and the point is to catch disease before it presents.

The screen flags babies at risk; it does not diagnose.

b1-w3-new-q13-13.html:
From 01 - Child Development and 08 - Developmental Milestones. The Nipissing (LookSee) checklist is a parent-completed questionnaire of yes/no questions about what the child can do, reviewed by the physician. One “no” is a positive screen, and it is very sensitive but not very specific. It is used repeatedly at well-child visits across early childhood (Nipissing Plus adds photos for less literate parents).

  • A true: short yes/no list about abilities.
  • B true: it tracks development over the early years at each visit.
  • C false: it is a screening tool; a positive screen leads to assessment, and only assessment diagnoses.

So D (A and B).

flags.title: Option B is only partly covered
flags.html: The notes describe the Nipissing as a repeated parent questionnaire but do not give its age range; “1 month to 6 years” is taken from the question, not the lecture.

b1-w3-new-q9-9.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening, as far as it goes. The lecture says Down syndrome risk rises with maternal age, uses 1:350 as the eFTS cut-off, and funds NIPT from age 40. The usual age-related figures run roughly 1:350 at 35, rising to about 1:175 around 38 and 1:100 at 40, so a 38-year-old sits between 1:175 and 1:100 (C).

  • A 1:900-1:600 is the risk of women around 30 or younger.
  • B 1:350-1:175 covers 35-37.
  • D greater than 1:100 applies from about 40 onward.

The logic to remember: the risk roughly doubles every 2-3 years after 35.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b1-w3-ra-q2-2.html:
From 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY: an extra X in a male, giving tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, learning disability and infertility with a normal appearance. The other options are the other syndromes in the lecture's table:

  • A 45,X = Turner syndrome (webbed neck, coarctation, short stature, primary amenorrhea).
  • C trisomy 13 = Patau (midline defects, cleft palate, polydactyly).
  • D trisomy 18 = Edward (rocker-bottom feet, overlapping fingers, cardiac defects).

B is the intended answer only if it reads 47,XXY.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The keyed option B reads “47, XX”, but 07 - Chromosome Disorder Testing and 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability (Week 4) both give Klinefelter as 47,XXY. The Y was probably dropped in transcription; as written, no option is correct.

b1-w3-ra-q3-3.html:
From 02 - Genetics. Autosomal recessive disorders need two variant alleles: affected children usually appear in one sibship of one generation with unaffected carrier parents, males and females equally, and consanguinity raises the chance. The lecture gives cystic fibrosis (CFTR, ΔF508) as the classic example, so A.

  • B Patau syndrome is trisomy 13, a numerical chromosome abnormality (aneuploidy), not a single-gene disorder.
  • C Turner syndrome is 45,X, a monosomy.
  • D Down syndrome is trisomy 21, usually from nondisjunction in meiosis I.

The discriminator: Mendelian inheritance patterns describe single genes; the three distractors are whole-chromosome errors.

b1-w3-sa-q16-16.html:
From 10 - Infant Nutrition. The lecture recommends that babies are breastfed exclusively until 6 months of age, with breastfeeding continued up to 2 years. Term infants have adequate iron stores from the mother up to 6 months, which is why iron-rich solids are added only after that. Breastfed infants need vitamin D 400 IU/day (01 - Child Development).

  • B cow's milk is not an infant diet in the first 6 months.
  • C, D formula is an alternative when breastfeeding is not possible, not the recommendation; iron is also less well absorbed from formula.
  • E rice cereal is a solid food, introduced from about 6 months.

b1-w3-sa-q4-4.html:
From 05 - Genetic Screening. Newborn screening detects babies at risk; it is NOT diagnostic, and screens carry false positives. A positive result therefore means clinical assessment plus definitive testing before anyone is labelled affected.

  • B wrong: a positive screen raises the probability; it is never dismissed because the disease is rare.
  • C wrong: one variant in a recessive gene usually means a carrier, but 02 - Genetics notes that two variants on different alleles (trans) cause disease, a second variant can be missed, and not every panel disorder is recessive.
  • D wrong: it treats a screen as a diagnosis.
  • E wrong: disorders are chosen by the Wilson and Jungner criteria (serious, asymptomatic stage, treatable), not by Ontario prevalence.

b1-w3-sa-q7-7.html:
From 08 - Developmental Milestones. Check each finding against the 18-month row and the red flags:

  • C concerning: poor eye contact is an early sign of autism spectrum disorder (with ritualistic behaviour and little symbolic play), and lack of eye contact and engagement is a listed red flag. Social-communication signs predict outcome more than motor ones.
  • A normal: 18 months expects 6-20 single words with meaning; 12 is in range. The red flag is no single words by 18 months.
  • B normal: 18 months is “walks well”; running comes at 24 months. Not walking at 18 months would be the flag.
  • D normal: temper tantrums and high activity are expected from 18 to 36 months.

b1-w4-module-q17-17.html:
From 01 - Child Development. Canada splits immunization into two layers. The national layer is advice: NACI (the National Advisory Committee on Immunization) issues the recommendations that the Rourke Baby Record's immunization reminders are built on. The delivery layer is provincial: health care, including buying, funding and giving vaccines, belongs to the provinces and territories, which is why the lecture shows an Ontario routine schedule (the 2-, 4-, 6-month infant series, the 1-year visit, 4-year boosters, school-based grade 7 HB, Men-C-ACYW and HPV-9).

  • National (A) confuses the source of the recommendation with the jurisdiction that delivers it.

flags.title: Only partly covered
flags.html: 01 - Child Development names NACI and the Ontario schedule, but no note states the constitutional split outright; the provincial-delivery point is from general knowledge.

b1-w4-module-q18-18.html:
From 01 - Child Development. There is a nationally recommended schedule: NACI (the National Advisory Committee on Immunization) publishes recommendations for all of Canada, and the lecture notes that the Rourke Baby Record's reminders of which immunizations are due at each age are based on NACI recommendations. That makes the statement true.

The trap is reading “recommended” as “delivered”. The national schedule is advice; each province decides what it funds and when (see the Ontario schedule in the same lecture), so the schedules actually given differ from province to province.

flags.title: Only partly covered
flags.html: 01 - Child Development names NACI as the source of the Rourke immunization reminders; that NACI's schedule is a national recommendation covering all provinces is from general knowledge.

b1-w4-module-q19-19.html:
From 01 - Child Development. False. NACI's recommendations are national, but each province and territory runs its own publicly funded program and sets its own schedule. The lecture's example is Ontario-specific: 2-, 4- and 6-month infant series, the 1-year MMR/Men-C/Pneu-C-13 visit, 4-year boosters, and school-based grade 7 hepatitis B, Men-C-ACYW and HPV-9. Other provinces choose different ages, products and school grades, and do not all fund the same vaccines.

Pair this with the two questions before it: national = recommendation (NACI); provincial = delivery and funding, so the schedules differ.

flags.title: Only partly covered
flags.html: 01 - Child Development shows only the Ontario schedule; that other provinces' schedules differ is from general knowledge.

b1-w4-module-q21-21.html:
From 04 - School Age. The lecture's key point is that preschoolers' semi-logical thinking produces self-blaming misconceptions (“my parents divorced because I was bad”). Sam at 4 is preoperational and egocentric, and even 11-year-old Mark, now concrete operational, may quietly wonder whether he caused it. Saying explicitly that it is not their fault addresses the misconception both ages share.

  • A listing alternative treatments is detail neither child can use.
  • B they should hear it with their parents' support, not alone.
  • C promising full recovery is false reassurance that breaks trust if the relative does not recover.
  • D raising their own risk adds fear without reason.

flags.title: Distractors reasoned from general principles
flags.html: 04 - School Age supports the self-blame point behind E; the reasons for rejecting A-D are not stated in any note.

b1-w4-module-q24-24.html:
From 04 - School Age and 01 - Child Development. Temperament is a child's characteristic, largely genetic way of responding, and the lecture lists the cautious (fearful) style alongside easy, difficult and mixed. Emily has always been shy and slow to warm up, yet once engaged she participates happily. The lecture's test is function: the difference between temperament and a disorder is usually the level of dysfunction, and assessment is needed only when behaviour or participation changes beyond what temperament explains.

  • A she does join in, so there is no impairment predicting isolation.
  • B a lifelong trait is not a passing phase.
  • C relatives with similar difficulties suggest inherited risk, not protection.
  • E punishment for anxiety-driven behaviour makes it worse.

b1-w4-module-q26-26.html:
From 04 - School Age. For a child with a chronic condition, the lecture's school-readiness role includes explaining the effect of illness on school performance to educators, so the school can plan for a disorder that will progress. His information is confidential, and for a child in foster care the consent to share it comes from the legal caregiver (child welfare or the foster parents). The best approach is therefore to get that permission first, then give the history, diagnosis and their expected effect on performance.

  • A narrows the audience but still shares without consent.
  • B puts a 5-year-old in charge of explaining his own disease.
  • C he has no learning difficulty, so insisting on comprehensive services overshoots.
  • D gives recommendations without the context the school needs to apply them.

flags.title: Only partly covered
flags.html: 04 - School Age supports explaining an illness's effect on performance to educators; the consent and confidentiality reasoning is from general principles.

b1-w4-module-q29-29.html:
From 05 - ADHD Primer. The lecture lists ADHD treatment as psychoeducation, parent training / behavioural management, school accommodation, stimulants and non-stimulants, used together. For a 10-year-old each of A, B and C is part of the initial plan:

  • A psychoeducation for parents and child: understanding the disorder underpins everything else.
  • B parental behavioural management strategies.
  • C a stimulant: first-line medication at school age.

So D, all of the above.

flags.title: Option E is also defensible
flags.html: “Treatment should be multimodal” describes the same combined plan the lecture lists, so E is true as a statement. The key prefers D because it names the specific treatments.

b1-w4-ra-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Adolescent Development and 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability. She has just reached menarche with little sex education, so the first visit starts from normal puberty and sexual development: the 7 Ps of sexual health and her developing identity apply to her as to any adolescent. The disability lecture warns against assuming a patient with a disability cannot make her own decisions, and the adolescent lecture lists family planning among the adult tasks to prepare for.

  • B, E her recurrence risk and folic acid (05 - Genetic Screening) matter for later preconception counselling, not as the first focus.
  • C telling her people with disabilities should not have children is discriminatory and false.
  • D brushing off her questions leaves her without knowledge she needs now.

b1-w4-sa-q12-12.html:
From 08 - Developmental Milestones. At 24 months the lecture expects running, climbing stairs, 50+ words, 2-word phrases, and imaginative play close to an adult. Checking the options against the table:

  • A hopping on one foot = 60 months (standing on one foot briefly is 36).
  • B riding a tricycle is a 3-year skill; at 30 months the lecture lists only a push car.
  • C using pronouns = 36 months (“asks questions, uses pronouns”).
  • D jumping on two feet is listed at 30 months, the nearest to 2 years, so it is the best answer.
  • E cooperative play = 48 months (parallel play at 36).

flags.title: The lecture dates jumping at 30 months
flags.html: 08 - Developmental Milestones and 07 - The Child with a (Dis)Ability both place jumping on two feet at 2.5 years, not 2. D is still the closest option to 24 months, but the key's “2-year motor milestone” is half a year early on the lecture.

b2-w5-module-q10-10.html:
From 12 - Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles. The screening-tool table gives the GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) as 7 questions on anxiety symptoms over the last 2 weeks, each scored 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day); 11-15 is moderate and warrants further evaluation.

  • A - depression is the PHQ-9's job, and it too uses 2 weeks, not 4.
  • D - alcohol is screened by CAGE or AUDIT, which have no fixed symptom window.
  • B, E - gastritis and gambling have no questionnaire in the lecture; the GAD-7 is not a GI or addiction tool.

review.t: Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles

b2-w5-module-q11-11.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (its mental-health framework). Stressors are formulated with the 4 Ps - predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective - each crossed with the biological, psychological and social domains. A lifelong belief is present before any illness, so it predisposes; a belief about the world and others is a cognition, so it is psychological.

  • A, D - biological would be genes, family history, medical illness or substances, not a thought pattern.
  • B, D - protective factors lower risk; distrust of others raises it.
  • C - perpetuating factors keep an existing illness going, and social ones are relationships, work or finances.

b2-w5-module-q13-13.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (its mental-health framework). Sort each option on the 4 Ps × biological/psychological/social grid: a family history of depression is inherited vulnerability present before the episode, so it is biological and predisposing.

  • A, B - the dog's death and the stock-market loss are recent social precipitating stressors that triggered the episode.
  • C - an “uptight” worrier personality predisposes, but it is psychological, not biological.
  • E - nightly cannabis is biological, but it began after the low mood and is keeping the sleep problem going: perpetuating, not predisposing.

b2-w5-module-q14-14:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results. The lecture's informed-consent section has three headed requirements: assess capacity (can the patient understand the nature of the test, its anticipated effects and the consequences of refusal), inform the patient of any special risks (benefits, material risks particular to that patient, alternatives, consequences of no treatment), and be sure consent is voluntary (no coercion, including by the physician, and time to deliberate). That is A, B and D.

  • C - a signed form documents consent but is not what makes it valid; it is not among the lecture's essentials, and a signature without understanding is not informed consent.
b2-w5-module-q17-17:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results (and 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine). An unexpected result is worked through by phase:

  • Pre-analytical - before the sample is analysed: wrong test, patient preparation, sample type/tube, order of draw, under-filling, mixing, hemolysis, storage, transport. The most common source of error.
  • Analytical - during measurement: random error, sample mix-up by the lab, methodology difference.
  • Post-analytical - after measurement: transcription error (44 for 4.4), patient mix-up in reporting, inappropriate reference interval.

Here the sample was run and a result produced; the error arose when Sr.'s result was reported under Jr.'s name as well - a patient mix-up in reporting, so post-analytical. Nothing went wrong with collection (pre-) or the measurement itself (analytical).
b2-w5-module-q18-18:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results (and 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine). An unexpected result is worked through by phase:

  • Pre-analytical - before the sample is analysed: wrong test, patient preparation, sample type/tube, order of draw, under-filling, mixing, hemolysis, storage, transport. The most common source of error.
  • Analytical - during measurement: random error, sample mix-up by the lab, methodology difference.
  • Post-analytical - after measurement: transcription error (44 for 4.4), patient mix-up in reporting, inappropriate reference interval.

Here blood drawn into a light-blue (citrate) tube was decanted into a green tube before it ever reached the analyser: the wrong sample type/tube additive at collection, so pre-analytical. The citrate already in the sample contaminates it whatever tube it ends up in. The measurement (analytical) and reporting (post-analytical) are not where the fault lies.
b2-w5-module-q21-21:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. Hyperplasia - an increase in cell number - occurs when there is “a need for compensatory increase after damage or resection”, and the lecture's own example is liver donation. Hepatocytes are stable cells sitting in G0 that re-enter the cycle when needed.

  • A hypertrophy enlarges existing cells without adding new ones; it is the muscle response to workload.
  • C atrophy is a decrease in size, the opposite direction.
  • D metaplasia swaps one mature tissue type for another; the regrown liver is still liver.
b2-w5-module-q22-22:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's two definitions separate every statement in this set: necrosis is always pathologic - loss of membrane integrity, leakage of contents, enzymatic digestion, and inflammation in the surrounding tissue; apoptosis may be physiologic or pathologic - a tightly regulated “suicide” program in which intrinsic enzymes degrade the cell's own DNA and proteins, and the fragments are devoured before they leak, so there is no inflammation.

“Always pathogenic” is necrosis: the lecture calls it a pathologic process, whereas apoptosis can also be physiologic.
b2-w5-module-q23-23:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's two definitions separate every statement in this set: necrosis is always pathologic - loss of membrane integrity, leakage of contents, enzymatic digestion, and inflammation in the surrounding tissue; apoptosis may be physiologic or pathologic - a tightly regulated “suicide” program in which intrinsic enzymes degrade the cell's own DNA and proteins, and the fragments are devoured before they leak, so there is no inflammation.

“May be physiologic or pathogenic” is apoptosis - it eliminates unwanted cells normally as well as after injury. Necrosis is only ever pathologic.
b2-w5-module-q24-24:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's two definitions separate every statement in this set: necrosis is always pathologic - loss of membrane integrity, leakage of contents, enzymatic digestion, and inflammation in the surrounding tissue; apoptosis may be physiologic or pathologic - a tightly regulated “suicide” program in which intrinsic enzymes degrade the cell's own DNA and proteins, and the fragments are devoured before they leak, so there is no inflammation.

“Programmed cell death following a tightly regulated program” is the lecture's definition of apoptosis. Necrosis is uncontrolled breakdown after membrane failure.
b2-w5-module-q25-25:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's two definitions separate every statement in this set: necrosis is always pathologic - loss of membrane integrity, leakage of contents, enzymatic digestion, and inflammation in the surrounding tissue; apoptosis may be physiologic or pathologic - a tightly regulated “suicide” program in which intrinsic enzymes degrade the cell's own DNA and proteins, and the fragments are devoured before they leak, so there is no inflammation.

“Loss of membrane integrity and leakage of cellular contents” is necrosis. In apoptosis the membrane holds until the fragments are phagocytosed, so nothing leaks.
b2-w5-module-q26-26:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's two definitions separate every statement in this set: necrosis is always pathologic - loss of membrane integrity, leakage of contents, enzymatic digestion, and inflammation in the surrounding tissue; apoptosis may be physiologic or pathologic - a tightly regulated “suicide” program in which intrinsic enzymes degrade the cell's own DNA and proteins, and the fragments are devoured before they leak, so there is no inflammation.

“Cells degrade their own DNA and proteins via intrinsic enzymes” is apoptosis - the cell activates its own enzymes. In necrosis the digestion is of a cell already failing, and it spills out.
b2-w5-module-q27-27:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's two definitions separate every statement in this set: necrosis is always pathologic - loss of membrane integrity, leakage of contents, enzymatic digestion, and inflammation in the surrounding tissue; apoptosis may be physiologic or pathologic - a tightly regulated “suicide” program in which intrinsic enzymes degrade the cell's own DNA and proteins, and the fragments are devoured before they leak, so there is no inflammation.

“Results in a host inflammatory reaction” is necrosis, because its contents leak into the tissue. Apoptotic fragments are cleared before leaking, so apoptosis provokes no inflammation.
b2-w5-module-q28-28:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The Celsus signs each trace to one vascular or mediator event: rubor (redness) = vasodilation and opening of capillary beds, so more blood flows; calor (heat) = that core-temperature blood arriving in cooler skin; dolor (pain) = mediators stimulating sensory nerve endings; tumor (swelling) = protein-rich fluid leaking through permeable vessels (or an abscess); functio laesa (loss of function) = Virchow's later addition, the consequence of the others.

“Vasodilation and increased blood flow” is the mechanism of rubor. Calor also depends on that flow, but its defining step is warm blood reaching the cooler skin; the rest are unrelated to flow.
b2-w5-module-q29-29:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The Celsus signs each trace to one vascular or mediator event: rubor (redness) = vasodilation and opening of capillary beds, so more blood flows; calor (heat) = that core-temperature blood arriving in cooler skin; dolor (pain) = mediators stimulating sensory nerve endings; tumor (swelling) = protein-rich fluid leaking through permeable vessels (or an abscess); functio laesa (loss of function) = Virchow's later addition, the consequence of the others.

“Blood at body core temperature entering the cooler skin” is calor. Rubor is the colour of the same increased flow, not its warmth.
b2-w5-module-q30-30:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The Celsus signs each trace to one vascular or mediator event: rubor (redness) = vasodilation and opening of capillary beds, so more blood flows; calor (heat) = that core-temperature blood arriving in cooler skin; dolor (pain) = mediators stimulating sensory nerve endings; tumor (swelling) = protein-rich fluid leaking through permeable vessels (or an abscess); functio laesa (loss of function) = Virchow's later addition, the consequence of the others.

“Mediator release that stimulates sensory nerve endings” is dolor. Swelling can add pressure pain, but the stimulus named here is chemical, not fluid.
b2-w5-module-q37-37:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration. Each circuit is named by where it delivers:

  • Coronary - coronary arteries (5% of CO) supply the heart muscle itself first, draining via the coronary sinus to the RA.
  • Portal - all venous blood leaving the GI tract enters the hepatic portal vein so the liver can process absorbed nutrients before the IVC.
  • Pulmonary - pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood to the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left heart for circulation.
  • Systemic - the arterial tree delivering O2, nutrients and hormones to every region, and carrying wastes away.

Supplying oxygen and nutrients to cardiac tissue is the coronary circulation.
b2-w5-module-q38-38:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration. Each circuit is named by where it delivers:

  • Coronary - coronary arteries (5% of CO) supply the heart muscle itself first, draining via the coronary sinus to the RA.
  • Portal - all venous blood leaving the GI tract enters the hepatic portal vein so the liver can process absorbed nutrients before the IVC.
  • Pulmonary - pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood to the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left heart for circulation.
  • Systemic - the arterial tree delivering O2, nutrients and hormones to every region, and carrying wastes away.

Carrying digested nutrients to the liver for processing is the portal circulation.
b2-w5-module-q39-39:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration. Each circuit is named by where it delivers:

  • Coronary - coronary arteries (5% of CO) supply the heart muscle itself first, draining via the coronary sinus to the RA.
  • Portal - all venous blood leaving the GI tract enters the hepatic portal vein so the liver can process absorbed nutrients before the IVC.
  • Pulmonary - pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood to the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left heart for circulation.
  • Systemic - the arterial tree delivering O2, nutrients and hormones to every region, and carrying wastes away.

Delivering oxygenated blood to the heart to be sent round the body is the pulmonary circulation, through the pulmonary veins. Coronary blood oxygenates the heart muscle rather than supplying blood for it to pump.
b2-w5-module-q40-40:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration. Each circuit is named by where it delivers:

  • Coronary - coronary arteries (5% of CO) supply the heart muscle itself first, draining via the coronary sinus to the RA.
  • Portal - all venous blood leaving the GI tract enters the hepatic portal vein so the liver can process absorbed nutrients before the IVC.
  • Pulmonary - pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood to the lungs; pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left heart for circulation.
  • Systemic - the arterial tree delivering O2, nutrients and hormones to every region, and carrying wastes away.

Delivering oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes to all regions of the body is the systemic circulation; the other three each serve a single organ.

b2-w5-module-q4-4.html:
From 08 - Choosing Wisely Review. The lecture frames Choosing Wisely as appropriate utilization - balancing under- and over-use - built on evidence-based recommendations generated by multidisciplinary stakeholders, with tool kits for putting them into practice, and it lists drivers of over-testing at every level (labs, health systems, physicians, patients). A change that has to reach every level needs each of A-C.

  • A - the physician drivers (malpractice fear, patient pressure, fee for service) start with the clinician, and the aim is patient-focused care.
  • B - engaging stakeholders and adapting evidence is how the recommendations themselves are made.
  • C - the system drivers (silo effect, historical practice) need openness to change and leadership support.
  • E - contradicts the premise that tool kits exist to implement it.

flags.title: The implementation strategies are only partly in the notes
flags.html: 08 - Choosing Wisely Review covers the principles and the drivers of over-testing, but does not list the three implementation strategies in A-C. The link from each driver to a strategy is reasoned, not quoted. Verify it before relying on it.

b2-w5-module-q42-42:
From 03 - Body Systems Integration. RBCs last about 100-120 days; the spleen identifies aged and defective cells and destroys them. In the red pulp, blood leaks into venous sinuses where macrophages destroy defective or aged cells, and only the healthy ones return to circulation.

  • B - clearing blood-borne antigens is the white pulp's job (adaptive immunity), and it acts on pathogens, not defective RBCs.
  • C - return to the systemic circulation is the fate of healthy RBCs.
  • D - defective cells are not repaired; new RBCs come from the marrow, not from recycled ones.

b2-w5-module-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Osmosis (Block 1, Week 2; Darrow-Yannet diagrams) and 01 - An Introduction to Body Fluids Regulation. The three items are, in order, excessive ingestion of pure [water] (the word was lost in transcription), hemorrhage, and excessive ingestion of salt.

  • 1 (pure water) → B - the water-overload diagram: more ECF volume, lower osmolality, water then moving into cells.
  • 2 (hemorrhage) → A - whole blood is lost as it is, so volume falls with no change in osmolarity.
  • 3 (salt) → C - a solute load raises ECF osmolarity; with no fluid taken to replace it there is no water added from outside.

flags.title: The Osmosis lecture has ECF volume rising after a solute load
flags.html: 02 - Osmosis (Block 1, Week 2) says a solute load gives more volume and higher osmolality of the ECF, as water is drawn out of the cells. So the “no change in volume” half of C holds only for total body water, not for the ECF. C is still the only option left for salt once water and hemorrhage are matched, but the option does not match the lecture exactly.

b2-w5-new-q10-10.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation (and 06 - Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway for vitals). Statement by statement:

  • i - HR, RR, temperature and BP are the classic vitals; every option includes i, so the question treats it as true (06 also lists O2 saturation).
  • ii true - systemic veins, the capacitance vessels, hold about 70% of the ~5 L blood volume.
  • iii true - biological gender is on the lecture's list of factors that affect BP.
  • iv - the lecture ties TPR to vessel diameter (larger diameter = lower resistance), and lists blood volume as a separate factor in BP. It never links TPR to blood volume.
  • v false - the PNS slows HR and contractility, so the heart has both SNS and PNS supply (the PNS just does not innervate the blood vessels).

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key (D) needs statement iv to be true, but 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation relates TPR to vessel diameter and lists blood volume as a separate determinant of BP alongside cardiac output, peripheral resistance, viscosity and vessel elasticity. On the lecture, iv is unsupported, which would make B (i, ii, iii) the answer. The key's own rationale addresses only statement v.

b2-w5-new-q12-12:
From 09 - Approach to Anxiety and Stress. The lecture's symptom-cluster tables sort each symptom into a sphere and a disorder. Avoidance (behavioural), worry (emotional) and catastrophizing (cognitive) belong to the anxiety cluster; impaired concentration and insomnia appear in both clusters, so they fit anxiety as well. Every symptom here fits anxiety.

  • A - the depression markers are missing: sadness, hopelessness, worthlessness, loss of interest, isolating, suicidal ideation.
  • B, D - there is nothing to suggest mania, or obsessions and compulsions; the lecture gives no cluster that matches this pattern better than anxiety.
b2-w5-new-q14-14:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results. The informed-consent section opens with the point: any test can find something bad, so the patient must understand what they are undergoing and what could result, and it is ultimately up to the patient whether to proceed. Explanation and consent therefore come before anything is ordered or collected.

  • A, B - knowing the collection steps and making the requisition are logistics that follow a decision the patient has not yet made.
  • D - telling the patient and then ordering skips consent: telling is not the same as the patient agreeing voluntarily with capacity.

b2-w5-new-q20-20.html:
From 12 - Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles. The lecture runs the inflammatory response as the 5 Rs, and the order follows the logic of the response: Recognition of the offending agent by host cells and molecules → Recruitment of leukocytes and plasma proteins from the circulation → Removal of the agent by the activated cells → Regulation, controlling and terminating the reaction → Resolution, repair of the damaged tissue.

  • A, B - cells cannot be recruited before the agent has been recognized.
  • C - nothing can remove the agent until leukocytes have been recruited.
  • E - regulation (termination) comes after removal; switching the response off first would leave the agent in place.

review.t: Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles

b2-w5-new-q3-3:
From 06 - Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway (its tube-colour chart; and 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine). The chart pairs the lavender (purple) K2 EDTA tube with the full blood count (FBC/CBC), along with HbA1c and ESR. 07 names collecting the proper specimen type in the correct tube, in the correct order of draw, as the basis of an accurate result; the wrong tube is a pre-analytical error.

  • A red - a clot activator, so the blood clots; the chart uses it for antibody screens and vitamin D.
  • C green - lithium heparin, for STAT biochemistry, electrolytes and renal function.
  • D navy (royal blue) - trace elements and heavy metals (zinc, copper, lead, mercury).

b2-w5-new-q5-5.html:
From 08 - Choosing Wisely Review (and 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine). The lecture defines Choosing Wisely as appropriate utilization, balancing underutilization and overutilization. Rationing withholds care to save resources, which is underuse: the reverse of what the campaign is for, so B is not a reason for it.

  • A - the volume of unnecessary testing is the problem the campaign exists to address.
  • C - a reason: 07 shows predictive value falls with prevalence, so testing low-probability patients makes a positive result increasingly likely to be false.
  • D - harm is a reason: inappropriate testing leads to unnecessary procedures and treatment, and so to patient harm.

flags.title: Two of the figures are not in the notes
flags.html: The “more than 1 million” figure (A) and the claim about harm from cascades after incidental findings (D) do not appear in 08 - Choosing Wisely Review, which states only that inappropriate testing causes unnecessary procedures and patient harm. Verify them before relying on them.

b2-w5-new-q6-6.html:
From 08 - Choosing Wisely Review. The lecture's “Why Choosing Wisely?” table gives drivers of over-testing at every level, and each option is one of them:

  • A the silo effect - health systems (culture and historical practice).
  • B revenue - labs.
  • C malpractice fear - physicians, alongside patient pressure, incentives and fee for service.
  • D “more is better” - patients, alongside wellness movements and Dr. Google.

Because every stakeholder contributes, all of the above is the answer, and no single option accounts for the problem alone.

b2-w5-ra-q10-10:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Weight training raises the workload on skeletal muscle, which cannot divide much, so it enlarges its existing fibres: hypertrophy. There are no new cells (not hyperplasia), no change of tissue type (not metaplasia), and the muscle is growing rather than shrinking (not atrophy).
b2-w5-ra-q7-7:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Estrogen driving more endometrial glands is increased cell number in a hormone-sensitive organ under hormonal stimulation: hyperplasia. The glands multiply rather than simply enlarging, and they stay endometrium.
b2-w5-ra-q8-8:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Chronic acid irritation replacing the esophagus's native squamous lining with intestinal-type epithelium is one mature tissue replaced by another not indigenous to that site: metaplasia. The change is in tissue type, not size or number.
b2-w5-ra-q9-9:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The four adaptations are told apart by what changes:

  • Hypertrophy - bigger cells, no new cells; the response of skeletal and cardiac muscle (limited division) to increased workload.
  • Hyperplasia - more cells, driven by hormones or growth factors, or compensatory after damage or resection.
  • Metaplasia - one mature tissue replaced by another not native to the site, a reversible response to chronic irritation.
  • Atrophy - loss of cell size and number; causes include disuse, denervation, diminished blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of endocrine stimulation, pressure.

Reduced brain volume from diminished blood supply is one of the lecture's named causes of pathologic atrophy: fewer and smaller cells, the opposite of both hyperplasia and hypertrophy.

b2-w5-sa-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The baroreceptor reflex is a fast neural loop: stretch sensors send signals to the brain, which answers by changing heart rate or vessel diameter (TPR). High-pressure receptors sit in the aortic arch and carotid sinus and monitor blood pressure (B); low-pressure receptors sit in the atria and report blood volume to the same centre (C).

  • A - hormones are the slow arm of BP control; the reflex itself needs no adrenal hormone.
  • D - reversed: the aortic arch and carotid sinus are both high-pressure sites.
  • E - fails because A and D are false.

flags.title: Option C is garbled and only partly matches
flags.html: Option C lost its verb in transcription (“Signals from low pressure baroreceptors to the cardiovascular centre to monitor...”). 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation assigns the low-pressure (atrial) receptors to blood volume and the high-pressure ones to blood pressure, so C's “blood pressure and blood volume” overstates the note. The stem also reads as single-answer while the key has two.

b2-wb-fom-q77:
From 01 - An Introduction to Body Fluids Regulation. The lecture's dehydration logic runs in reverse here. Losing solute from the ECF makes the ECF hypo-osmotic, so water follows its gradient into the cells: ICF volume rises, ECF volume falls. Water keeps moving until the two compartments are iso-osmotic again, so osmolarity ends up lower in both - the cells cannot hold a different osmolarity from their surroundings.

  • A, D - ECF volume cannot rise when water is leaving it for the cells.
  • B - both volumes cannot fall with no net fluid loss; water shifts, it does not vanish.
  • C - right volumes, but osmolarity equilibrates, so it cannot fall in the ICF alone.
b2-wb-fom-q89:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. After injury, tissue either regenerates (normal function restored) or is repaired by scar. Regeneration happens in tissues made of labile and stable cells when the injury is not too severe - which covers most tissues (skin and GI epithelium constantly, hepatocytes from G0). Only permanent cells (cardiac myocytes, neurons, skeletal muscle) always heal by scarring.

  • A - fibrous scarring is the fallback for permanent cells, severe injury or damaged supporting structures, not the majority.
  • B, C - hyperplasia and hypertrophy are adaptations to stress (more cells, bigger cells), not the healing outcome after cell death.
b2-w6-meds2024-q13-13:
From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. The lecture defines screening in one sentence: we screen for relatively common problems in people who are asymptomatic, using cheap and easy tests, for conditions where early detection allows effective but less invasive treatment. A rare problem breaks that model - a test run on a low-prevalence population yields few true cases for the cost and many false positives.

  • A - cheap and easy: a stated feature.
  • B - asymptomatic population: a stated feature.
  • C - less invasive: stated, both of the test and of the treatment early detection allows.
b2-w6-meds2024-q16-16:
From 05 - Cancer From Macro to Molecular. The lecture lists the modifiable (“lifestyle”) risk factors: smoking, obesity, physical activity, diet, alcohol, injection drug use, sexual history (HPV and cervical cancer) and tanning beds (melanoma). Non-modifiable factors follow the GGRAPES mnemonic, whose R is reproductive history (breastfeeding, menarche, menopause), as spelled out in the chart in 03 - Cancer Genetics.

  • A - sexual activity: modifiable, via HPV exposure.
  • C - obesity: modifiable.
  • D - tanning beds: modifiable, melanoma.
  • E - smoking: the #1 modifiable risk factor.
b2-w6-module-q10-10:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass. A fibroadenoma is a benign neoplasm presenting as a single nodule that is well circumscribed, well demarcated, firm and mobile - exactly this lump, with no symptoms and no skin or nipple change.

  • A - an abscess is a pus collection with warmth, redness, tenderness and swelling.
  • B - a discrete 2 cm lump is not normal breast tissue.
  • C - fat necrosis is the trauma (T) of VITAMIN C&D; there is no trauma history.
  • E - malignancy is typically hard, irregular, poorly circumscribed and may be fixed.
b2-w6-module-q26-26:
From 05 - Cancer From Macro to Molecular. Among systemic treatments the lecture defines immunotherapy as drugs that stimulate the body's immune system to recognize cancer cells as foreign (e.g., PD-L1 inhibitors).

  • A - drugs aimed at specific genes or their products are targeted therapy (e.g., imatinib against BCR-ABL1).
  • C - cancer vaccines are listed separately, and they are not against “cancer antibodies”.
  • D - sequencing the patient's tumour belongs to precision medicine; immunotherapy drugs are not built from each patient's sample.
b2-w6-new-q11-11:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass (its benign-lesion table). The stem lists the terms as 1 Cyst, 2 Fibrocystic change, 3 Abscess, 4 Fibroadenoma.

  • A = 4, fibroadenoma - a benign neoplasm: a single nodule, well circumscribed and demarcated, firm and mobile.
  • B = 3, abscess - a collection of pus (acute inflammation, neutrophils) with warmth, redness, swelling and tenderness.
  • C = 1, cyst - a sac of air, fluid or semi-solid, well demarcated with smooth margins, collapsing when the fluid is drawn off.
  • D = 2, fibrocystic change - lumpy, nodular breasts whose pain or tenderness varies with the menstrual cycle; not a neoplasm.
b2-w6-new-q3-3:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass. A cyst is a sac of air, fluid or semi-solid that is well demarcated and well circumscribed with smooth margins. Rough or irregular edges are the malignant feature in the lecture's benign-vs-malignant table, so B is false twice over: wrong margin, and the wrong inference from it.

  • A - true: the sac can hold air.
  • C - true: it collapses once the fluid is removed (e.g., by fine-needle aspiration).
  • D - true: well demarcated from surrounding tissue.
  • E - true: cysts can be single or multiple, as in fibrocystic change.
b2-w6-new-q8-8:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics. A tumour suppressor gene normally inhibits the cell cycle, slows proliferation or promotes apoptosis; cancer needs it lost (two hits, loss of function). Up-regulating the cycle describes an oncogene, so D is the false statement.

  • A - true: a proto-oncogene mutation is gain of function and one hit suffices.
  • B - true: tumour suppressor mutations are loss of function.
  • C - true: BRCA1 (chr 17) and BRCA2 (chr 13) are described as autosomal dominant.
  • E - true: promoting apoptosis is one of their normal roles.

b2-w6-sa-q11-11.html:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics. In p.L458X the “X” denotes a stop codon: leucine 458 is replaced by a premature stop, truncating the MSH2 protein. A point change that creates a stop is a nonsense mutation - the truncation the stem says causes colon cancer.

  • A - anticipation is earlier or worse disease each generation, a feature of triplet-repeat disorders (Block 1, 02 - Genetics); this is a point change, and the ages do not fall steadily.
  • C - affected relatives across generations on one side fit autosomal dominant hereditary cancer, which the lecture's red flags describe.
  • D - Audrey is the affected relative the lecture says to test first; once her mutation is known, relatives can be offered predictive testing.
  • E - X is a stop, not xanthine, which is not an amino acid.

flags.title: Nonsense-mutation notation is not in the notes
flags.html: 03 - Cancer Genetics covers hereditary red flags and testing an affected relative first, and Block 1's 02 - Genetics covers anticipation, but no note defines a nonsense mutation or the p.…X notation; that part is from general principles. The transcribed stem also lost the “>” in c.1373T>G, and option D names a sister although the stem gives Audrey only a brother.

b2-w6-sa-q4-4:
From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass. A firm, mobile, non-tender 2.5 cm mass in a 28-year-old, stable for months and unchanged by feeding, is the lecture's fibroadenoma: a benign single nodule, well circumscribed, firm and mobile. Young age already makes a benign cause most likely.

  • A, J - abscess and mastitis are common in breastfeeding, but they are warm, red, swollen and tender.
  • E - a cyst is a smooth fluid sac, not described as a firm solid mass.
  • I - carcinoma is usually hard, irregular and may be fixed, and is less likely at 28.
  • G, L - a node would sit in the axilla; normal lactation change is diffuse, not a discrete lump.
  • B, C, D, F, K, M, N - remaining VITAMIN C&D categories with nothing in the history to support them.
b2-wb-fom-q132:
From 02 - Approach to Neoplasia. A neoplasm is an abnormal mass arising from excessive cell division and evasion of apoptosis. A slowly enlarging lump whose biopsy shows atypical cells with a raised mitotic rate is that - abnormal cells proliferating autonomously.

  • A - hypertrophy is larger cells with no new cells (05 - Cellular Stress & Repair).
  • B - hyperplasia is more cells, but normal ones driven by hormones or growth factors, not atypical ones.
  • C - metaplasia replaces one differentiated cell type with another; it adds no mass of atypical cells.
b2-w7-module-q25-25:
From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer (Week 6). Average-risk breast screening is a mammogram every 2 years for women 50-74; screening is reserved for relatively common problems. At 30, breast cancer is rare (B), and in a low-prevalence group most positive results are false (C): positive predictive value depends on how many true cases the population holds.

  • A - true, but a reason for screening, not against it.
  • D - also true, and also an argument for screening in general; it does not explain withholding it at 30.
b2-w7-module-q27-27:
From 03 - Mental Health Through Aging (& Depression in Older Adults). The lecture states that dementia and depression are risk factors for each other (A, B), and gives major depression in 20-25% of people after stroke (F).

  • C - false: bereavement more than triples the risk of depression, the largest effect of any factor examined.
  • D - false: it is economic disadvantage and deteriorating finances that raise depressive symptoms.
  • E - false: the protective list includes no alcohol abuse, and substance use is a common comorbidity of late-life depression.
b2-w7-module-q28-28:
From 03 - Mental Health Through Aging (& Depression in Older Adults). The lecture says screening older adults is beneficial because depressive symptoms are associated with suffering, poorer health outcomes, increased mortality (B) and disability (D). It is also hard to recognize (C): older adults deny or minimize low mood, express distress physically, and present with cognitive and somatic changes.

  • A - false: the lecture calls depression being “normal” with age a large misconception, and one of the barriers to recognizing it.

b2-w7-module-q29-29.html:
From 03 - Mental Health Through Aging (& Depression in Older Adults). Late-life depression hides: older patients are less likely to report affective symptoms, deny depressed mood, and are more likely to endorse cognitive and physical changes. Depression without sadness is common and somatization is quite common.

  • A - true on the lecture: prominent somatic complaints are common in older adults.
  • B - false on the lecture: older adults are less, not more, likely to complain of depressed mood.
  • C - true: cognitive changes are more often the presenting concern.
  • D - false: MDD prevalence is lower after 65 than in younger groups.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives B and C, but 03 - Mental Health Through Aging (& Depression in Older Adults) says older patients “typically deny depressed mood” and are “less likely to report affective symptoms”, which makes B false, and that somatization is “quite common”, which makes A true. On the lecture the answer is A and C.

b2-w7-new-q16-16:
From 02 - Periodic Health Encounter for Older Adults. Hypercholesterolemia screening starts at 40 for men and 50 for women, repeated every 5 years if risk factors do not change other than age, with risk estimated by the Framingham calculator.

  • A - 40 is right for men only; women start later.
  • B - 50 is right for women only; men start earlier.
  • C - the ages are swapped between the sexes.
b2-w7-new-q18-18:
From 01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease. The normal changes of aging include variable loss of cortical and spinal cord neurons with a decrease in brain weight and functional reserve, so an increase is not part of healthy aging.

  • A - normal: older adults shiver less, sense cold late, sweat less and vasoconstrict/vasodilate poorly.
  • B - normal: body water/fat ratio shifts, alongside reduced thirst and ADH sensitivity.
  • C - normal: pupils shrink and the lens thickens, lowering acuity and night vision.
  • E - normal: maximal heart rate falls with age, and the ventricles stiffen.

b2-w7-ra-q3-3.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Delirium. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention with a precipitant to find, and the 4-AT scores an acute change or fluctuation on its own. Dementia is a decline that impairs independence in ADLs/IADLs and, by definition (03 - Mental Health Through Aging), does not occur exclusively during delirium - it develops over months to years, not hours to days.

  • A - IADL difficulty is the functional criterion for dementia, and an acutely delirious patient cannot manage IADLs either.
  • B, D, E - agitation, apathy and delusions can accompany either condition, so none separates them.

b2-w7-sa-q12-12:
From 09 - Interdisciplinary Teams & Community Resources for Older Adults. Home and Community Care (LHIN) care coordinators determine the right supports and coordinate long-term care admission (B), and it provides OHIP-funded nursing, OT, PT, social work and personal support at home - OTs assess function, mobility and safety in the home (C).

  • A - homemaking is a pay-per-service community service the LHIN coordinates access to, not one it provides at extra cost.
  • D - referral can come from the physician, patient or caregiver.
  • E - nothing in the lecture has home care giving daily medications; the lecture's answer to adherence is the pharmacist's blister packs.
  • F - false: home nursing is funded, which covers wound care.
b2-w7-sa-q17-17:
From 02 - Periodic Health Encounter for Older Adults, with the cervical program from Week 6's 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. At 65 a woman is still inside the Pap program (25-70, every 3 years; A), is due lipids (women from 50, every 5 years; B), starts bone mineral density at 65 (C), and is screened for diabetes with HbA1c (E).
