  • D, F - CBC and chest X-ray are on the lecture's explicit “not routinely ordered for screening” list, as is ECG.
  • G, K - magnesium and B12 are not screening tests in either lecture.
  • H, I, J - CT head, stress test and pelvic ultrasound are diagnostic tests with no screening role in a healthy woman.
b2-w7-sa-q3-3:
From 10 - Introduction to Neurofunction. First step: CNS or PNS. Leg hyperreflexia and upgoing plantars are upper motor neuron signs, so the lesion is central. Second step: the pattern. Weakness confined to both legs (paraparesis) localizes to the thoracic cord or lumbar roots; normal arm reflexes and power spare the cervical cord, and impaired leg vibration fits a cord lesion below the arms.

  • A - brainstem gives cranial nerve signs and usually affects the arms too.
  • B - a cervical lesion causes quadriparesis with arm UMN signs.
  • D - lumbar roots are LMN: reduced reflexes, no Babinski.
  • E - peripheral nerves are LMN too: hyporeflexia and atrophy, not hyperreflexia.
b2-w7-sa-q4-4:
From 10 - Introduction to Neurofunction. Impaired vision in the right hemifield of both eyes localizes behind the optic chiasm, since after the chiasm each optic tract carries the opposite hemifield from both eyes. The right hemifield travels on the left, ending in the left occipital lobe. She missed a car on her right for exactly this reason.

  • A, B - retina and optic nerve are anterior to the chiasm, giving loss in one eye only.
  • C - a chiasmal lesion hits the crossing fibres from both nasal retinas, taking out both temporal fields rather than one hemifield.
  • E - the right occipital lobe processes the left hemifield.
b2-w8-module-q35-35:
From 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response. Asians have about twice the plasma level of rosuvastatin at the same dose, and high statin levels raise the risk of rhabdomyolysis, so the 40 mg dose is contraindicated in Asians (a 5 mg pill exists for them).

  • A - false: most people carry at least one variant affecting drug effect or harm.
  • B - false: warfarin dose runs African American > Caucasian > Asian, so Asians need lower doses, because of more common VKORC1/CYP2C9 variants.
  • D - false: BiDil is isosorbide dinitrate + hydralazine; ACE inhibitors are the drugs to use cautiously as monotherapy in Black patients.

b2-w8-module-q36-36.html:
From 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response. Three statements match the lecture, which leaves D as the false one.

  • A - consistent: the PK differences are described as “slightly” more efficient elimination, with named drugs (zolpidem, ACE-inhibitor cough, QT prolongation) where they matter.
  • B - true: zolpidem starts at 5 mg for women and 5 or 10 mg for men, because women metabolize it more slowly.
  • C - true: diazepam's half-life rises with age from reduced clearance and a larger volume of distribution, since it is stored in fat.
  • D - the lecture does say to reduce doses and monitor renal function routinely in the elderly, but it gives no figure for kidney disease at 70.

flags.title: Why D is false is not in the notes
flags.html: 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response supports A, B and C, but has no prevalence of kidney disease at age 70, so the note cannot confirm what makes the 30% figure in D wrong. The key is followed here on the strength of the other three.

b2-w5-module-q12-12.html:
From 12 - Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles. On the PHQ-9 (depression symptoms over the last 2 weeks), 0-4 is minimal. A score of 3 calls for no treatment; action starts at 5-9 with watchful waiting and at 10 or more with pharmacotherapy or CBT.

  • C, E - psychotherapy is for moderate scores, not minimal ones.
  • B, D - the PHQ-9 screens for depression; drug and gambling addiction are not what it measures, and inpatient or residential care is far beyond any score.

review.t: Adult Screening and Preventative Care Principles

b2-w5-module-q15-15.html: From 03 - Examination of a Well Newborn & Infant (Block 1). The note is explicit: there is no age of consent in Ontario. Once a child can show that they understand the risks and benefits of a medical intervention, they can consent for themselves, which is how some teenagers choose vaccination their parents declined. Capacity, not a birthday, decides - so a fixed age of 12 is false.

review.t: Examination of a Well Newborn & Infant

b2-w5-module-q16-16.html:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results. Confidentiality applies to individuals, not families: you may disclose only with your patient's implied or expressed consent, and the exceptions are mandatory reporting (a child in need of protection, serious harm to others). A 15-year-old who understands the risks and benefits of the pill can consent to it herself, since Ontario has no age of consent (Block 1, 03 - Examination of a Well Newborn & Infant). She is the patient, so her mother cannot be told without her permission.

  • A - being her parent is not one of the exceptions.

b2-w5-module-q19-19.html:
From 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results. Faced with an unexpected result, work through pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical explanations. Analytical explanations include random error, lab mix-up and methodology differences - “do you know the analytical method and anything that could interfere?” A very high plasma protein load that distorts the measured sodium is interference with the method: the sample was right, the measurement was not.

  • A - pre-analytical errors come before analysis: wrong test, patient preparation, collection, transport, processing.
  • C - post-analytical errors come after: transcription, reporting mix-up, wrong reference interval.

b2-w5-module-q20-20.html:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The Warburg effect is increased glucose (and glutamine) uptake and glycolysis in dividing cells, and it is fixed in cancer cells. PET exploits exactly that: FDG, a glucose analogue, is taken up preferentially by rapidly dividing tissue, and the Block 3 lymphoma lectures use it as a functional scan of tumour glucose uptake.

  • A - CT reconstructs anatomy from X-ray attenuation; it does not measure metabolism.
  • C - MRI images structure with a magnet and radio waves.
  • D - ultrasound images structure with sound waves.

b2-w5-module-q34-34.html:
From 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair. The lecture's response to vascular injury is intimal thickening, and it lists the harms of intimal thickening as luminal stenosis, vascular obstruction and reduced blood flow. The cells doing the thickening are smooth muscle cells from the media that migrate into the intima, proliferate and lay down matrix, while endothelium re-covers the new “neointima”.

  • A - the intima is the layer that thickens and narrows the lumen.
  • B - the media supplies the migrating smooth muscle cells; that is the only reading on which it is “responsible”.
  • C - the adventitia plays no part in the lecture's account.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives the media, but 05 - Cellular Stress & Repair (and the chart in 09 - Approach to Anxiety and Stress) attribute luminal narrowing to intimal thickening. The media is defensible only as the source of the smooth muscle cells that move into the intima. On the lecture's wording the answer is A.

b2-w5-module-q56-56.html:
From 10 - Body System Organization (Block 1). Lead time is the interval between diagnosis by a screening program (preclinical phase) and diagnosis when signs and symptoms appear. Screening moves the diagnosis date earlier, so survival measured from diagnosis lengthens even if the patient dies on the same date - longer survival without any fall in mortality.

  • A - survival from diagnosis is exactly the measure lead time inflates; only mortality shows real benefit.
  • B - screening more often adds lead time; it does not prove more cures.
  • C - an invented claim that goes beyond the scenario.

b2-w5-module-q57-57.html:
Length-time bias: a slow-growing tumour spends a long time in the detectable preclinical phase, so periodic screening is more likely to catch it, whereas fast tumours surface as symptoms between screens. Screen-detected cases are therefore enriched for indolent disease and survive longer regardless of the screening - exactly the prostate scenario described.

  • A - the healthy-worker effect is employed populations being healthier than the general one.
  • B - the volunteer effect is people who choose screening being healthier and more health-conscious; the stem is about tumour speed, not who volunteers.
  • D - lead time is earlier diagnosis of the same tumour (Block 1, 10 - Body System Organization); this is about different tumours.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b2-w5-module-q6-6.html:
From 01 - An Introduction to Body Fluids Regulation. ADH acts on the kidney to reabsorb more water and produce less urine, and as that water is retained the plasma osmolarity falls - the solutes become diluted. Excess ADH therefore retains free water out of proportion to sodium, and the measured sodium falls: dilutional hyponatremia.

  • A - the opposite: ADH produces a small volume of concentrated urine; large volumes of dilute urine mean too little ADH.
  • C - in the lecture, raised extracellular K+ is a trigger for the RAAS, not an effect of ADH.
  • D - ADH also vasoconstricts and expands volume, so an excess pushes blood pressure up, not down.

review.t: An Introduction to Body Fluids Regulation

b2-w5-module-q9-9.html:
From 06 - Adult Screening - Diagnostic Pathway. The pathway opens with “Stable? Vitals?”, and the vitals it lists are blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature (plus O2 saturation, which is not among the options). All four are measured at the bedside without a sample and describe circulation, breathing and thermoregulation.

  • A, C, D, E - the four primary vital signs.
  • B - blood glucose is a point-of-care laboratory test, not a vital sign; it is checked when the presentation calls for it, not as part of every set of vitals.

b2-w5-new-q16-16.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Laboratory Medicine. The lecture states that most laboratory errors occur in the pre-analytical phase - everything that happens before the analyser measures the sample: wrong sample type, wrong order of draw, under-filled tubes, tubes not mixed after collection, hemolysis, extreme temperature or improper storage, delayed transport, and long times from collection to analysis.

  • B - the analytical phase is the measurement itself; errors occur there but are the smaller share.
  • C - post-analytical errors (reporting, transcription, interpretation) are also real but not the largest source.
  • D - the lecture is explicit that the phases are not equal.

That is also why 10 - Approach to Abnormal Test Results checks pre-analytical explanations first when a value looks wrong.

b2-w5-new-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The lecture splits blood pressure control in two: the autonomic nervous system is the short-term, rapid response, and hormonal mechanisms are the long-term, slow one. A fall in pressure unloads the high-pressure baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus, and the brain responds by raising heart rate and sympathetic tone to the arterioles - raising CO and TPR, and so MAP (MAP = CO x TPR).

  • A, D - the RAAS and aldosterone are hormonal: renin must generate angiotensin II, and aldosterone works by changing Na+ reabsorption and volume - the slow arm.
  • B - a fall in GFR is a consequence of reduced renal perfusion, and any renal volume-conserving effect is slow, not a reflex.

b2-w5-sa-q1-1.html:
From 09 - Approach to Anxiety and Stress (charted as Effects of Stress and Inflammation on Blood Vessels). Sustained high pressure is hemodynamic stress on the endothelium; the vessel's repair response is intimal thickening, which narrows the lumen and cuts blood flow to the organ the vessel supplies. The complications are therefore vascular, organ by organ: atherosclerosis and MI, cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure, multi-infarct dementia, aortic dissection, cerebrovascular hemorrhage and renal failure.

  • B, C - renal failure and cerebrovascular disease are on the lecture's list.
  • A, E - erectile dysfunction and retinal hemorrhages are not named in the note, but they are the same small-vessel damage in the penile and retinal circulations.
  • D - cirrhosis is a disease of the liver parenchyma, not a consequence of arterial pressure.

b2-w5-sa-q2-2.html:
From 10 - Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees (Block 1). After migration a refugee must adjust to a new language and culture, secure housing and financial stability, and use a health system that is hard to access and poorly understood. Any of these can stop a blood test from happening, so an uncompleted requisition is a prompt to ask about barriers, not a sign of disinterest.

  • A, D - childcare and employment constraints (shift work, lost wages, no one to watch the children) compete with a lab visit during opening hours.
  • B - transit access decides whether she can physically reach the lab.
  • C - the lecture names not understanding the healthcare system and language barriers; a test whose purpose was never explained in her language is easy to set aside.
  • E - each is plausible, so all apply.

review.t: Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees

b2-wb-fom-q76.html:
From 02 - Introduction to Blood Pressure Regulation. The lecture's formula is MAP = DP + 1/3 (SP - DP). Here the pulse pressure is 160 - 93 = 67; a third of it is 22.3; and 93 + 22.3 = 115.3 mmHg.

  • A (114.7), B (121.4), D (109.3) - none follows from the formula.

The check worth remembering: MAP is weighted toward diastolic pressure, so it always sits below the simple average of systolic and diastolic (here 126.5). The abdominal pain in the stem is a distractor; the question is pure arithmetic.

b2-w6-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 07 - Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer. For average-risk adults aged 50-74 (asymptomatic, no high-risk features), the screening test is the FIT - the fecal immunochemical test, which detects human heme (sensitivity 92.3%) - repeated every 2 years.

  • A - an incisional biopsy samples a known lesion; it is diagnostic, never a screen.
  • B - the lecture does list flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy every 10 years as an alternative, which is why this distractor is tempting, but it is not how the average-risk population is typically screened. High-risk patients (prior CRC or adenomatous polyps, IBD, a first-degree relative, FAP or Lynch) sit outside this program altogether.
  • D - false: CRC is on the screening schedule precisely because early detection changes outcomes.

review.t: Well Person Care and Screening for Cancer

b2-w6-module-q25-25.html:
From 05 - Cancer From Macro to Molecular. The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which the lecture names as the first human genetic abnormality directly linked to a cancer: chronic myeloid (myelogenous) leukemia. 03 - Cancer Genetics adds the mechanism - the fusion deletes ABL's regulatory region, turning a proto-oncogene into an oncogene - and the payoff: imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor and the first targeted therapy aimed at it, raised response rates from about 30% with chemotherapy to over 90%.

  • A - multiple myeloma is a plasma-cell neoplasm, not a BCR-ABL1 disease.
  • B, C - colon and breast carcinomas are solid tumours; the lecture's breast examples are HER2 and BRCA1/2, not t(9;22).

b2-w6-new-q16-16.html:
From 06 - Communication of the Pathology Report. When a diagnosis is not clear-cut the pathologist writes a narrative report using a graded vocabulary of malignancy risk. The lecture's scale runs positive → suspicious → atypia (cannot exclude malignancy) → atypia (favour reactive) → negative; reversed for least-to-most:

  • 1 - E, negative for malignancy.
  • 2 - C, atypia present, favour reactive: abnormal cells, but the pathologist leans benign.
  • 3 - A, atypia present, cannot exclude malignancy: abnormal cells with malignancy left open.
  • 4 - B, suspicious for malignancy: probably cancer, short of certainty.
  • 5 - D, positive for malignancy.

The two atypia terms are the trap: favour reactive leans benign, cannot exclude does not.

b2-w6-new-q17-17.html:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics (its interprofessional management table). Numbering the answer list in the order shown, 1 = clinical geneticist through 11 = social worker:

  • A - 2, general surgeon: diagnostic biopsy, removal and staging, lymph node dissection.
  • B - 8, primary care physician: screening, symptom relief, counselling and referrals - the lecture's wording almost exactly.
  • C - 11, social worker: counselling through education, resources and supports, and advocacy in navigating recovery.
  • D - 6, palliative care physician: relieves suffering and improves quality of life in curable, chronic or life-threatening illness - at any stage, not only at the end of life.

The near-miss is C: the Indigenous health navigator (3) also counsels and advocates, but the lecture defines that role as navigating the health care system. The pathologist (7) makes the diagnosis on the tissue but does not perform the biopsy or the removal.

flags.title: The answer list lost its numbers
flags.html: The stem runs the eleven professions together without the numbers the key (A=2; B=8, C=11; D=6) refers to. The mapping above assumes they are numbered 1-11 in the order shown; check it against the original.

b2-w6-new-q7-7.html:
From 03 - Cancer Genetics (the surgical pathology report). The synoptic report is a concise, standardized checklist of the most important findings - the ones that predict outcome and guide treatment and further testing. The lecture lists its contents as specimen, tumour, margins, lymph nodes, stage, additional findings and comments.

  • A - specimen: the site and type of tissue.
  • B - tumour grade is recorded in the tumour section of the checklist.
  • C - margins show whether the excision was complete.
  • D - lymph node involvement feeds the stage.

All four are on the checklist, so E. 06 - Communication of the Pathology Report adds that synoptic reporting suits clear-cut diagnoses, while ambiguous ones get a narrative report.

b2-w6-new-q9-9.html:
Breast cancer 5-year survival falls with stage: essentially 100% at stage 1, about 92-93% at stage 2, about 72-74% at stage 3 and about 22-23% at stage 4 (Canadian Cancer Society figures). The shape follows the staging logic in 02 - Approach to Neoplasia: stage I has no nodal or distant spread, while stage IV means metastasis and is usually incurable.

  • A - false: 90% would put stage 1 below stage 2, which cannot be right.
  • B, C, D - match the published stage figures.
  • E - true; A and E cannot both hold, and E is the correct figure.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

The stage-specific survival figures come from Canadian Cancer Society statistics, not a vault note.

b2-w7-meds2024-q15-15.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Basic ADLs are the self-care tasks, DEATH: Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting/continence, Hygiene. Instrumental ADLs are the more cognitively demanding tasks of running a household, SHAFT: Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/transportation.

  • C - housework is the H of SHAFT, an IADL.
  • A, B, D - toileting, dressing and eating are all DEATH items.

The distinction matters clinically: because IADLs need more cognitive skill, they are the first to need help as cognition declines (the Clinical Frailty Scale's “mildly frail” step is defined by it).

b2-w7-ra-q2-2.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Delirium (the embedded delirium note's risk factors). The material separates predisposing factors, which make a patient vulnerable, from precipitants (DIMESPPP), which tip them over. The predisposing list: cognitive impairment, comorbidity burden, age over 65, male sex, living in an institution, functional impairment, prior delirium, hearing and visual impairment, reduced education, alcohol use disorder, dehydration or malnutrition, and polypharmacy.

  • A - pre-existing dementia is cognitive impairment, the first item.
  • D - hearing impairment is on the list; it is also why glasses and hearing aids are part of management.
  • B, C, E - Crohn's disease, osteoarthritis and smoking are not named risk factors (arthritic pain would count as a precipitant, not a predisposition).

b2-w7-ra-q4-4.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Delirium. The lecture lists delirium's consequences as a longer length of stay; long-term cognitive and functional decline; higher mortality; and a higher risk of institutionalization, falls and ulcers, nursing time, and developing dementia.

  • B, E - both are on the list.
  • A - reversed: delirium increases nursing time per patient.
  • C - reversed: nothing lowers restraint use here; agitation and fall risk push it the other way.
  • D - stroke is a structural cause of delirium (the S of DIMESPPP), not a listed consequence.

b2-w7-sa-q13-13.html:
From 01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease. Ageism is negative (or positive) stereotyping, prejudice or discrimination on the basis of age. The lecture's examples in care are clinicians under-treating illness as “normal aging” and patients under-reporting symptoms for the same reason. The keyed options are stereotypes of that kind:

  • A - “older adults overuse the system” frames their care as a burden.
  • C - “poor historians” leads clinicians to discount what the patient reports.
  • B - not a common ageist belief; if anything substance use is assumed to be a younger person's issue.
  • D - a statistic about living arrangements, not a belief.
  • E - as worded, the opposite of the ageist assumption, which is that illness is an expected part of aging.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

01 - Healthy Aging vs. Disease defines ageism but does not list these five beliefs. If option E originally read “should expect to live with illness”, it would be an ageist belief and the key would be incomplete; check the source.

b2-w7-sa-q2-2.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Basic ADLs are DEATH - Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene - and the options use synonyms for some of them:

  • B Mobility and I Transfers - both are Ambulating, which the ADL note defines as moving from one position to another and walking independently.
  • E Grooming - Hygiene (bathing, grooming, dental, nail and hair care).
  • F Eating and J Toileting - named directly.
  • A, C, D, G, H - managing medications, shopping, cooking, housework and managing finances are IADLs (SHAFT plus medications), the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-w7-sa-q6-6.html:
From 08 - Frailty and Falls. The Clinical Frailty Scale turns on dependence. CFS 5, mildly frail, is more evident slowing with help needed for higher-order IADLs while basic ADLs remain independent. Mr Sandos's spouse has had to take over finances and medications because of his mistakes, he is independent in basic ADLs, and he walks with a cane after a fall. The lecture also notes that frailty corresponds to the degree of dementia, and his is mild.

  • A (3) - managing well means controlled medical problems and no dependence at all.
  • B (4) - vulnerable means not dependent on others for daily help; he now is, for IADLs.
  • D (6) - moderately frail needs help with all outside activities and housekeeping, stairs and bathing; his basic ADLs are intact.

Cooking and cleaning do not count against him: 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment says to judge change, and his spouse always did those.

b2-wb-fom-q94.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Ambulating is the A of DEATH, a basic ADL: moving from one position to another (transfers) and walking independently. It is physical self-care, not a household task that needs planning.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q95.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Cooking is the F of SHAFT (Food preparation), an IADL: it needs planning, sequencing and safety judgment, not just the physical ability to feed oneself. Do not confuse it with eating, which is a basic ADL.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q96.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Dressing is the D of DEATH, a basic ADL: selecting appropriate clothing and putting it on.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q97.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Eating is the E of DEATH, a basic ADL: the ability to feed oneself. Preparing the food is a different task - cooking is an IADL.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q98.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Finances are the A of SHAFT (Accounting), an IADL: the ability to pay bills and manage money, a cognitively demanding task of running a household rather than self-care.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q99.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Hygiene is the H of DEATH, a basic ADL: bathing and grooming oneself and keeping up dental, nail and hair care.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q100.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Managing medications is the extra M the SHAFT note adds to the IADLs: obtaining medications and taking them as prescribed. It depends on memory and organization rather than physical self-care.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q101.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Shopping is the S of SHAFT, an IADL: acquiring food and clothing.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q103.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Using the telephone is a T of SHAFT, an IADL, along with mail, internet and email.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q104.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Toileting is the T of DEATH, a basic ADL: getting to and from the toilet, using it appropriately and cleaning oneself, plus continence - control of bladder and bowel.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q105.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Transportation is a T of SHAFT, an IADL: driving or using public transport.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

b2-wb-fom-q102.html:
From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment. Social engagement is not one of the named SHAFT items, but it belongs on the IADL side by the same logic: it is a higher-order activity of living in the community, not basic self-care of the body - and none of the DEATH items (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene) covers it.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

The vault's ADL and IADL lists (DEATH, SHAFT plus medications) do not name social engagement; the IADL classification follows the key and the logic of the split, not a lecture statement.

b2-w8-module-q37-37.html:
From 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response. D is the false statement because the enzyme is wrong: grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4, the enzyme that metabolizes felodipine (04 - Introduction to Pharmacokinetics: bioavailability rises about threefold), and erythromycin is a CYP3A4 inhibitor that raises felodipine levels 2.5-fold. CYP2C9 is the lecture's warfarin enzyme.

  • A - true: creatinine clearance predicts renal clearance (penicillin: usual dose above 50 mL/min, 75% at 10-50, 20-50% below 10).
  • B - true: in severe liver disease reduced albumin production increases drug distribution to tissues, since less drug is protein-bound.
  • C - true: calcium, magnesium and iron form complexes with some drugs and decrease their absorption, so milk can.

b2-w8-module-q38-38.html:
From 08 - Therapeutics Across the Lifespan and 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response.

  • Increase: sensitivity to opioids (A; benzodiazepines too, so more sedation); body fat (B; the fat-to-water ratio rises, so fat-soluble drugs such as digoxin and benzodiazepines are stored and released for longer); risk of polypharmacy (I).
  • Decrease: liver blood flow (C) and liver enzyme metabolism (D), so hepatically cleared drugs such as diazepam linger; GFR (F), so renally cleared drugs need dose reduction; serum albumin (G), leaving more free drug; body water (H).
  • Creatinine (E) - keyed as increasing, but see the flag: the lecture warns that in older adults a normal creatinine does not mean a normal GFR.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key puts creatinine among the factors that increase with age. 08 - Therapeutics Across the Lifespan lists a falling GFR with the caveat normal creatinine ≠ normal GFR: serum creatinine tends to stay in the normal range while GFR declines, which is exactly why it misleads. No vault note says creatinine rises with age. If the option meant creatinine clearance, that decreases, which also contradicts the key.

b2-wb-fom-q131.html:
From 05 - Principles of Clinical Pharmacology (its prescription abbreviations table).

  • A PO - 5, orally.
  • B BID - 1, twice a day; the frequency series is q.d., b.i.d., t.i.d., q.i.d. for once to four times a day.
  • C PRN - 2, as needed; 01 - Approach To Prescribing adds that a PRN order still needs a maximum frequency.
  • D AC - 4, before meals; p.c. is after meals.
  • E OD - 3, right eye, paired with O.S. (left eye) and O.U. (both eyes).

OD is the trap: it reads like “once daily”, but the lecture's once-daily abbreviation is q.d.

flags.title: The meanings were fused onto option E
flags.html: The five meanings were run into option E during transcription, so E reads “OD 1) Twice a day 2) As needed ...”. The intended list is 1 Twice a day, 2 As needed, 3 Right eye, 4 Before meal, 5 Orally.

b3-w9-module-q1-1:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia. Hemolysis releases heme, globin and iron, and leaves a fixed chemical fingerprint: high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin. Those three are products or scavengers of the destroyed cell itself.

  • A LDH - a cytoplasmic enzyme spilled into plasma when RBCs lyse.
  • C haptoglobin - falls because it binds and clears free hemoglobin.
  • D indirect bilirubin - heme is degraded to bilirubin by the reticuloendothelial system.
  • B reticulocytes - also high in hemolysis, but as the marrow's response to the anemia, not a marker of hemoglobin breakdown; the lecture uses the retic count to separate increased turnover (bleeding or hemolysis) from decreased production.
b3-w9-module-q10-10:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias. An acidic environment in the stomach increases iron absorption, so vitamin C helps; 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome adds that ascorbic acid helps duodenal cytochrome B reduce Fe3+ to the absorbable Fe2+.

  • A with food - dietary chelators reduce absorption, per the lecture.
  • B antacid - raises gastric pH, removing the acid that aids absorption.
  • D enteric coating - iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, so a coating that delays release past that site works against absorption.

b3-w9-module-q11-11.html:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias and 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome. The main route for B12 is intrinsic-factor dependent: IF binds B12 after pancreatic proteases free it from R protein, and the IF-B12 complex is taken up at receptors in the terminal ileum. A small fraction is absorbed along the gut without IF by passive diffusion, which is why high-dose oral B12 (1 mg in the treatment table) can work.

  • B - B12 absorption does not depend on folate; they share a role in DNA synthesis, not a transporter.
  • C - green leafy vegetables are the lecture's source of folate; B12 comes from meat, fish, eggs, dairy and bacterial synthesis.
  • D - replacement produces a hematologic response (reticulocytosis) within days rather than taking over a week.

flags.title: Partly not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: The vault notes describe only IF-mediated ileal absorption; none mentions passive diffusion of B12 or the timing of the hematologic response, so the reasoning for A and D is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w9-module-q2-2:
From 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia. The smear for G6PD deficiency shows bite cells, blister cells and Heinz bodies: without glutathione, oxidants (infection, antimalarials, sulfonamides, fava beans) denature hemoglobin, which precipitates on the membrane and is plucked off by the spleen.

  • A sickle cell anemia - sickle cells (elongated, pointed ends).
  • B MDS - a marrow disorder; its film clue is hypogranular, hyposegmented neutrophils (pseudo-Pelger-Huët).
  • D malaria - direct parasitization of RBCs, which lyse as merozoites escape; no oxidant bite or blister.
b3-w9-module-q3-3:
From 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia. Spherocytes are shared by hereditary spherocytosis and warm AIHA: in both, membrane is removed (a structural defect in HS, IgG-coated membrane taken by splenic macrophages in warm AIHA) and the remaining cell rounds into a sphere. The DAT separates them - negative in HS, positive (IgG) in warm AIHA.

  • A DIC - microangiopathic, so schistocytes.
  • C G6PD - bite and blister cells, Heinz bodies.
  • D thalassemia - target cells and basophilic stippling (03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia).
b3-w9-module-q9-9:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias (and the treatment table in 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia). The iron still has to be replaced, only by another route: IV iron is indicated for inadequate absorption (including intolerance of oral forms) and rapid blood loss.

  • B transfusion - reserved for brisk, clinically significant blood loss, not as routine iron replacement.
  • C vitamin B12 - treats megaloblastic anemia; it does not correct an iron deficit.
  • D phlebotomy - removes red cells and iron, the opposite of what an iron-deficient patient needs.
b3-w9-new-q19-19:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias and 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome. Folate does all three jobs:

  • A DNA synthesis - as tetrahydrofolate it is the cofactor for uracil → thymine; deficiency hits rapidly dividing cells.
  • B RBC synthesis - that is why its lack produces megaloblastic anemia (large erythroid precursors with immature nuclei).
  • C methylation - methyl-THF donates its methyl group via methionine synthase (homocysteine → methionine), the pathway behind the body's methylation reactions, DNA included.

So D is the complete answer; E (A and B only) drops the methylation role.
b3-w9-new-q22-22:
From the vault's sickle cell disease reference note (the lecture notes cover crises but not lifestyle advice). Vaso-occlusive episodes are triggered by dehydration, cooling of the skin, stress and infection, because cold slows flow and promotes sickling and vasoconstriction. The advice is therefore a warm compress, never a cold one, on an injury, and not swimming in cold water.

  • A - it is cold water, not warm, that patients should avoid.
  • B - a warm compress is the recommended physical measure.
  • D - wrong, because C is correct advice.

b3-w9-new-q7-7.html:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Microcytosis means Hb synthesis has fallen behind cell division, from too little heme or too little globin. The differential is TAILS: thalassemia, anemia of chronic inflammation, iron deficiency, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia.

  • A iron deficiency, C sideroblastic, D lead - all reduce heme synthesis (lead acts through the sideroblastic mechanism), so F is right.
  • B hemolytic anemias - classed with the normocytic anemias (the D of ABCD in 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia) and are not a heme or globin synthesis defect, so they are not on TAILS.
  • E - fails because it includes B.

flags.title: Hemolysis is not always normocytic
flags.html: 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia says hemolytic anemia can be microcytic, normocytic or macrocytic depending on the cause, and thalassemia itself involves hemolysis. The key holds for hemolysis as a category of causes, but B is not strictly impossible.

b3-w9-ra-q9-9:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. The discriminator is the normal RDW: thalassemia makes uniformly small cells, and its smear shows target cells and basophilic stippling, with normal platelets and an RBC count higher than in iron deficiency.

  • B iron deficiency - the Schulich pattern is high RDW (anisocytosis), low ferritin and often high platelets.
  • C hypothyroidism - an endocrine cause of macrocytosis (05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia).
  • D renal disease with impaired EPO (“APO” is a typo) - underproduction with no marrow pathology, a normocytic picture (04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia).

b3-w9-sa-q10-10.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia and 08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome. MDS is a marrow diagnosis: anemia without reticulocytosis leads to a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, and an abnormal marrow names MDS. The workup is CBC, ferritin, BM aspirate/biopsy, flow cytometry and cytogenetics, which feed the IPSS score that then decides treatment (supportive care for lower risk, hypomethylating agents or HSCT for higher).

  • A - chemotherapy before a tissue diagnosis and risk score skips both steps.
  • B, C - observation without a marrow sample cannot confirm MDS; an abdominal ultrasound adds nothing to the diagnosis in a symptomatic man with Hb 76.

b3-w9-sa-q6-6.html:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. A sleep study is the investigation for obstructive sleep apnea: the erythrocytosis history asks about snoring, gasping or stopped breathing at night, and the workup lists a sleep study to confirm OSA as a hypoxic, secondary cause.

  • A generalized anxiety disorder, B acute insomnia - clinical diagnoses from the history; polysomnography looks for a sleep-breathing or sleep-architecture disorder, not worry or short-term sleeplessness.
  • D hypothyroidism - a thyroid problem diagnosed with blood work, not a sleep study.

b3-w9-sa-q7-7:
From 05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia (prevention: folic acid in pregnancy) and the supplement table in 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia (pregnancy dose 0.4 mg). Folate is the one nutrient given routinely to everyone pregnant or planning pregnancy, because demand rises and folate stores last only months.

  • B iron - requirements rise in pregnancy (3-4 mg/day), but iron is replaced when deficiency is found, not uniformly before conception.
  • C vitamin D, D essential fatty acids, E calcium - none is the universal preconception supplement the lectures name.
b3-wb-heme-q1:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis. Of the four, only erythroblasts are nucleated - they are the nucleated RBC precursors in the marrow, and they are absent from normal peripheral blood.

  • Reticulocytes - have extruded the nucleus; they keep only RNA and ribosomes (seen on supravital stain).
  • Erythrocytes - no nucleus, organelles or granules.
  • Thrombocytes - fragments of megakaryocytes; like RBCs they lack a nucleus, though they do have granules.

Every option that adds reticulocytes, erythrocytes or thrombocytes (A, B, D, E) is therefore wrong.
b3-wb-heme-q102:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology. The 4 Rs of radiobiology explain why fractionation works: repair of sublethal damage between fractions, repopulation between fractions, redistribution of cells into radiosensitive cell-cycle phases, and reoxygenation of hypoxic tumour cells. Repair and repopulation spare normal tissue; redistribution and reoxygenation sensitize the tumour.

  • A - the recycling slogan, not radiobiology.
  • C - swaps in “recalibration” for repopulation.
  • D - drops repopulation for “review”.
b3-wb-heme-q14:
From 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias. The liver holds 2-5 mg of B12 against a requirement of only 1-2 mcg per day, so stores last 3-5 years (08 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome agrees; 05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia rounds it to 3-4). That is why B12 deficiency after a diet change or gastrectomy appears years later.

  • A 1 month, B 6 months - closer to folate, whose 10-12 mg store lasts only 3-4 months.
  • C 1-2 years - too short for a store roughly a thousand times the daily need.

b3-wb-heme-q25.html:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Alpha thalassemia is common in Southeast Asian and African populations; beta thalassemia in Mediterranean populations. Option C reads the blanks as “South-East Asia [and] Africa” and “Mediterranean”.

  • A - puts Africa nowhere and places Europe with alpha.
  • B - Australia is not an alpha-thal population, and beta is not SE Asian.
  • D - reverses the pair, putting Mediterranean on alpha.

flags.title: The two blanks were run together
flags.html: Each option's two answers lost their separator during transcription (e.g. “South-East Asia Africa, Mediterranean”), so where the first blank ends is inferred. The bank also stores no machine-readable key for this question; only the key line gives C.

b3-wb-heme-q9:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Sideroblastic anemia is iron trapped in mitochondria around the precursor nucleus. Its acquired causes are toxins, vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency, MDS, chronic alcohol, drugs (anti-TB, alkylating chemotherapy) and lead poisoning - so B, C and D are all associated.

A hydroxyurea is not on that list. The lectures meet it as a treatment for sickle cell disease (04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia), where it raises HbF; it is also a drug cause of macrocytosis, not of ringed sideroblasts.
b3-wb-heme-q98:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The lecture's features concerning for malignancy include every option: systemic symptoms such as weight loss over 10% (with fever, night sweats), generalized lymphadenopathy, an abnormal CXR (mediastinal mass, hilar adenopathy) and an abnormal CBC (lymphoblasts, cytopenias). Other red flags are fixed, non-tender, matted nodes of 2 cm or more, supraclavicular location, and nodes that do not settle after antibiotics.

So none of A-D can be the one that is not a red flag, which is what E's double negative says. Context matters: over 98% of enlarged nodes in primary care are benign, and these flags are what pick out the few needing biopsy.

b3-w10-module-q12-12.html:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (its VTE section). Duration depends on why the clot formed, and the shortest course in the lecture is a minimum of 3 months for a VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor.

  • A 10 days - the scale of post-operative prophylaxis (7-10 days), not treatment.
  • C 6 months - the minimum for cancer-associated VTE, and the review point for idiopathic VTE in women (HERDOO2).
  • D indefinite - for idiopathic VTE in men (and women with HERDOO2 of 2 or more), not the minimum.

b3-w10-module-q13-13.html:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia, which lists the VTE agents by setting: LMWH for cancer and pregnancy, warfarin for renal failure. Warfarin works through vitamin K epoxide reductase and is not dependent on renal clearance, and it is monitored with the INR.

  • A LMWH - renally eliminated; half-life is prolonged in renal failure.
  • B fondaparinux - renal elimination and contraindicated in severe renal failure.
  • D edoxaban - a direct Xa inhibitor, renally eliminated and prolonged in renal failure.

(Unfractionated heparin, cleared by the RES in the liver, is also safe in renal failure, but it is not offered here.)

b3-w10-module-q14-14.html:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (the VTE algorithm). When DVT is likely on the Wells score, the next test is compression ultrasound: non-invasive, and a positive scan leads to anticoagulation.

  • A D-dimer - useful only when negative, to exclude VTE in an unlikely patient; a positive result means nothing, so it does not help once DVT is likely.
  • B CTPA - the test for suspected PE, not a leg clot.
  • C ascending venogram - the gold standard, but invasive with radiation, so not the first test.

flags.title: The case was lost
flags.html: The stem is only “What will you do next?”; the vignette it followed did not survive transcription. The explanation assumes the missing case was a suspected DVT with a likely Wells score, which is what the key implies.

b3-w10-module-q16-16:
From 02 - Hemostasis. The cell-based model runs on the activated platelet surface in four phases:

  • Initiation (A) - tissue factor + FVIIa activate a little FIX and FX, making a small amount of thrombin.
  • Amplification (F) - that thrombin activates FV, FVIII, FXI and more platelets.
  • Propagation (E) - tenase (IXa + VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa + Va) generate a burst of thrombin.
  • Stabilization (D) - thrombin turns fibrinogen to fibrin and activates FXIII, which cross-links it.

B adhesion (vWF-GPIb) and C aggregation (fibrinogen-GPIIb/IIIa) are steps of primary hemostasis, the platelet plug, not phases of coagulation.
b3-w10-module-q23-23:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. This is ITP: acute, very severe thrombocytopenia (below 10 carries spontaneous bleeding risk) with mucocutaneous bleeding - epistaxis, purpura, petechiae - and every other CBC line normal. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

  • A splenomegaly - sequestration gives only moderate thrombocytopenia, and bleeding is rare.
  • B DIC - needs an underlying trigger (sepsis, malignancy, trauma, obstetric) and deranged coagulation, with bleeding and clotting together.
  • D TTP - the patient is very sick, with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes) and neurologic features, so the other parameters would not be normal.

b3-w10-module-q4-4.html:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (its VTE section). VTE follows Virchow's triad - stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability. Surgery and trauma (10-20% of VTE, with hip fracture and arthroplasty the highest risk) and cancer (30% of patients) are listed risks.

D is the exception: a patient who is ambulating, with or without a walker, is moving, and early mobilization is the lecture's first measure for preventing VTE. Prophylaxis is given only while a patient is not ambulatory.

b3-w10-module-q7-7.html:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (DVT imaging). Compression ultrasound is the non-invasive test used to confirm DVT; a positive scan leads to anticoagulation.

  • A ascending venogram - the gold standard, but invasive and needs radiation, so it is not the routine confirmatory test.
  • C CT leg - not a DVT test in the lecture.
  • D D-dimer - can only exclude VTE when negative; a positive result is non-specific and confirms nothing.

b3-w10-module-q8-8:
From 02 - Hemostasis. D-dimer is the breakdown product of cross-linked fibrin, made when plasmin lyses a clot. A negative D-dimer rules out VTE; a raised one is non-specific (surgery, trauma, cancer, infection, pregnancy, old age, DIC).

  • B fibrinogen - the substrate thrombin converts to fibrin; its level does not exclude a clot.
  • C thrombin - the central enzyme of coagulation, not a rule-out test.
  • D plasmin - the fibrinolytic enzyme that produces D-dimers; it is not what is measured.

b3-w10-module-q9-9.html:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (PE imaging). The two non-invasive confirmatory tests are the V/Q scan, showing a ventilation-perfusion mismatch (preferred for younger women and renal failure), and the CT pulmonary angiogram, the default test.

  • A pulmonary angiogram - the gold standard, but invasive (right heart catheterization), which the question excludes.
  • D D-dimer - rules PE out when negative; a positive result means nothing and cannot confirm the diagnosis.

b3-w10-ra-q6-6.html:
Blood products in Canada are collected, tested and supplied by two national operators: Canadian Blood Services for every province and territory except Quebec, and Héma-Québec within Quebec. 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient covers what happens next - the hospital blood bank tests and issues the right product to the right patient - but not who supplies it.

  • A Canadian Red Cross - ran the blood system until the tainted-blood inquiry led to its replacement in 1998.
  • C International Red Cross - does not run national blood supply.
  • D hospital blood banks - they store, crossmatch and issue units; they are not the supplier.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w10-sa-q8-8.html:
Partly from 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient, which makes the blood bank responsible for issuing the right product and the nursing staff for giving it to the right patient at the bedside. The vault's acute hemolytic transfusion reaction note adds only that ABO incompatibility is often human error.

The single commonest error is at sample collection: the tube is drawn from one patient but labelled as another (wrong blood in tube). The lab then types and crossmatches correctly against the wrong person's blood, so every later check passes.

  • A laboratory testing errors, C supplier mislabelling - rare, because testing and unit labelling are controlled and double-checked.
  • D bedside misidentification - a real cause, but less frequent than a mislabelled sample.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w11-module-q10-10.html:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia.

  • A - true as intended: neutropenia is an ANC below 1.5 × 109/L, graded mild 1-1.5, moderate 0.5-0.99 and severe below 0.5.
  • B - true: after stabilizing and drawing blood and urine cultures, start empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (IV imipenem or piperacillin-tazobactam), adding vancomycin for line or skin infection or instability.
  • C - true: febrile neutropenia (a single temperature of 38.3°C, or 38.0°C or more sustained over 1 hour) is an oncologic emergency and the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy.

flags.title: Statement A seems to have lost its “<”
flags.html: A reads “an ANC is 0.5 × 109/L”. In the lecture's grading an ANC of exactly 0.5 is moderate; severe is below 0.5. The less-than sign was probably lost in transcription, and A is true only in that form.

b3-w11-module-q11-11:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis and 10 - Pharmacological Treatment of Anemias. After birth EPO comes from the interstitial fibroblasts of the kidney (about 90%), switched on by hypoxia-inducible factor when tissue oxygen falls.

  • B bone marrow - EPO's target: erythroid progenitors carry the receptor and mature instead of undergoing apoptosis.
  • C liver - the source in fetal and perinatal life, and only a small share in adults; the adult liver makes thrombopoietin.
  • D lung - not a source; lung disease raises EPO only indirectly, through hypoxia.
b3-w11-module-q12-12:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. In primary (bone marrow) erythrocytosis the marrow is autonomous and EPO-independent. The excess red cells feed back on the kidney to make less EPO, so the serum EPO level is low. That is the one test the lecture uses to split primary from secondary.

  • A fails: negative feedback does change EPO. It falls.
  • B describes secondary erythrocytosis, where hypoxia or a tumour drives renal EPO up, giving a normal or high level.
  • C fails: the liver is the EPO source only in fetal and perinatal life. After birth it comes from renal interstitial fibroblasts, and hepatic EPO in an adult means a tumour (HCC), which is a secondary cause.
b3-w11-module-q13-13:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. Polycythemia vera is primary, acquired erythrocytosis. A somatic JAK2 mutation makes the marrow autonomous and EPO is low. Secondary erythrocytosis is the opposite: a normal marrow driven by normal or high EPO.

  • A chronic lung disease (COPD) causes systemic hypoxia, which drives EPO. Secondary.
  • C renal cell carcinoma is one of the pathologic EPO-secreting tumours, along with HCC, cerebellar hemangioblastoma and pheochromocytoma. Secondary.
  • D testosterone falls under the lecture's drug causes (EPO, androgens). Secondary.
b3-w11-module-q14-14:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. PV is driven by an acquired JAK2 mutation. JAK2 V617F is found in 90-95% of cases, and JAK2 exon 12 mutations account for most of the rest. Both appear in PV major criterion 3.

  • B BCR-ABL (the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22)) defines CML. The MPNs other than CML are Philadelphia-negative.
  • D MPL and E CALR are the other drivers of ET and primary myelofibrosis, alongside JAK2 in 50-60%. They are not listed for PV.
b3-w11-module-q17-17:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis (MPN table) and 06 - Approach to Thrombocytosis. ET carries the best outlook of the MPNs. The lecture gives untreated prognosis as slightly below normal and treated as close to normal, so a near-normal lifespan is the expected course.

  • A is backwards: untreated PV survives 2-3 years, and myelofibrosis arises from ET/PV and is the more serious disease.
  • C describes PV, where all three lines can rise. In ET the platelets rise markedly, RBCs are normal, and WBCs are normal or mildly raised.
  • D fails: ET is Philadelphia-negative. Only CML is positive.
b3-w11-module-q24-24:
From 10 - In-Class and 04 - Approach to Leukemia. Auer rods are the pink, needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions that mark a blast as myeloid. APL (AML M3) blasts carry many of them, bundled into “faggot cells”, and multiple (2+) Auer rods per blast is the lecture's suggestive feature of APL.

  • A, B and C (“our needles”, “hour rods”, “hour needles”) are homophone distractors built on the eponym (Auer). None of them is a real structure.
b3-w11-module-q29-29:
From 06 - Approach to Thrombocytosis. Secondary (reactive) thrombocytosis is more common than primary, so an MPN is not the likely diagnosis in a patient with a high platelet count. That makes C the incorrect statement. The workup assesses secondary causes first.

  • A is correct: infection is a leading reactive cause, and bacterial infection is the most common.
  • B is correct: red cell fragments (schistocytes, microspherocytes) can be miscounted as platelets by the Coulter counter. That spurious thrombocytosis is “extremely rare” in the lecture's words.

b3-w11-module-q31-31.html:
From 06 - Approach to Thrombocytosis. The approach runs: repeat the CBC, assess secondary causes, then consider a primary cause only if no secondary cause is found. In practice the two are assessed together.

  • A is correct: a CBC and peripheral smear are core investigations, with iron studies, a hemolytic screen and CRP.
  • B is incorrect: it reverses the order. Secondary causes are far more common, so they are sought first.
  • C is incorrect: “all” is too absolute. Extreme thrombocytosis (>1000) can cause an acquired von Willebrand defect, which raises bleeding risk, so ASA is not automatic in every patient.

flags.title: Option C is not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: 06 - Approach to Thrombocytosis leaves ET management blank, and no FoM note discusses ASA in extreme thrombocytosis or acquired von Willebrand syndrome. The reasoning for C is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w11-module-q32-32.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 10 - In-Class. Clonal thrombocytosis comes from an MPN (ET, PV, PMF, CML), and the MPNs' main danger is thrombosis. The in-class session calls them cancers that “mostly just increase the risk of blood clots”. PV management is built around preventing it with ASA and a hematocrit target, and its complications are arterial and venous clots. Reactive thrombocytosis resolves when its cause is treated and is not framed as a thrombotic risk.

  • B (False) fails: the platelet count alone does not carry the clot risk. What carries it is the clonal, abnormal megakaryopoiesis behind it.

flags.title: Only partly covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No note directly compares thrombotic risk in clonal versus reactive thrombocytosis. The answer is inferred from the MPN material in 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 10 - In-Class.

b3-w11-module-q39-39.html:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology (Week 12, research-methods section). The lecture draws the line cleanly: chance = random error; bias = systematic error. Bias is minimized by randomization, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis.

  • A confounding is a distortion from a third variable. It is associated with the exposure, is a risk factor for the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway. It is not a design or conduct error as such.
  • C interaction (effect modification) is a real difference in effect across strata, not an error.
  • D stratification is an analytic technique for handling confounding, not an error.

b3-w11-module-q4-4:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. In a child, lymphocytosis is almost always reactive. By far the most common cause is infection, and EBV mononucleosis is the classic one in the young, diagnosed by the Monospot test. The history point the lecture stresses is age: CLL is not a disease of the young.

  • A flow cytometry establishes clonality. It is kept for lymphocytosis that persists after 4-6 weeks with no secondary cause.
  • C autoimmune testing and D malignancy screening belong to the broader workup, not the first test in a 10-year-old.
b3-w11-module-q5-5:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Reactive lymphocytosis usually clears. If it persists (repeat in 4-6 weeks) with no secondary cause, suspect a chronic lymphoproliferative disorder. In an older man that is most likely CLL. The confirming step is to show clonality by flow cytometry on the peripheral blood (CLL: CD5, CD19, dim CD20, CD23, light-chain restriction).

  • A cytogenetics (FISH, p53) refines prognosis once the diagnosis is made. It does not establish it.
  • B autoimmune testing looks for a secondary cause, and the stem says none was found.
  • C CT stages disease. It does not prove clonality.
b3-w11-module-q6-6:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. The lecture's benign causes of eosinophilia come first because they are common: drug reaction (penicillins and other antibiotics), allergic disorders (asthma, eczema), pulmonary disease, parasitic infection, and collagen vascular disease or vasculitis.

  • B lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) and E/F leukemia or myeloproliferative neoplasm are the malignant eosinophilias. They are considered only after the common benign causes are excluded.
b3-w11-module-q7-7:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia.

  • A is correct: neutrophils are granulocytes, one of the two categories of leukocyte.
  • B is incorrect: leukopenia is most commonly due to low neutrophils, because neutrophils are the most abundant WBC. Lymphopenia is only an occasional cause.
  • C is correct: the lecture says neutropenia “is used interchangeably with leukopenia because it is the most common cause.”
b3-w11-module-q8-8:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia.

  • A is incorrect as the lecture frames it: counts of the five leukocyte types, the neutrophil count among them, come from the differential, not the total WBC on a basic CBC.
  • B is incorrect: constitutional neutropenia, which is linked to ethnic background, is benign and not associated with an increased risk of infection.
  • C is correct: B12 deficiency, like folate and copper deficiency and malnutrition, is a nutritional cause of acquired neutropenia.
b3-w11-module-q9-9:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia. Severe neutropenia (ANC <0.5) opens the door to three classes of infection, so any statement restricting it to one class is wrong.

  • A is correct: fungal infection (Candida, Aspergillus, mucormycosis) is listed.
  • B is incorrect: gram-negatives (E. coli, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella) matter, but so do gram-positives (S. aureus, streptococci, enterococci), fungi and viral reactivation. “Only” is the error.
  • C is correct: reactivation of HSV, CMV and VZV is a listed complication.

b3-w11-new-q1-1.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. Macrophages live for months rather than hours, and the lecture credits them with extra killing tools that neutrophils lack: acidification of the phagosome by vacuolar ATPase, iron and manganese efflux, copper and zinc influx, and reactive nitrogen intermediates.

  • B fails: nitric oxide synthase making nitrogen radicals is listed under M1 macrophages, not neutrophils.
  • D fails: neutrophils are polymorphonuclear, with a multi-lobed nucleus.
  • A is also true: both are phagocytes, and the lecture contrasts them with NK cells, which “DO NOT phagocytose like neutrophils or macrophages”.

flags.title: Option A is also true
flags.html: 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs supports A (both macrophages and neutrophils phagocytose) as well as the keyed C. The stem asks for similarities and differences but allows one answer, so the question has two defensible choices.

b3-w11-new-q11-11:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Low EPO puts this in the primary (marrow-autonomous) group, and acquired primary erythrocytosis is PV. V617F is found in only 90-95% of PV. JAK2 exon 12 mutations are the other qualifying lesion in major criterion 3, so a negative V617F does not exclude PV.

  • A overreaches for the same reason: exon 12 testing is still pending.
  • C fails: EPO receptor mutations (ECYT1) are a congenital primary cause, and congenital causes are very uncommon.
  • D fails: secondary erythrocytosis has normal or high EPO, not low.
b3-w11-new-q13-13:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. Secondary erythrocytosis needs something that drives EPO: hypoxia or an EPO-secreting lesion. A lipoma does neither. It is a benign fatty tumour with no EPO production.

  • A high altitude and B obstructive sleep apnea both cause systemic hypoxia, which drives renal EPO.
  • C pheochromocytoma is on the lecture's list of pathologic EPO producers, with RCC, HCC and cerebellar hemangioblastoma.

b3-w11-new-q2-2.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. Neutrophils kill by iron restriction, by damaging the cell wall and membrane, and by oxidation with toxic free radicals. The keyed C casts the free radicals' role as disabling the bacterial respiratory and energy machinery.

  • A fails: NADPH oxidase does not act alone. Its superoxide becomes H2O2, which myeloperoxidase combines with a halide to make hypochlorite. The lecture calls it the NADPH oxidase/myeloperoxidase system.
  • D fails: an NADPH oxidase defect (chronic granulomatous disease) leaves phagocytosed bacteria undestroyed. The defect is in killing, not migration.
  • B is not addressed in the notes. See the flag.

flags.title: The key is not supported by the lecture, and B may also be true
flags.html: 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs never says free radicals target bacterial cytochromes, so the keyed C is unverified. Option B looks transcription-damaged: “OH-” has probably lost its radical dot (OH·, the hydroxyl radical). As written, it is the textbook contrast between a highly reactive hydroxyl radical and a comparatively weak oxidant, H2O2, and so may also be true. Check the source before relying on the key.

b3-w11-new-q3-3.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. PAMPs are recognized by the innate system through germline-encoded PRRs such as TLRs. Adaptive immunity recognizes antigens, the fine structural detail of molecules, through somatically recombined, clonal TCRs and BCRs. So C is false.

  • A: healthy cells express MHC I, which engages the NK inhibitory receptor, so the NK cell does not kill. That is the lecture's mechanism.
  • B: PRRs are found on the cell surface (TLR 2, 4, 5, 6) and on endosomes (TLR 3, 7, 8, 9).
  • D is true: TLR 3, 7, 8 and 9 recognize microbial and viral nucleic acids.

flags.title: Option B's wording does not match the lecture
flags.html: 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs places PRRs on the cell surface and on endosomes (intracellular), not “extracellularly”. The word may be a transcription error for “intracellularly”. Soluble extracellular PRRs do exist, but the note does not cover them. Either way, C is the clearly false statement.

b3-w11-new-q4-4:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. All three are on the lecture's list of emergencies. The hematologist wants to hear about them the day an acute leukemia is found.

  • A DIC is especially tied to APL, whose promyelocyte granules release procoagulant and fibrinolytic activity. Early APL deaths are mostly from hemorrhage, often intracerebral.
  • B leukostasis: large, sticky blasts lodge in small vessels, causing dyspnea, hypoxia, confusion and visual change. It is managed with fluids, leukapheresis and cytoreduction.
  • C tumour lysis: high K, PO4 and urate with low Ca, leading to renal failure and arrhythmia. It is managed with hydration, rasburicase or allopurinol, and dialysis.

b3-w11-new-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Features that favour reactive neutrophilia: toxic granulation, toxic vacuolation and Döhle bodies, no promyelocytes or myeloblasts in the blood, and negative cytogenetic and molecular studies.

  • A a WBC above 30 favours neoplasia.
  • B raised eosinophils and/or basophils favour neoplasia, classically CML.
  • D Auer rods mark myeloid blasts, which means leukemia.

flags.title: Option A has lost its comparison sign
flags.html: Option A reads “WBC 30”. The source almost certainly read WBC >30 × 109/L, which is the neoplastic clue in 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. The answer is unaffected.

b3-w11-new-q9-9:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia. Febrile neutropenia is an oncologic emergency, and the most common serious complication in hematologic cancer and chemotherapy. You stabilize, draw blood and urine cultures, and start empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (imipenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) promptly, before the source is known.

  • A fails: viral reactivation (HSV, CMV, VZV) and fungal infection are listed complications, alongside bacterial infection.
  • C fails: constitutional neutropenia is benign and not associated with infection risk.
  • D therefore fails.
b3-w11-ra-q8-8:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. An acute leukemia is a cancer of an early, blast-stage cell. In AML, myeloid cells fail to differentiate beyond the blast stage: the cell cycle arrests where cells normally proliferate, giving rapid proliferation and high turnover. The lineage runs myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → neutrophil.

  • B myelocytes and C metamyelocytes are later, more mature stages. Their excess in the blood is the left shift of CML or a reactive process, not an acute leukemia.
  • D bands and segmented granulocytes are mature cells.
b3-w11-sa-q1-1:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 04 - Approach to Leukemia. A middle-aged man with marked lymphocytosis (48 × 109/L), left upper quadrant pain (splenomegaly) and B symptoms has a mature lymphoproliferative disorder, most likely CLL, until proven otherwise. The diagnosis needs two things: mature lymphocytes on the peripheral blood film (smudge cells; immature cells would point to ALL), and clonality by peripheral blood flow cytometry.

  • B, E: liver or spleen biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when the clone is circulating.
  • D CT stages disease. It does not diagnose it.
  • F serum electrophoresis looks for a myeloma paraprotein.
  • G BCR-ABL is for CML, a myeloid disease.

b3-w11-sa-q3-3.html:
From 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. PV is diagnosed when all 3 major criteria are met, or the first 2 major plus the minor criterion. The major criteria are a raised Hb, a hypercellular marrow and a JAK2 mutation. The minor criterion is a subnormal EPO. Option A has a JAK2 mutation and a low EPO: the clonal driver and the primary-erythrocytosis pattern.

  • B: a high EPO points to secondary erythrocytosis, which argues against PV despite the JAK2 result.
  • C and D: without a JAK2 mutation, and with Hb 160 at the top of the female reference range, neither is diagnostic.

flags.title: Hemoglobin thresholds are borderline
flags.html: The PV criterion in 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis has lost its comparison sign (“Hb 165 (M)”), and the WHO threshold is usually given as greater than 165 g/L. Option A's Hb of exactly 165 therefore sits on the cut-off, and the erythrocytosis chart in 05 uses 170 g/L for men. A is still the only option combining JAK2 positivity with a low EPO. No option mentions the marrow criterion.

b3-w11-sa-q5-5:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. This is PV: Hb 190, all three lines raised, aquagenic pruritus, JAK2 positive, low EPO. Management is aimed at preventing thrombosis. Every patient gets ASA 81 mg daily and a hematocrit target under 0.45. At 51 with no prior thrombosis he is low risk, so the hematocrit is brought down by phlebotomy.

  • B hydroxyurea is cytoreduction for high-risk PV (age 60 or over, or prior thrombosis).
  • C IV chemotherapy is for acute leukemia and has no role in PV.

b3-w11-sa-q8-8.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Fever, sore throat, cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes in a young adult is EBV mononucleosis until proven otherwise. The lecture's test for it is the Monospot. Flow cytometry on peripheral blood is the non-invasive way to settle reactive versus clonal lymphocytosis if the picture persists. It is kept for persistence after 4-6 weeks, so in practice the Monospot comes first.

  • A/B marrow biopsy and C/H node excision or FNA are invasive, which the stem excludes.
  • G EBV IgG marks past exposure, not acute infection.

flags.title: Options were duplicated in transcription
flags.html: A and B are identical (marrow biopsy), and so are E and F (peripheral blood flow cytometry). The keyed F is the same test as E. The IgG-versus-acute-serology point for G is not in the vault notes and comes from general principles.

b3-w12-meds2024-q2-2:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Where a node sits tells you what it drains, and so what to look for. Inguinal nodes drain the lower abdomen, external genital skin, anal canal, lower third of the vagina and lower limb. The lecture's inguinal list leads with benign reactive nodes, STIs and skin or lower-limb infection. Inguinal nodes are also the only ones normally palpable in adults.

  • A tuberculosis is the classic cause of mediastinal nodes.
  • B breast carcinoma drains to the axillary nodes.
b3-w12-meds2024-q3-3:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Axillary nodes drain the breast, upper limb and chest wall. The lecture lists breast cancer (adenocarcinoma) first among axillary causes, with melanoma and lymphoma. Axillary adenopathy should prompt a breast exam.

  • A tuberculosis sits with sarcoidosis under mediastinal nodes.
  • C STIs drain to the inguinal nodes. Syphilis appears under axillary and epitrochlear, but STIs as a group point to the groin.
b3-w12-meds2024-q4-4:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The lecture's causes of mediastinal nodes are Mycobacterium tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and primary or secondary malignancy. Hilar or mediastinal adenopathy on CXR is also one of the features concerning for malignancy.

  • B breast carcinoma spreads first to the axillary nodes.
  • C STIs drain to the inguinal nodes.
b3-w12-module-q13-13:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The anterior mediastinum lies between the sternum and the pericardium. It contains the thymus, internal thoracic artery, lymph nodes, connective tissue and fat. That is why thymoma, with the other “T”s, heads the anterior-mass differential.

  • A the heart and pericardium, B the pulmonary veins and D the SVC all lie in the middle mediastinum. It also holds the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, IVC, phrenic nerve and recurrent laryngeal nerve.
b3-w12-module-q15-15:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. Sort by compartment boundaries: the anterior lies between sternum and pericardium, the middle is the pericardium and what it holds, the posterior is behind the heart against the spine.

  • Anterior (A, H): the internal thoracic artery and thymus (with nodes, connective tissue and fat: “I CAN'T”).
  • Posterior (G, I): the T3 vertebra (the spine is the posterior border, and posterior masses implicate spine and nerves) and the hemiazygos vein, with the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct and sympathetic trunk.
  • Middle (B, C, D, E, F): SVC, pericardium, phrenic nerve, pulmonary veins and heart, with the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, IVC and recurrent laryngeal nerve.
b3-w12-module-q16-16:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The anterior-mass differential is the 5 T's: thymus/thymoma, “terrible” lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin), teratoma/germ cell tumour, thyroid (goitre, thyroiditis, neoplasm) and thoracic aortic aneurysm. Transitional cell carcinoma is a urothelial (bladder) cancer; it starts with a T but belongs to none of these.

  • A thymoma, B lymphoma and C germ cell tumour are three of the five, so each is on the list.
b3-w12-module-q17-17:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. Middle-mediastinal masses are mostly nodal (lymphadenopathy), then benign cysts (bronchogenic, pericardial or enteric, about 20% of middle masses), esophageal tumours and vascular masses. A bronchogenic cyst is the classic middle-compartment cyst.

  • B thyroid goitre and D teratoma are two of the anterior 5 T's.
  • C parathyroid adenoma is on the lecture's list of uncommon anterior differentials, with hemangioma, lipoma and fibroma.
b3-w12-module-q18-18:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. A posterior mass implicates the spine and nerves: neurogenic tumours, meningoceles and thoracic spine lesions. A plasmacytoma of a thoracic vertebra is a spine lesion, so it sits posteriorly.

  • B thymoma is the first anterior T.
  • C a pericardial cyst is one of the benign middle-compartment cysts.
  • D lipoma is an uncommon anterior differential.
b3-w12-module-q19-19:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. Age sorts the anterior masses. Over 40, in both sexes, thymomas predominate, followed by thyroid masses, and lymphomas become much less common. A woman in her 60s therefore points to thymoma.

  • A lymphoma is the leading mass in women aged 10–39, not over 40.
  • C thyroid masses come second after thymoma in this age group.
  • D teratoma is the most likely mass in children.

b3-w12-module-q20-20.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The portal's summative chart (mirrored in 06 - Multiple Myeloma) tags lymphoma for women, men and children, and germ cell tumours for children and men; thymoma is the over-40 mass. That supports the key: lymphoma is a leading anterior mass in a young man.

  • C thymoma rises in the 30–39 group but only predominates after 40.
  • A, D germ cell tumours (non-seminomatous and seminoma) are the main competitor in young men; see the warning below.

flags.title: The notes disagree on young men
flags.html: The prose of 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass says that in the 10–39 group lymphomas lead in women “while in men, germ cell tumors are more common.” On that reading, A or D would be keyed. The summative chart lists lymphoma for men too. Check the original age-by-decade figure before relying on this key.

b3-w12-module-q21-21.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass.

  • Anterior (B, C, D, E): teratoma, thyroid goitre, thymoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumour, which are all 5 T's.
  • Posterior (A, G, I): meningocele, a neurogenic tumour and a T5 plasmacytoma. The posterior compartment is spine and nerves: neurogenic tumours, meningoceles and thoracic spine lesions.
  • Middle (F, H): the esophageal lesion (the lecture lists esophageal tumours with the middle-compartment masses) and the pericardial cyst, one of the benign middle cysts.

flags.title: Option G probably means neurogenic
flags.html: The lecture lists neurogenic tumours in the posterior compartment, not neuroendocrine ones. Option G reads best as a transcription slip for “neurogenic tumour”.

b3-w12-module-q22-22:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the middle mediastinum, and a mass there can compress it. That paralyses the ipsilateral vocal cord and causes hoarseness, one of the lecture's mass-effect symptoms.
