  • A the phrenic nerve, also in the middle mediastinum, supplies the diaphragm. Compression gives diaphragmatic palsy and dyspnea, not a hoarse voice.
  • C the greater splanchnic nerve is a posterior sympathetic nerve to the abdominal viscera.
  • D the sciatic nerve is in the lower limb, nowhere near the thorax.

b3-w12-module-q23-23.html:
From the mediastinal-mass chart in 06 - Multiple Myeloma (see also 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass). SVC syndrome gives face, neck and chest edema, dilated chest-wall collaterals, dyspnea and cough, and a Pemberton sign: raising both arms narrows the thoracic inlet further and brings on facial plethora or distress.

  • A Rumpel-Leede is petechiae below a tourniquet: capillary fragility or thrombocytopenia.
  • C Chvostek's is facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve: hypocalcemia.
  • D Darier's is urtication on stroking a lesion: mastocytosis.

flags.title: The distractors are not in the vault notes
flags.html: The notes name the Pemberton sign under SVC syndrome but do not describe the three distractor signs. Their meanings above come from general principles, so verify them before relying on them.

b3-w12-module-q24-24.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass and its summative chart (in 06 - Multiple Myeloma). Horner syndrome comes from involvement of the sympathetic chain, which runs in the posterior mediastinum. The chart gives its signs as miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis and enophthalmos, and notes it is not specific to a mediastinal mass (Pancoast tumours do it too). So E, F and I are all Horner signs.

  • G hoarseness comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • H dysphagia is esophageal mass effect, typical of posterior masses.

flags.title: The key looks incomplete
flags.html: The key gives only E (miosis). The summative chart for 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass lists miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis together as Horner signs, so F and I are equally correct. The options starting at E suggest a select-all question whose key was truncated in transcription. Check the source.

b3-w12-module-q25-25:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. Tumour markers help most when a thymoma or germ cell tumour is suspected. Anti-AChR points to a thymic tumour, especially with myasthenia gravis, so it will not help with a germ cell tumour.

  • A LDH is raised in lymphomas and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours.
  • B AFP marks germ cell tumours, 60–80% of non-seminomatous ones. A raised AFP excludes pure seminoma.
  • C β-hCG is positive in 10% of seminomas and 30–50% of non-seminomatous tumours.
b3-w12-module-q26-26:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. Not every mediastinal mass needs a biopsy. The lecture's rule is that if you suspect lymphoma, you definitely biopsy and send the tissue to pathology and flow cytometry, because typing the lymphoma dictates treatment.

  • B a bronchogenic cyst is a simple cyst, and a simple cyst needs no biopsy.
  • C for a suspected thymoma you may skip biopsy and go straight to resection.
  • D an aneurysm needs no biopsy, and needling one would be dangerous.

b3-w12-module-q28-28.html:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent, a nitrogen mustard. It cross-links guanine so the DNA strands cannot separate, and the cell cannot enter S phase. It arrests and undergoes apoptosis. The lecture's framing therefore places its hit at the G1-to-S step.

  • A “only dividing cells” is the general statement about chemotherapy, not the phase this drug targets.
  • B is wrong: cytotoxics spare non-cycling tissue, which is why their toxicity falls on hair, mucosa and marrow.
  • D S phase is where antimetabolites act, by starving DNA synthesis of nucleotides.

flags.title: Alkylators are usually called cell-cycle nonspecific
flags.html: Standard pharmacology teaching treats alkylating agents as cell-cycle nonspecific. The key follows this lecture's “cannot enter S phase” wording. Expect the lecture's version on this exam, but be aware that other sources frame it differently.

b3-w12-module-q29-29:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid, an antimicrotubule agent. It blocks microtubule assembly in metaphase, when microtubules line the chromosomes up. The spindle never forms, the cell arrests in M phase and dies by apoptosis.

  • A is true of chemotherapy in general but does not name the phase.
  • B is wrong: resting cells are spared, which is why the toxicity lands on rapidly dividing tissue (hair, mucosa, neutrophils) and, for vincristine, on nerves.
  • C the G1-to-S block is the alkylating agents' step.
b3-w12-module-q31-31:
From 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas and 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. DLBCL is the most common NHL and is treated with R-CHOP, which contains every class listed:

  • A prednisone: glucocorticoids are cytotoxic to lymphocytes, and the lecture names aggressive B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) among the malignancies they treat.
  • B cyclophosphamide, an alkylating agent.
  • C vincristine (Oncovin), a vinca alkaloid. The H is doxorubicin (hydroxydaunomycin).
  • D rituximab, the anti-CD20 naked mAb used for any B-cell malignancy, DLBCL included.

No single class is the answer, so E is.

b3-w12-module-q32-32.html:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. The letters were shifted in transcription: J to N stand for A to E, so the key “A, B, C, E” means AML, multiple myeloma, B-cell lymphoma and CLL. The lecture supports three of these clearly:

  • Multiple myeloma: daratumumab (anti-CD38).
  • B-cell lymphoma: rituximab (anti-CD20), and obinutuzumab for follicular lymphoma.
  • CLL: rituximab, obinutuzumab, ofatumumab (CD20) and alemtuzumab (CD52).
  • AML has no monoclonal antibody in the note. Its targeted drugs there are FLT3 inhibitors.
  • T-cell lymphoma: brentuximab (CD30) is listed for anaplastic large cell lymphoma, which is a T-cell lymphoma.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies names no monoclonal antibody for AML, yet the key includes it. It does list brentuximab for anaplastic large cell lymphoma, a T-cell lymphoma, and the key leaves that out. The key may reflect slide content the note lacks, such as an anti-CD33 antibody for AML. Check the source before trusting it.

flags.title: Option letters are damaged
flags.html: Option A (“J. Acute myeloid leukemia”) was absorbed into the stem, and the rest are lettered K to N, while the key uses A to E.

b3-w12-module-q33-33.html:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. A naked mAb is antibody alone and kills by complement-mediated cytotoxicity and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity or phagocytosis. A conjugated mAb carries a radioisotope to the CD marker for extra killing power.

  • Conjugated (E, F): tositumomab (Bexxar) and ibritumomab tiuxetan (Zevalin), the radio-immunoconjugates.
  • Naked (A, B, C, D): brentuximab (CD30), daratumumab (CD38), obinutuzumab (CD20) and rituximab (CD20).

flags.title: Brentuximab is filed as naked
flags.html: The lecture lists brentuximab vedotin with the naked antibodies. The “vedotin” is actually a cytotoxic drug payload, so outside this course brentuximab is usually called an antibody-drug conjugate. The key follows the lecture, where “conjugated” means radioisotope-labelled.

b3-w12-module-q34-34:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • Imatinib: B, E. This tyrosine kinase inhibitor blocks the constitutively active BCR-ABL of the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), in CML, and is also used in GIST.
  • BTK inhibitor: A. Ibrutinib (and idelalisib) is used for CLL specifically. Its toxicities are bruising, atrial fibrillation and diarrhea.
  • FLT3 inhibitor: C, for AML.
  • ATRA: D. It dissociates the PML-RARA block so promyelocytes mature in APL, and is given with chemotherapy to prevent a very high WBC count.
b3-w12-module-q40-40:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology. The technology is described correctly. SABR and SRS are highly focused external beam radiation with about 1 mm accuracy and very high doses in 1–5 treatments, on platforms like Gamma Knife and CyberKnife. The false part is who uses it: this is radiation oncology, not hematology.

In hematologic malignancy, radiotherapy is used to palliate (for example, myeloma bone pain) or to cure limited-stage lymphoma and give CNS prophylaxis in ALL. Hematologists treat with systemic drugs. The statement is False.
b3-w12-module-q5-5:
From 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas. Fine needle aspiration is easy, needs no surgeon or OR, is the least invasive and least expensive, and gives faster results. That is why it can be done quickly in clinic. Its weakness is that it loses nodal architecture: it cannot subclassify, can give false negatives with localized disease, and may yield too few cells for flow, cytogenetics and molecular studies.

  • A, B needing an OR and being expensive are disadvantages of excisional biopsy.
  • D “always representative” is excisional biopsy's advantage, and the opposite of FNA's false-negative problem. That is why excisional biopsy is the best option.

b3-w12-module-q7-7.html:
From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma. B symptoms are exactly three: fever (over 38°C), drenching night sweats and weight loss. They add the “B” suffix to the stage, and they carry prognostic weight.

  • E/G poor appetite and I fatigue (low energy) are the lecture's non-specific symptoms, not B symptoms.
  • F pruritus is a Hodgkin history clue, with node pain after alcohol, but it is listed under “other symptoms”.
  • B headache and H skin rash are not part of the definition.

flags.title: Duplicated option
flags.html: Options E and G are both “Poor Appetite”. Both are incorrect, so the key is unaffected.

b3-w12-new-q16-16:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The mediastinum is the space between the lungs, bounded by the thoracic inlet above and the diaphragm below. The anterior compartment, between sternum and pericardium, contains the thymus, internal thoracic arteries, lymph nodes, connective tissue and fat (“I CAN'T”). The tongue is in the oral cavity, above the thoracic inlet, so it is not in the mediastinum at all.

  • A, C, D, E are all listed anterior-mediastinal contents.
b3-w12-new-q17-17:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. For suspected ectopic thyroid tissue or goitre, the lecture says to consider a technetium scan, which shows functioning thyroid tissue. MRI's role is to distinguish compression from invasion of structures.

  • A is true: CT chest with IV contrast is the standard next step after a plain-film abnormality.
  • B is true: PET/CT if lymphoma is suspected.
  • C is true: scrotal ultrasound if a germ cell tumour is suspected.
  • E is true: a widened mediastinum is 6 cm or more on an upright PA film (8 cm on a supine AP film).
b3-w12-new-q19-19:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. Antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-FU, 6-MP, 6-thioguanine) interfere with nucleic acid metabolism, so the nucleotides needed to build DNA and RNA are not made. 5-FU's block of thymidine synthesis is the classic example.

  • A garbles the mechanism: alkylators cross-link guanine so strands cannot separate. They do not convert hydrogen bonds.
  • C preventing DNA relaxation is topoisomerase inhibition (anthracyclines, etoposide), not alkylation.
  • D intercalation belongs to the antitumour antibiotics. Topoisomerase inhibitors act by blocking topoisomerase.
  • E taxanes stabilize microtubules to cause M-phase/metaphase arrest, not prophase.
b3-w12-new-q20-20:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. Nivolumab is a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor. The lecture lists checkpoint inhibitors for myeloma, Hodgkin lymphoma and lung cancer, not T-cell lymphoma, so E is the mismatched pair.

  • A daratumumab (anti-CD38) targets plasma cells in myeloma.
  • B, C rituximab (anti-CD20) treats CLL and follicular lymphoma, like any B-cell malignancy.
  • D Zevalin, the radio-conjugated anti-CD20 mAb, is used for relapsed follicular lymphoma.
b3-w12-new-q5-5:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Most enlarged nodes are reactive: over 98% in primary care are non-malignant. So the first step is history and physical, not a test. Location tells you the drainage area to examine. A neck node leads to the oral cavity, oropharynx and scalp. The history screens for constitutional symptoms and exposures, and the exam checks size and character: hard or soft, tender, mobile or fixed.

  • A, B CT and X-ray come after the clinical assessment, guided by what it finds.
  • D biopsy is for nodes with red flags, and FNA is not the lecture's preferred biopsy anyway.
b3-w12-new-q7-7:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. Several features on the lecture's list are concerning for malignancy:

  • A systemic symptoms: fever over a week, night sweats, weight loss over 10%.
  • C fixed, non-tender, matted nodes.
  • E a supraclavicular node, which drains the GI tract, GU tract and lungs, so think abdominal or thoracic malignancy.
  • B is not a red flag. Regional (localized) nodes usually reflect infection in the drainage area. It is generalized lymphadenopathy that is concerning.
  • D is not either. Tenderness suggests an inflammatory or reactive node, and the worrying node is non-tender.
b3-w12-new-q9-9:
From 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas. Reed-Sternberg cells are scattered in a mostly reactive background and do not express light-chain monoclonality. Flow cytometry therefore sees only polyclonal lymphocytes, reads as normal, and cannot detect classical HL.

  • A immunohistochemistry is how classical HL is shown: CD15+ and CD30+, with CD20 and CD45 negative.
  • C FISH is one of the three standard ancillary tests (with IHC and flow) used for diagnosis and prognosis in lymphoma.
b3-w12-sa-q1-1:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • i Imatinib: D (CML). This tyrosine kinase inhibitor blocks the constitutively active BCR-ABL made by t(9;22).
  • ii ATRA: A (APL). APL's PML-RARA fusion arrests maturation at the promyelocyte stage, and ATRA dissociates that block so the cells differentiate.
  • iii Nivolumab: C (Hodgkin lymphoma). This PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor is listed for HL, myeloma and lung cancer.
  • iv Ibrutinib: B (CLL). This Bruton kinase inhibitor is used for CLL specifically.

b3-w12-sa-q6-6.html:
From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • i Imatinib: B (diarrhea), with muscle cramps, periorbital edema, cytopenias and effusions.
  • ii Rituximab: D (infusion reactions), the remaining pair once the others are placed.
  • iii ATRA: A (differentiation syndrome). ATRA drives all the leukemic promyelocytes to mature at once, which is why the lecture says it is given with chemotherapy to prevent a very high WBC count.
  • iv Nivolumab: C (colitis). PD-1 blockade releases immune toxicity: colitis, pneumonitis, rash, hepatitis, hypophysitis, nephritis. It is treated with steroids.
  • v Ibrutinib: E (bruising), with atrial fibrillation. Ibrutinib also causes diarrhea, so bruising is the discriminating match.

flags.title: Two pairings are only partly in the notes
flags.html: The note does not mention rituximab infusion reactions or name “differentiation syndrome”. It only describes the mass differentiation that ATRA causes. These two pairs are reasoned by elimination and general principles.

b3-w12-sa-q9-9.html:
From 07 - Individual Variability in Drug Response (Week 8). A clinically actionable pharmacogenetic pair is one where the genotype changes the dose or the drug choice. Ethanol metabolism through ADH is not used this way, so D is the odd one out.

  • A CYP2C9 metabolizes the active S-warfarin. Its variants (*2, *3) cut clearance by up to 85% and are present in up to 18% of people. Together with VKORC1, it underlies genotype-guided warfarin dosing, which LHSC offers.
  • B clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19 (PoM 1 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs), so poor metabolizers get less antiplatelet effect.
  • C DPYD deficiency blocks 5-FU breakdown, causing severe toxicity.

flags.title: Partly not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers DPYD and 5-fluorouracil, or ADH and ethanol, so those lines come from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

b3-wb-heme-q96:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The 5 T's of an anterior mediastinal mass are thymus/thymoma, “terrible” lymphoma, teratoma/germ cell tumour, thyroid and thoracic aortic aneurysm. A tracheal growth is not one of them, and the trachea is not an anterior-compartment structure.

  • A thymus: thymomas are about 20% of mediastinal masses, slow-growing, and linked to myasthenia gravis.
  • B lymphoma, Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin.
  • D thyroid: goitre, thyroiditis or neoplasm.
  • E thoracic aorta: an aneurysm can present as an anterior mass.

b3-wb-heme-q99.html:
From 02 - Approach to Lymphadenopathy. The workbook's options read Size < 3 cm and Persistence > 4 weeks; the portal copy lost both signs. With them restored, A is the only feature that is not a red flag: a smaller node is reassuring, and the lecture's size threshold for concern is a non-tender node ≥ 2 cm that is growing or not settling after 2 weeks of antibiotics.

  • B persistence: a node that fails to resolve is concerning.
  • C supraclavicular nodes drain the chest and abdomen, so think thoracic or abdominal malignancy.
  • D, E hard, fixed (immobile), matted, non-tender nodes are the malignant character on exam.

flags.title: Option text lost its signs
flags.html: The vault workbook copy reads A) Size < 3 cm and B) Persistence > 4 weeks, and its key line says “concerning if size was >3cm”. As printed here, a 3 cm node would itself be a red flag (the lecture's threshold is ≥ 2 cm). The key is right for the original wording.

b3-w9-module-q12-12:
From 05 - Approach to Macrocytic Anemia. An MCV of 133 with a very low B12 is a megaloblastic anemia: impaired DNA synthesis leaves nuclear maturation behind the cytoplasm, and the film shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. That neutrophil finding is what separates megaloblastic from non-megaloblastic macrocytosis (liver disease gives round macrocytes with normal neutrophils).

  • B teardrop cells mean marrow fibrosis or infiltration (myelofibrosis, myelophthisis).
  • C target cells point to liver disease, hyposplenism or thalassemia.
  • D spherocytes mean hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune hemolysis (01 - Hematopoiesis morphology table).
b3-w9-module-q13-13:
From 06 - Approach to Hemolytic Anemia (pharmacologic treatment table). EPO is made mainly by the kidney in response to hypoxia, so failing kidneys leave the marrow under-driven. The lecture's EPO indications are chronic renal failure, AIDS patients on antivirals, chemotherapy-associated anemia, pre-op to avoid transfusion, and MDS to reduce transfusions.

  • A iron deficiency is treated by replacing iron (oral or IV) and finding the source of loss; EPO would have no iron to work with.
  • B sideroblastic anemia is managed with transfusion, removing the toxin, and occasionally pyridoxine (03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia).
  • D EPO is indication-specific, not a treatment for every anemia.
b3-w9-module-q4-4:
From 07 - Hemoglobinopathies and 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Beta thalassemia is a quantitative defect: 2 normal alpha chains with absent beta chains. In the homozygous (major) form this gives ineffective erythropoiesis and hemolysis, an overactive marrow with bone deformities (extramedullary expansion), and iron overload from transfusion and absorption, treated with chelation (deferoxamine). HbF is raised.

  • A sickle cell disease is also a beta-globin mutation, but a qualitative one (Glu to Val); its hallmark is vaso-occlusion, not the transfusion-driven iron overload the stem describes.
  • C alpha thalassemia involves the alpha-globin genes on chromosome 16, not beta.
b3-w9-module-q5-5:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. Alpha thalassemia is the quantitative defect of the alpha-globin genes (4 genes, 2 on each chromosome 16). Severity tracks the number deleted: 1 silent carrier, 2 trait (mild anemia), 3 HbH disease (hemolysis, splenomegaly), 4 hydrops fetalis. Hb electrophoresis shows a normal HbA2; gene sequencing and the HbH inclusion test confirm it.

  • A sickle cell disease is a qualitative beta-chain mutation (HbS, Glu to Val).
  • B beta thalassemia major is a beta-globin defect, with raised HbF.
b3-w9-module-q6-6:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis and 07 - Hemoglobinopathies. The option text here ran the three descriptions together. The pairing is A (HbF) = ii, 2 alpha + 2 gamma; B (HbS) = iii, 2 alpha + 2 abnormal beta; C (HbA) = i, 2 alpha + 2 beta.

  • HbF (α2γ2) is the intrauterine hemoglobin. Gamma chains are replaced by beta chains in the first 3-6 months, leaving < 2% HbF in adults.
  • HbS has normal alpha chains with a mutant beta chain (position 6 Glu to Val). That is why sickle disease hides until about age 3, while HbF still protects.
  • HbA (α2β2) is about 95% of adult hemoglobin; HbA2 (α2δ2) is about 3%.
b3-w9-module-q7-7:
From 07 - Hemoglobinopathies. Beta globin is encoded by one gene on each chromosome 11, 2 copies in total. Beta thalassemia major is the homozygous state, with both copies mutated; one mutated copy gives beta thalassemia minor (trait), with raised HbA2.

  • A, D are wrong on the count. There are 4 alpha-globin genes (2 on each chromosome 16). Alpha thalassemia scales with the number deleted: 1 = silent carrier, 2 = trait, 3 = HbH disease, 4 = hydrops fetalis. So neither “2 genes” statement holds.
  • C there are not 4 beta genes; 4 is the alpha count.
b3-w9-module-q8-8:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia. The lecture's VOC management is oxygen, IV fluids, opioids/NSAIDs, and treating the trigger, so A, B, C and E are correct. Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes and sickled cells occlude vessels, so each step works against that. Oxygen limits deoxygenation, fluids correct dehydration and viscosity, analgesia treats the ischemic pain, and removing the precipitant (such as infection) stops the cycle.

  • D ice is not part of the lecture's plan. Cold causes vasoconstriction, which works against the goal of restoring flow.
  • F a VOC is an acute ischemic event and needs active treatment; it is not left to settle with rest.
b3-w9-new-q21-21:
From 03 - Approach to Microcytic Anemia. In beta thalassemia the unpaired excess alpha chains precipitate in red-cell precursors and circulating cells. The lecture lists all three consequences under thalassemia: ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and iron overload, so D is correct.

  • A ineffective erythropoiesis: precursors die in the marrow, and the marrow expands in response (bone deformities, short stature).
  • C hemolysis: damaged cells are cleared early, giving jaundice and splenomegaly.
  • B iron overload: from transfusion and increased absorption driven by the ineffective erythropoiesis, hence chelation with deferoxamine.

b3-w9-sa-q8-8.html:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis (abnormal RBC morphology). The image is not reproduced here, but per the key it shows sickle cells: elongated cells with pointed ends and no central pallor. They form because the HbS beta-globin mutation (position 6 Glu to Val) lets deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerize and stretch the cell. An 8-year-old fits too, since HbF protects until about age 3.

  • B thalassemia major gives a hypochromic microcytic film with target cells, teardrops and basophilic stippling, not sickled forms.
  • C thalassemia minor is mild and hypochromic, with a normal RDW and a high RBC count.
  • D HbC (Glu to Lys) is named in the lecture, but no film feature is given for it; sickled cells point to HbS.

flags.title: Image not available
flags.html: The question refers to a blood film that is not shown in the bank; the explanation relies on the key's statement that it shows sickled red cells.

b3-wb-heme-q26.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia. The key gives A, C, D, F. Sickle cell disease is a chronic hemolytic anemia (A). Sickled, adhesive cells cause sickle and vaso-occlusive crises (C, D: dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, stroke). Chronic organ damage explains the shorter life expectancy (F).

  • I is backwards: heterozygotes have increased resistance to malaria.
  • E, H IBS and COPD are unrelated to sickling.
  • G bronze skin belongs to iron-overload states (hemochromatosis), not sickle disease; jaundice is the hemolytic skin sign.
  • B fever is not listed in the lecture as a sickle feature. It signals a complication (infection, acute chest), and it is the likeliest intended fifth answer.

flags.title: Stem asks for five; the key gives four
flags.html: The question says “Choose 5” but the workbook key lists only A, C, D and F, and the bank records no correct letters for grading. Fever (B) is the most plausible fifth, but no lecture note says so.

b3-w10-module-q10-10:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (VTE section). The lecture reserves the V/Q scan for younger women and patients with renal failure, so B and D are correct. A CTPA needs iodinated contrast, which is a problem in renal failure, and it delivers a chest radiation dose that matters for young breast tissue. A V/Q scan avoids both, and it diagnoses PE as a ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

  • A, C suspected lung cancer or an abnormal chest x-ray argue for CTPA. It also images the parenchyma and can find the alternative diagnosis. A V/Q scan is hard to interpret when the lung fields are already abnormal (general principle; not stated in the note).
b3-w10-module-q11-11: From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (VTE section). False: the lecture lists DVT as an outpatient condition. Treatment is anticoagulation at home, with the limb elevated as needed, activity encouraged, compression stockings for post-thrombotic syndrome, and an NSAID for pain. LMWH and the oral Xa inhibitors are given subcutaneously or orally without monitoring, which makes home treatment practical. Admission is the rule only for PE with hemodynamic instability or an oxygen requirement.
b3-w10-module-q15-15:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (Treatment of VTE). This follows the preceding case: a 37-year-old woman, 16 weeks pregnant, with a right-leg DVT. The lecture's anticoagulant choice is LMWH for cancer and pregnancy. It is given subcutaneously at home with predictable pharmacokinetics and no routine monitoring.

  • A apixaban and the other DOACs are not the lecture's choice in pregnancy.
  • B UFH is IV or SC and hospital-based, with aPTT monitoring 2-4 times a day. It is also 10 times more likely than LMWH to cause HIT.
  • D warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy.
b3-w10-module-q17-17:
From 02 - Hemostasis. FXII is a contact factor that is “not required in the body”: in vivo, coagulation starts with tissue factor and FVIIa, and FXII plays only a minor role. The aPTT uses a contact activator, so FXII deficiency profoundly prolongs the aPTT without causing bleeding.

  • A FV is a common-pathway cofactor (the prothrombinase complex); its deficiency prolongs both the PT and aPTT, and it bleeds.
  • B FVII deficiency prolongs the PT/INR and bleeds, because FVIIa initiates coagulation.
  • C vWF deficiency causes mucosal bleeding. It can lower FVIII and prolong the aPTT, and the bleeding is real.
b3-w10-module-q18-18:
From 03 - Approach to Coagulopathy in Adults. A bleeding disorder found in adulthood is typically one mild enough to have been missed, because severe congenital forms are identified earlier in life. Mild vWD (type 1, partial quantitative deficiency) fits this pattern, so A is true.

  • B the platelet plug is primary hemostasis. Tertiary hemostasis is clot stabilization, the FXIII cross-linking of fibrin (01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient).
  • C is reversed. Mucosal bleeding points to a primary defect (platelets, vWF); deep joint and muscle bleeding points to a secondary one (coagulation factors, e.g. hemophilia).
b3-w10-module-q19-19:
From 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient. Normal PT and aPTT do not exclude a bleeding disorder. The INR and PTT only test factor-driven fibrin generation, and they miss platelet number and function and clot stabilization. The lecture's normal-INR-and-PTT list includes thrombocytopenia (A), congenital or acquired platelet function disorders (D), and FXIII deficiency (B). FXIII cross-links fibrin after the clot has formed, which the clotting-time tests never measure.

  • C fails both halves. FXII deficiency prolongs the aPTT, because the test uses a contact activator, and it does not cause bleeding (02 - Hemostasis).
b3-w10-module-q20-20:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. The thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS and DIC in this lecture) all shear red cells through microthrombi, so schistocytes are the shared finding. The other options each belong to only one of them.

  • B low ADAMTS-13 defines TTP. HUS has a normal level, and that is how the two are separated.
  • C Shiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7) causes HUS, after a diarrheal prodrome.
  • D an elevated INR marks DIC, where consumption depletes factors. TTP and HUS leave the coagulation tests normal.
b3-w10-module-q21-21:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. HIT is antibody against the heparin-PF4 complex. It activates platelets, so the patient clots rather than bleeds. Management is to stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban (an IV direct thrombin inhibitor listed for HIT), fondaparinux or danaparoid.

  • A UFH is the cause, and it is 10 times more likely to trigger HIT than LMWH.
  • B LMWH is still heparin and cross-reacts, so all heparin must stop.
  • D warfarin is started only once platelets have normalized, never as monotherapy at diagnosis.
b3-w10-module-q22-22:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. In ITP, antibody-coated platelets are cleared by splenic macrophages, so removing the spleen removes the main site of destruction. The lecture's treatment ladder runs from glucocorticoids and IVIg to splenectomy, rituximab, TPO mimetics and immunosuppression. That makes A the next step for a stable patient who has failed the first two.

  • B antibiotics have no role; the lecture says to avoid them in HUS.
  • C replacing ADAMTS-13 (by plasma exchange) treats TTP.
  • D platelet transfusion in ITP is kept for emergency bleeding. Transfused platelets are destroyed just as quickly, so they do nothing for a stable patient.
b3-w10-module-q24-24:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia and 02 - Hemostasis. DIC is over-activation of coagulation that consumes factors and platelets. Depleted factors prolong the clotting times, so the INR rises (ISTH score: platelets < 100, raised D-dimer, fibrinogen < 1 g/L, raised INR).

  • A platelets are consumed and fall.
  • B fibrinogen is consumed and falls, and cryoprecipitate is given if it drops below 1.0 in a bleeding patient. It is also factor I, not factor II; prothrombin is II.
  • D FVIII is consumed along with the other factors. The lecture's multiple-factor pattern is a fall in factor levels, not a rise.
b3-w10-module-q3-3: From 06 - Thrombosis and 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. False: over 50% of patients with PE have no symptoms of DVT. A DVT can embolize before it causes leg pain or swelling, and in some patients the source is never found clinically. So the absence of leg symptoms does not lower the pretest probability of PE enough to skip the workup. The Wells PE score gives 3 points for signs of DVT when they are present, but PE can be scored and pursued without them.
b3-w10-module-q5-5: From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (VTE section). False: the signs of DVT (pain, swelling, erythema, warmth) are non-specific, and trauma, cellulitis, Baker's cyst, lymphedema and external compression all mimic them. Clinical assessment only sets the pretest probability through the Wells score (likely > 1, unlikely ≤ 1). If DVT is unlikely, a negative D-dimer excludes it. If DVT is likely, or the D-dimer is positive, the diagnosis needs imaging: compression ultrasound, or an ascending venogram as the gold standard.
b3-w10-module-q6-6:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia (VTE section). The lecture's DVT symptoms are pain, limb swelling, erythema and warmth, so B, C and D are correct. Obstructed venous outflow raises pressure in the limb and pushes fluid into the tissues (swelling). The inflammation around the clot produces redness and heat.

  • A itching is not a DVT feature. Its presence should point toward a skin cause, one of the mimics (with cellulitis and trauma) that must be ruled out.
b3-w10-ra-q8-8:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia and 02 - Hemostasis. Warfarin blocks VKORC1, so factors II, VII, IX and X are not activated. FVII has the shortest half-life, so the extrinsic pathway falls first, and the PT rises. The INR standardizes the PT across labs specifically to monitor vitamin K antagonists (target 2.0-3.0).

  • A the aPTT monitors UFH and the IV direct thrombin inhibitors.
  • C fibrinogen is not a vitamin K-dependent factor.
  • D D-dimer measures fibrin breakdown; a negative result is used to exclude VTE, not to dose drugs.
b3-w10-sa-q10-10:
From 01 - Hematopoiesis (components of blood). Plasma is the non-cellular fluid of blood: water, albumin, coagulation factors and immunoglobulins. Serum is what is left after the blood has clotted, which is plasma minus the coagulation factors and fibrinogen used up in the clot. That is also why coagulation tests are drawn into a citrate (blue-top) tube and run on plasma.

  • B complement proteins are present in both.
  • C, D both plasma and serum are cell-free. Erythrocytes and platelets are spun out of plasma, and they are trapped in the clot for serum.
b3-w10-sa-q6-6:
From 05 - Approach to Thrombocytopenia. LMWH is the lecture's indication for long-term treatment of cancer-associated thrombosis, and cancer-associated VTE is treated for a minimum of 6 months, stopping only if the cancer is cured.

  • A the lecture names warfarin for renal failure. In active cancer, interactions and variable nutrition make INR control unreliable.
  • C UFH is an IV, hospital drug with aPTT monitoring 2-4 times a day, so it is not a long-term option.
  • D aspirin is an antiplatelet drug (it blocks COX and lowers thromboxane A2), and it is not a treatment for venous thrombosis.
b3-wb-heme-q107:
From 01 - Approach to a Bleeding Patient (blood components). The lecture's platelet contraindications are refusal; not indicated; and TTP, HUS, HIT, so all four options apply.

  • A transfusion requires written informed consent from a capable patient, so refusal ends it.
  • B a normal count without bleeding is not an indication. Platelets are given at < 10, for symptomatic or massive bleeding, or before surgery at < 50 (neurosurgery < 100).
  • C, D TTP and HUS are consumptive, clotting microangiopathies, and transfused platelets feed further thrombosis. The same applies to HIT.
b3-w11-module-q15-15:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis (myeloproliferative neoplasms). MPNs are defined by clonal marrow stem cells giving rise to an excess of one or more myeloid lines. That clonal hematopoietic stem-cell origin is the only feature every MPN shares.

  • B PV expands red cells, and primary myelofibrosis can cause pancytopenia, so a high WBC or platelet count is not universal.
  • C splenomegaly is rare in ET. JAK2 is present in 90-95% of PV but only 50-60% of ET and PMF.
  • D no mutation is required. The ET and PMF criteria accept another clonal marker, or the absence of a reactive cause, in place of a JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation.
b3-w11-module-q16-16:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis (PV management). The goal in PV is preventing thrombosis, and the lecture's baseline for all patients is ASA 81 mg daily with the hematocrit kept below 0.45, plus reduction of cardiovascular risk. The other options depend on risk group.

  • B phlebotomy is the approach for low-risk patients; it lowers the hematocrit.
  • D hydroxyurea (cytoreduction) is for high-risk patients: age ≥ 60 or prior thrombosis.
  • A allogeneic stem cell transplant is the curative option for primary myelofibrosis, not routine PV care.
b3-w11-module-q18-18:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia and 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Nucleated red cells plus immature white cells in the blood is the definition of a leukoerythroblastic picture. It means precursors are being pushed out of the marrow early, because the marrow is replaced (myelofibrosis, hematologic cancer, metastatic solid cancer) or under strain. The option is the name of the film pattern, not a diagnosis.

  • A teardrop cells are a separate red-cell shape, often seen alongside this pattern.
  • B myelofibrosis is one cause of the picture, not its name.
  • C AML is a diagnosis made on blasts, not on this pattern.
b3-w11-module-q19-19:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. PV is JAK2-driven overproduction of red cells, often with raised white cells and platelets. The resulting hyperviscosity and activated platelets make thrombosis the dominant complication, both arterial (MI, unstable angina, stroke, TIA) and venous (DVT, PE). That is why every patient gets ASA with a hematocrit target below 0.45.

  • C, D AML and myelofibrosis are listed as PV complications. They are later transformations in a minority, not the most likely manifestation.
  • A infections are not a feature of PV. White cells are increased, not deficient.

b3-w11-module-q2-2.html:
From 01 - Innate Immunity and WBCs. Neutrophils are the “first responders” to bacterial and fungal infection: 50-70% of circulating WBCs, with 55-60% of the marrow given over to making them. They kill bacteria by iron restriction, destruction of the cell wall and membrane, and the oxidative burst (NADPH oxidase plus myeloperoxidase, which colours pus).

  • A lymphocyte - adaptive immunity; the lecture ties them chiefly to viral defence.
  • C eosinophil - parasites and allergic reactions.
  • D basophil - allergic responses through histamine release.

b3-w11-module-q20-20.html:
From 07 - Specialized Testing for Hematological Malignancies. One marrow sample (from the PSIS) feeds every test listed, which is why the answer is all five.

  • A morphology - all stages of hematopoiesis, the M:E ratio (normally 1:1 to 3:1) and dysplasia.
  • B flow cytometry - the immunophenotype: immaturity, myeloid, B, T and NK markers.
  • C cytogenetics - chromosome changes in structure or location (karyotype, FISH).
  • D molecular diagnostics - mutations in the genetic material.
  • E core biopsy pathology - architecture and cellularity (about 100 minus age, %).

A-D are done on the liquid aspirate; only E needs the solid core.

b3-w11-module-q22-22.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia. Aplastic anemia (pancytopenia with a hypocellular, fat-replaced marrow) has hereditary forms, and the lecture names two:

  • A Fanconi anemia - short stature, triphalangeal thumb, skin pigmentation, congenital heart and kidney defects.
  • D dyskeratosis congenita - oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, lacy pigmentation of the neck and back.
  • C 5q deletion - an acquired clonal change: MDS with del(5q), with macrocytic anemia, thrombocytosis and a response to lenalidomide (09 - Myelodysplastic Syndrome).
  • B SF3B1 - likewise an acquired somatic mutation found in MDS, not an inherited marrow-failure syndrome.

flags.title: Option B is not in the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note mentions SF3B1. Calling it an acquired MDS mutation is from general knowledge; verify it before relying on it.

b3-w11-module-q25-25.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. The lecture splits the APL workup into tests that suggest it and tests that confirm it:

  • A suggestive: blasts with multiple (2+) Auer rods (“faggot cells”).
  • C suggestive: on flow, the myeloblasts are HLA-DR negative.
  • D confirmatory: t(15;17) on karyotype.
  • E confirmatory: the PML-RARα fusion on FISH (or NGS).
  • B del 5q - marks MDS with del(5q), not APL.
  • F HBB - the β-globin gene. Its changes cause hemoglobinopathies, not leukemia.

b3-w11-module-q26-26.html:
From 07 - Specialized Testing for Hematological Malignancies. The aspirate is the liquid part of the marrow, and it is used for four tests: morphology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics. FISH is a form of cytogenetics, so it is run on the aspirate.

  • A CBC - done on peripheral blood, not marrow.
  • B immunohistochemistry - a pathology stain on tissue sections, so it belongs to the core biopsy, not the aspirate.
  • D bone density - a test of mineralised bone, not of marrow cells.

b3-w11-module-q27-27.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia. Pancytopenia with a normal MCV, very low reticulocytes and a markedly hypocellular marrow is aplastic anemia: the marrow is empty, not deficient. The lecture's management is supportive blood products, plus antibiotics for febrile neutropenia, then immunosuppression (ATG, cyclosporine, steroids) or a marrow transplant if the patient is eligible. A 12-year-old is a strong transplant candidate.

  • B, C - iron fixes iron deficiency, which he does not have, and EPO cannot drive a marrow that has no progenitors.
  • D - support is given as individual blood components. Transfused neutrophils live about 10 hours (01 - Innate Immunity), so whole blood cannot restore a white count.

b3-w11-module-q28-28.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. DIC together with numerous blasts carrying multiple Auer rods is the lecture's picture of APL (AML-M3). The malignant promyelocyte granules release procoagulant and fibrinolytic activity. It is confirmed by t(15;17), the PML-RARα fusion, and treated with ATRA plus arsenic, because early deaths are mostly from hemorrhage.

  • A t(9;22) - the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL) of CML.
  • B t(11;14) - cyclin D1 overexpression in mantle cell lymphoma (05 - Approach to Lymphoma).
  • D t(8;21) - a different AML translocation. The notes link the DIC-plus-Auer-rods picture only to t(15;17).

b3-w11-module-q30-30.html:
From 06 - Approach to Thrombocytosis. The lecture states that secondary (reactive) causes are more common than primary ones, and it makes no exception for extreme counts (≥ 1000 × 109/L, up to 5% of cases). The workup is the same at any height: repeat the CBC, then look for infection (bacterial is the most common), inflammation, tissue damage, hemorrhage, iron deficiency, hyposplenism, non-hematologic cancer or rebound after myelosuppression.

An MPN (ET, PV, PMF, CML) becomes the working diagnosis only when no secondary cause is found, or when the count persists after the cause is treated. “Likely primary” is therefore false.

b3-w11-module-q33-33.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. The lecture's AML diagnostic workup is built around the disease and its emergencies. Bone density is in none of it: it is an osteoporosis test and plays no part in planning induction.

  • A marrow studies - aspirate, flow, karyotype and FISH make the diagnosis and set the cytogenetic risk.
  • B MUGA or echo, plus ECG - required before chemotherapy, because anthracyclines are cardiotoxic.
  • D TLS labs - LDH, urate, PO4, Ca and K, since rapid cell turnover can trigger tumour lysis.
  • E DIC labs - INR, aPTT, fibrinogen and FDP. The lecture calls coagulopathy (especially in APL) the difference between life and death.

b3-w11-module-q43-43.html:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology (the critical appraisal section). The primary endpoint is the main outcome of the trial, and it drives the power calculation and sample size (B).

  • A - endpoints are part of the written study protocol, fixed before enrolment, in the same way the non-inferiority margin is pre-specified. Choosing an endpoint after seeing the data is a source of bias.
  • C - outcomes should ideally be assessed blind to allocation, and a trial is only as useful as the relevance of what it measures.
  • D - power depends on the number of events in each group, so an endpoint that rarely occurs during follow-up leaves the trial underpowered.

All four statements are true.

b3-w11-new-q10-10.html:
From 03 - Approach to Leukopenia. The lecture numbers the febrile neutropenia protocol in this order:

  • 1. C stabilize - ABCs, IV fluids, and O2 for hypoxia.
  • 2. B investigate - CBC and differential, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, transaminases and bilirubin, blood and urine cultures, and a CXR.
  • 3. A focused history and exam - mouth, pharynx and sinuses, lungs, GI (no DRE), GU, skin and catheter sites, and mental status.
  • 4. D empiric antibiotics - IV imipenem or piperacillin-tazobactam, adding vancomycin for a line or skin infection or instability.

Cultures come before antibiotics so the organism can still be grown, but the antibiotics must not be delayed: this is an oncologic emergency.

b3-w11-new-q12-12.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Every PV patient gets ASA 81 mg daily and a target Hct below 0.45, and the risk category then decides everything else. High risk (age ≥ 60 or prior thrombosis) means hydroxyurea with or without phlebotomy. Low risk means phlebotomy. At 45 with no prior clot she is low risk, so she needs phlebotomy plus ASA.

  • A - leaves out the ASA that every patient receives.
  • C, D - hydroxyurea (cytoreduction) is reserved for high-risk patients, and she is not one.

b3-w11-new-q15-15.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 10 - In-Class. The lecture gives primary myelofibrosis a characteristic blood film: teardrop cells (A) and a leukoerythroblastic picture (B), usually with splenomegaly and cytopenias.

  • C reticulin fibres - these are a marrow finding. Reticulin or collagen fibrosis (grade 2/3) on the core biopsy is a major diagnostic criterion, but fibres do not circulate and cannot be seen on a blood film.
  • D - pairs a true film finding with that marrow finding.

As the stem is worded, the supportable set is A and B, and no option offers that pair.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is E, which includes C. 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis places reticulin fibrosis on the marrow biopsy (a PMF major criterion), not on the blood film, which shows teardrops and a leukoerythroblastic picture. The key only works if the stem means “film or marrow”. As written, A and B are the true findings, and no option offers that pair.

b3-w11-new-q16-16.html:
From 04 - Approach to Normocytic Anemia.

  • A true - dyskeratosis congenita is one of the two hereditary forms the lecture names, with Fanconi anemia. It presents with oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy and lacy pigmentation.
  • B false - aplastic anemia is marrow failure: a hypocellular marrow replaced by fat, most often idiopathic. It is not a clonal neoplasm, which is what separates it from MDS (an abnormal marrow) and from myelophthisis (a replaced marrow).
  • C true as keyed - aplastic anemia is more common outside Western countries.

With A and C true and B false, the answer is D, and E fails because of B.

flags.title: Not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: No lecture note gives regional incidence figures for aplastic anemia, so statement C (Mexico vs the United States) rests on general knowledge. Verify it before relying on it.

b3-w11-new-q8-8.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia. In tumour lysis, dying tumour cells spill their contents into the blood. High K causes arrhythmia. High PO4 binds calcium, and the resulting hypocalcemia causes seizures and arrhythmia. Uric acid and phosphate injure the kidney, and the result is metabolic acidosis, renal failure and death, which together amount to multiorgan failure.

  • A decreased tissue perfusion - the mechanism of leukostasis: large, sticky blasts lodge in small vessels and cause local hypoxemia.
  • B very high blast count - a risk factor for TLS and leukostasis, not a consequence of either.
  • D intracranial hemorrhage - the typical early death in APL, caused by DIC.

b3-w11-ra-q4-4.html:
From 06 - Multiple Myeloma. The spine is the most common site of myeloma bone disease, so back pain with tender vertebrae fits. Add anemia below 100 g/L (the A of CRAB) and rouleaux on the film, and the picture is myeloma. The next steps are SPEP/UPEP for an M spike, serum free light chains, calcium and creatinine, and a skeletal survey.

  • B follicular lymphoma - indolent painless lymphadenopathy. It causes neither rouleaux nor vertebral disease.
  • C AML - marrow failure with circulating blasts. It can cause sternal bone pain, but rouleaux are not an AML finding.
  • D MDS - cytopenias with dysplasia in an older patient, and no paraprotein to stack the red cells.

b3-w11-sa-q2-2.html:
From 04 - Approach to Leukemia and 10 - In-Class. Auer rods are the finding that marks a blast as myeloid. The AML film shows large blasts with Auer rods, and they are how the lecture tells M blasts from L blasts, with flow cytometry to confirm. The CBC here already shows blasts, so seeing Auer rods is what makes it AML.

  • B BCR-ABL - t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome of CML.
  • C JAK2 - the driver of the MPNs (PV in 90-95% of cases, ET and PMF in 50-60%).
  • D dysplasia - the defining feature of MDS, not of AML.

b3-w11-sa-q4-4.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. A raised WBC count does not say which white cell is raised. The lecture says that is exactly what the differential is for, and its approach begins by sorting the cells by lineage (neutrophil, lymphocyte, eosinophil and so on) and by maturity. Every later decision depends on that answer.

  • A reticulocyte count - measures red cell production and is used to work up an anemia. Her hemoglobin is normal.
  • B INR - a coagulation test with no bearing on the white count.
  • D flow cytometry - establishes clonality later, for example in a lymphocytosis that persists after 4-6 weeks or when blasts are seen. It is not a first test.

b3-w11-sa-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis. Granulocytes mature through myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band and neutrophil, and all of those stages belong in the marrow. The lecture says only fully developed neutrophils should be seen in the peripheral blood.

Having no myeloblasts or promyelocytes in the blood is one of the features of a reactive process. Any circulating blasts favour a neoplasm, which is why 10%, 5% and 3% are all abnormal. Even the “under 10%” blast count of chronic-phase CML is a disease finding, not a normal range.

b3-w11-sa-q7-7.html:
From 02 - Approach to Leukocytosis and 05 - Approach to Erythrocytosis. Itching after a bath or shower is aquagenic pruritus, and early satiety with abdominal discomfort suggests splenomegaly. In a man over 60 with fatigue, that is the lecture's picture of polycythemia vera, and JAK2 (V617F or exon 12) is present in 90-95% of cases.

  • A Philadelphia chromosome - CML, which presents with a high WBC and basophilia rather than aquagenic itch.
  • B t(15;17) - APL, an acute leukemia that presents with bleeding and DIC.
  • C marrow fibrosis - PMF also causes early satiety and splenomegaly, but it is not linked to aquagenic pruritus and carries JAK2 in only 50-60% of cases. JAK2 is the more likely finding.

b3-w12-module-q10-10.html:
From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma. Once the biopsy has made the diagnosis, the workup stages the lymphoma and checks that the patient can tolerate treatment. PET (FDG uptake by the tumour) with CT is the staging scan. The CBC belongs to the baseline bloods, with chemistry, LDH, HBV/HCV and HIV, and shows any marrow involvement as low counts. A marrow biopsy, cardiac wall-motion study and LP are added when indicated.

  • B skeletal survey - the standard of care for the lytic lesions of myeloma (06), not for lymphoma staging.
  • D, E - bone density and cholesterol play no part in staging or in fitness for chemotherapy.

b3-w12-module-q12-12.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass and the mediastinal chart in 06 - Multiple Myeloma. The lecture divides the mediastinum into three compartments:

  • A anterior (prevascular) - thymus, internal thoracic arteries, nodes and fat.
  • D middle (visceral) - heart, pericardium, great vessels, phrenic and recurrent laryngeal nerves.
  • B posterior (paravertebral) - esophagus, descending aorta, vagus nerves, azygos system and sympathetic trunk.
  • C inferior - not a compartment in this scheme. The diaphragm is only the inferior border of the mediastinum.

On the lecture, the option that is not a compartment is C.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is D (middle). Both 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass and the chart in 06 - Multiple Myeloma list the middle mediastinum as one of the three compartments, with named contents. The one option absent from the lecture's model is C, inferior. The classical anatomical scheme, which splits the mediastinum into superior and inferior, would make inferior a division too, but under neither scheme is “middle” not a compartment. The key is probably a relettering error for C.

b3-w12-module-q14-14.html:
From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. The lecture lists the vagus nerves among the contents of the posterior mediastinum. The chart's mnemonic for that compartment is TADA, 2 GUS'S: thoracic aorta and duct, the azygos, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, esophagus, vagus, sympathetic trunk, and greater and lesser splanchnic nerves.

  • A anterior - thymus, internal thoracic arteries, connective tissue, nodes and fat (I CAN'T).
  • C middle - its nerves are the phrenic nerves and the recurrent laryngeal nerve (whose compression causes hoarseness), not the vagus trunks.

b3-w12-module-q27-27.html:
From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma and 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies. In lymphoma, surgery is used to make the diagnosis. An excisional biopsy of a node is the best sample, ahead of a core biopsy and far ahead of a needle aspirate, because it preserves the architecture and provides tissue for flow, FISH and molecular studies. The pharmacology lecture's modality table gives surgery the role “diagnosis ONLY”. It is only occasionally used to control symptoms or complications.

A fails because lymphoma is a systemic disease. Removing the visible nodes leaves the rest of the disease untouched, which is why chemotherapy, not resection, is the main modality.

b3-w12-module-q6-6.html:
From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for 85% of lymphomas and Hodgkin for 15%. The single most common subtype is an NHL, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, followed by follicular lymphoma.

The two also differ in who they affect. Hodgkin is a disease of young adults (median age at diagnosis 26, males more than females) that spreads contiguously from node to node. NHL mostly affects older patients and can be nodal or extranodal.

b3-w12-module-q8-8.html:
From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma. Ann Arbor staging depends on the number of regions involved and where they sit relative to the diaphragm (the dashed line in each figure).

  • Image 2 is stage 1 (D) - a single node region.
  • Image 4 is stage 2 (C) - three regions, all above the diaphragm.
  • Image 1 is stage 3 (A) - nodes both above and below the diaphragm.
  • Image 3 is stage 4 (B) - the most extensive figure, with disease scattered on both sides, including a larger central abdominal lesion.

Stage IV means diffuse extralymphatic involvement, such as the bone marrow. A or B is added for the absence or presence of B symptoms.

flags.title: Image 3 is stage 4 mostly by elimination
flags.html: Images 1 and 3 both show disease on both sides of the diaphragm, which is stage III. The lecture defines stage IV as diffuse involvement of an extralymphatic organ, and the drawing does not clearly show one. The central abdominal cluster may be meant as an organ. Read Image 3 as the most extensive figure and match it to stage 4 by elimination.

b3-w12-module-q9-9.html:
From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma. The lecture names chemotherapy as the main treatment modality: more than 100 drugs, given orally or IV, in repeated cycles such as R-CHOP every 21 days for B-cell NHL and ABVD for Hodgkin. It works systemically, which suits a disease spread through the lymphatic system.

  • A surgery - used for diagnosis (biopsy), not treatment.
  • C radiation - acts only inside the radiation field. It follows chemotherapy in stage I/II disease or is used for palliation.
  • D stem cell transplant - not among the lecture's standard modalities, which are chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy (rituximab), combinations, surgery, and watch and wait.

b3-w12-new-q10-10.html:
From 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas (the table of main differences between HL and NHL).

  • i true - classical HL spreads contiguously, from one node to the adjacent node. NHL can spread contiguously or non-contiguously.
  • ii false - the statement is reversed. HL is nodal, and extranodal disease is rare. NHL is the one that is nodal or extranodal.
  • iii true - in classical HL all cells are mature, while NHL can be mature (lymphocytic) or immature (lymphoblastic).

So the true statements are i and iii, which is B.

flags.title: Statements ii and iii have lost their numerals
flags.html: Only the first statement carries its label (“i)”). The other two appear as a numbered list (1, 2) below it, so read list item 1 as ii and item 2 as iii when matching them to the options.

b3-w12-new-q15-15.html:
From 06 - Multiple Myeloma. R-ISS stage 3 requires β2-microglobulin ≥ 5.5 together with high-risk FISH or a high LDH. The high-risk FISH abnormalities the lecture lists are t(4;14), t(14;16) and del(17p).

  • A t(4;14) and C t(14;16) - both on that high-risk list, so both point towards stage 3.
  • B t(14;6) (usually written t(6;14)) and D t(11;14) - neither is on the list, so neither makes a patient stage 3. These are the abnormalities that do not indicate R-ISS 3.

flags.title: The key gives two letters, but option E already combines them
flags.html: The bank keys this as “B, D”, yet option E is “B and D”. Read as a single-best-answer question, the intended choice is E. The two agree in content.

b3-w12-new-q21-21.html:
From 08 - Radiation Oncology and 04 - Classification and Testing for Lymphomas. Early-stage HL is now treated with combined-modality therapy: a short course of chemotherapy followed by involved-field radiation. Radiation doses and field sizes are being reduced, especially in favourable cases, and bulky disease is treated like advanced disease.

  • A - radiation alone (sub-total nodal irradiation) was the historical cure. It was abandoned because of late toxicity: second cancers and cardiac disease.
  • B - gets the order backwards. Chemotherapy comes first.
  • C and D - both describe chemotherapy before radiation, the lecture's sequence. The notes do not give cycle numbers.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is D, but the bank's own note says “chemotherapy for unfavourable is 4 cycles”, which makes D (“2 cycles”) false as written. 08 - Radiation Oncology supports chemotherapy before radiation for favourable early-stage disease, which is what C says. The vault notes give no cycle counts. In the standard regimen (from general knowledge, not the notes), favourable disease gets 2 cycles and then radiation, and unfavourable disease gets 4. On that reading C is the answer. Check the lecture slides.

b4-w13-module-q19-19:
From 07 - The Normal Healthy Microbiome. The note defines the four terms by where the microbe is and whether it causes disease: commensal = usual habitat; coloniser = unusual habitat, no disease; infection = wrong compartment or outside invader causing disease; dysbiosis = a shifted community.

  • A S. epidermidis on skin: a usual resident, so i (commensal).
  • B S. aureus on skin: Staphylococcus is listed among skin commensals (i), and eczema is the skin dysbiosis where too few coagulase-negative staphylococci let S. aureus expand (iv). It becomes infection only once it breaches the skin (cellulitis, abscess).
  • C E. coli in the peritoneum: a gut organism breaching its compartment, i.e. peritonitis, so iii (infection).
  • D Candida overgrowth in the vagina: vulvovaginal candidiasis is the note's example of iv (dysbiosis).
  • E Pseudomonas in a chronic wound: the note's textbook ii (coloniser).
b4-w13-module-q23-23:
From 14 - Pathology of Acute Inflammation. An abscess is purulent (suppurative) inflammation: pus, made mainly of neutrophils, localised to a cavity created by tissue destruction, typically from pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus causing liquefactive necrosis.

  • Fibrinous: marked permeability lets fibrinogen out, giving fibrin deposits in the pleura, pericardium or meninges (e.g. post-MI pericarditis).
  • Serous: cell-poor fluid - effusion, ascites, blister.
  • Ulcer: a local defect in a mucosal surface, not a walled-off pus collection.
  • Granulomatous: a pattern of chronic inflammation (epithelioid macrophages ringed by T cells; 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation), not an acute pus collection.

b4-w13-module-q26-26.html:
From 14 - Pathology of Acute Inflammation and 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. Neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at a site of inflammation, drawn by chemotactic factors such as IL-8, and pus - the hallmark of acute purulent inflammation - is mainly neutrophils.

  • Eosinophils: allergic reactions and parasitic infections (major basic protein).
  • Lymphocytes and plasma cells: cells of chronic inflammation and adaptive immunity. 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation makes the contrast explicit: neutrophils are not typically seen in chronic inflammation unless an acute process is running alongside it.

b4-w13-module-q4-4:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. Culture is a direct method that grows the organism: its stated purpose is to isolate individual colonies, and it is the only one of the three main methods that gives susceptibility results, since isolates go on to antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

  • B is serology: an indirect method that detects the host's antibody and so gives proof of exposure. Culture shows a living, growing pathogen instead.
  • D fails because culture is not rapid - plates are first read at 24 h, anaerobes at 48 h. Molecular methods are the rapid option.
b4-w13-module-q5-5:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The two antibody classes need different sampling. IgM is made early and briefly after first exposure, so a single acute serum (drawn at onset) can indicate current infection. IgG is also left over from past exposure, so it needs paired acute and convalescent sera (2-6 weeks apart), and a fourfold rise in titre is what diagnoses current infection.

  • A: one IgG only shows infection at some unknown time, or immunity. It cannot date the infection.
  • D: IgM does not need pairing. It is short-lived, and its presence in one acute sample is the whole point.
b4-w13-module-q6-6:
From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. Skeletal muscle contraction generates heat (ATP → ADP + Pi + energy). When core temperature is raised, the body tries to minimise heat production by muscle, which the note gives as the reason we cut back physical activity on hot days. It is a behavioural effector.

  • B: sweating is a heat-loss effector, so the body wants more of it in the heat, not less.
  • C: brown adipose tissue thermogenesis is inhibited in the heat, but that is metabolic (thyroid-driven), not a consequence of activity. It is also minor in adults.
  • D: evaporation and warm exhalation from the lungs also lose heat, so reducing them would be counterproductive.
b4-w13-module-q8-8:
From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. Each effector in the note runs in one direction for heat production and the other for heat loss.

  • i BAT → D: brown fat metabolism (driven by T3/T4) produces heat internally.
  • ii Sweat glands → C: cholinergic sweating cools by evaporation of water from the skin.
  • iii Skeletal muscle → B: contraction and shivering generate heat.
  • iv Lungs → E: airway evaporation and exhalation of warm air lose heat (dogs rely on panting).
  • v Cutaneous vessels → A: sympathetic vasoconstriction shunts blood from the skin to conserve heat, and vasodilation increases skin blood flow to lose it.

b4-w13-new-q7-7.html:
From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. The note frames thermoregulation as a negative-feedback loop: thermoreceptors → hypothalamus → effectors, holding the regulated variable at its set point.

  • Effector → D: sweat glands carry out heat loss.
  • Thermoreceptors → B: sensory neurons activated by warmth or cold, found in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera and brain.
  • Regulated variable → A: core temperature held at about 37°C (normal 35.5-37.7°C).
  • Feedforward → C: this pairing is left by elimination. The note defines feedforward as the body acting in anticipation of a thermal change (e.g. responding to a cold breeze before core temperature drops).

flags.title: Option C is a poor fit for feedforward
flags.html: 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature defines a feedforward mechanism as acting before the change happens. “Body temperature during hyperthermia” is a state of the regulated variable, not an anticipatory response, so the fourth pairing only works by elimination. Learn the definition, not this pairing.

b4-w13-sa-q2-2.html:
From 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. Antigen from an organism a macrophage has ingested is handled by the antigen-presenting-cell route. The APC internalises the organism, breaks it into peptides with lysosomal enzymes, and displays them in the groove of MHC class II (HLA class II) to CD4+ helper T cells. The note restricts MHC II to APCs such as macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells.

  • B: MHC class I samples the cell's own internal contents for CD8+ T cells, not phagocytosed material.
  • C, D, E: cytosolic proteases, the endoplasmic reticulum and TAP transporters are the loading machinery of that class I route, so they go with B.

flags.title: The class I machinery is not in the notes
flags.html: 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher supports A (lysosomal processing onto MHC II in APCs). It does not describe the proteasome, TAP or ER loading steps of class I presentation, so the reasoning against C-E comes from general immunology.

b4-w13-sa-q5-5.html:
From 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. Co-stimulation is the APC's second signal, B7 (CD80/86) binding CD28, delivered alongside TcR-antigen-MHC binding. It drives the helper T cell into growth and clonal proliferation, largely through more IL-2 and IL-2 receptors. Part of what keeps the activated clone expanding is pro-survival proteins such as Bcl-XL.

  • A: loading antigen into MHC II is the first signal's job, done by the APC before co-stimulation matters.
  • B: anergy is what happens when co-stimulation is blocked (09 - Autoimmunity, 06 - Approach to Allergy: CD28:CD80 blockade).
  • D: co-stimulation increases IL-2 transcription rather than inhibiting it.
  • E: activated T cells ramp up metabolism for proliferation. They do not slow it.

flags.title: Bcl-XL is not in the vault notes
flags.html: The notes cover co-stimulation through B7-CD28 and IL-2, and anergy when it is blocked, which rules out B and D. The Bcl-XL survival mechanism in the keyed option is not mentioned in any Block 4 note, so that part is from general immunology. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w13-sa-q6-6:
From 10 - Approach to the Assessment of a Patient with Fever. The rule is to investigate when the diagnosis is uncertain. Dysuria, frequency and urgency with no fever or flank pain look like simple cystitis, but a new sexual partner puts urethritis from N. gonorrhoeae or C. trachomatis on the differential, and those present the same way. So test the site of inflammation:

  • Urinalysis/dipstick: the targeted test the lecture names for suspected UTI.
  • Urine culture and sensitivity: confirms the organism and guides the antibiotic.
  • NAAT for GC/CT: the molecular test for an STI, which culture of urine will not find.

E fails for this patient: the lecture allows skipping culture only for a clearly likely UTI, and the sexual history makes this one unclear.
b4-w13-sa-q8-8:
From 02 - Classification of Different Microbes. The note gives one seven-step cycle for virtually all viruses: attachment → entry → uncoating → protein synthesis → genome replication → assembly → release.

The logic fixes the order. The genome must be uncoated before the host ribosomes can translate it. Viral proteins, including the polymerases, are needed to replicate the genome. Only then can new genomes and structural proteins be assembled into virions.

  • A, B, C put protein synthesis before uncoating, which cannot happen while the genome is still inside the capsid. C also assembles virions before there are genomes to package.
  • E replicates the genome before making the proteins that replication depends on.
reviews-b4-Q12:
From 14 - Pathology of Acute Inflammation. An abscess is walled off, and its pus-filled necrotic centre has no blood vessels, so antibiotics struggle to reach it. That is why the definitive treatment is incision and drainage: open the skin and clear the contents. Deep organ abscesses may need a more invasive surgical approach.

In-Class - Fever gives the S. aureus-specific reason. Coagulase and fibrinogen-binding proteins build a fibrin pseudocapsule around the abscess community, which keeps leukocytes out and blocks antibiotics. Abscesses therefore will not resolve on antibiotics alone. Antibiotics follow drainage, to treat surrounding cellulitis or spread, and contact precautions apply if the patient is flagged for MRSA.
b4-w14-meds2024-q11-11:
From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents and 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. Herd immunity protects the few susceptible people because the pathogen is unlikely to find them. The proportion who must be immune depends on the agent's transmissibility. Highly infectious, high-R0 diseases such as measles need the highest coverage. Measles is airborne, and transmission has been reported up to 90 minutes after the index case left the room.

  • B: a short incubation period changes how fast an outbreak unfolds, not how many secondary cases each case produces.
  • C: lethality is not transmissibility. A virus that kills its host is not thereby easier to spread.
  • D: a stable antigen, if anything, makes durable herd immunity easier to reach, not harder.
b4-w14-meds2024-q12-12:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. Sepsis is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response. The cardiovascular picture is tachycardia with hypotension, as the heart compensates for arteriolar vasodilation and capillary leak, so a falling heart rate is the odd one out.

  • A: low BP from vasodilation and loss of intravascular fluid. When it does not respond to fluids, it is septic shock.
  • C: oliguria is the kidney pillar of early recognition.
  • D: hypoxia (and ARDS) is the lung pillar, alongside tachypnea.
  • E: microcirculatory dysfunction clogs capillaries, so tissues are underperfused, the mechanism behind multi-organ failure.

b4-w14-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture separates early treatment (early, appropriate, broad-spectrum antibiotics) from life support, which is invasive support for failing organs that buys time and fixes nothing. Vancomycin is an antibiotic that treats the infection itself, so it belongs to early treatment, not life support.

  • Vasopressors: cardiovascular support for hypotension that fluids have not corrected.
  • Dialysis (or CRRT): renal support.
  • Mechanical ventilation: pulmonary support, along with prone positioning, lung-protective ventilation and ECMO.

flags.title: The bank's key line misnames vancomycin
flags.html: The key line calls vancomycin an “antibody treatment”. It is an antibiotic (a glycopeptide that blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking; 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1). The keyed letter is right, but the reason given with it is not.

b4-w14-meds2024-q16-16:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. MRSA carries mecA, which makes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein that β-lactams cannot bind. Every β-lactam therefore fails. Vancomycin binds peptidoglycan directly and covers most Gram-positives including MRSA, and the lecture's cellulitis case says to consider it when the patient has MRSA risk factors.

  • Cloxacillin: an anti-staphylococcal penicillin, good for MSSA and GAS cellulitis, but it is exactly the drug MRSA resists.
  • Amoxicillin: an aminopenicillin without anti-staphylococcal activity.
  • Carbapenem: the broadest spectrum of all, but the lecture notes it still misses MRSA and VRE.

b4-w14-meds2024-q2-2.html:
From 06 - New Vaccine Platforms and 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. A subunit vaccine uses one component of the pathogen as the antigen rather than the whole organism. The Pfizer vaccine makes the immune system respond to a single protein, the spike, so of these four classes it fits subunit best. It contains no live virus, so it cannot shed or cause a positive PCR test.

  • A: live attenuated vaccines (MMR) contain a weakened, replicating pathogen.
  • B: inactivated whole-cell vaccines (IPV, hepatitis A) contain the entire killed organism.
  • C: toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria) target an inactivated bacterial toxin, and SARS-CoV-2 is a virus.

flags.title: The lecture treats mRNA as its own platform
flags.html: 06 - New Vaccine Platforms lists RNA vaccines as a next-generation platform, separate from the traditional protein subunit vaccines (Novavax, seasonal influenza), whose protein is made in bacteria and injected. “Subunit” is only the best of the four options offered. If “mRNA vaccine” is an option, choose it.

b4-w14-meds2024-q20-20:
From 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 2 and 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. E. coli is an aerobic Gram-negative bacillus. Metronidazole (Flagyl) is the anaerobe drug on the spectrum map. In the peritonitis case it is added to ceftriaxone precisely because ceftriaxone lacks anaerobic cover, and it does nothing for an aerobic E. coli UTI.

  • Aminoglycosides: on the map for Gram-negatives.
  • Amoxicillin: has Gram-negative activity against susceptible E. coli. The cystitis case says to check prior susceptibility reports because of resistance such as ESBLs.
  • Meropenem and piperacillin-tazobactam: both cover E. coli, but they are broader than needed, so they are appropriate yet not first choice.
b4-w14-meds2024-q23-23:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Enzymatic degradation means the bacterium makes an enzyme that destroys the drug. ESBL (extended-spectrum β-lactamase) inactivates most β-lactams except carbapenems, and ESBL E. coli is the lecture's example. This is a major resistance mechanism in Gram-negatives, and the ESBL gene is often acquired on a plasmid.

  • A: D-Ala-D-Ala → D-Ala-D-Lac is target alteration (VRE). The drug stays intact but cannot bind.
  • C: porin mutation restricts entry (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas).
  • D: efflux pumps remove the drug (P. aeruginosa).
b4-w14-meds2024-q24-24:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Efflux pumps actively move antibiotic back out of the bacterial cell. This is one arm of “preventing antibiotic accumulation”, whose net effect is lower intracellular drug levels. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the lecture's example.

  • C: porin mutation belongs to the same family but works by decreasing entry through the outer membrane, not by removing drug already inside.
  • A: target alteration (D-Ala-D-Lac in VRE), so the drug cannot bind.
  • B: ESBL destroys the drug enzymatically.
b4-w14-meds2024-q25-25:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Vancomycin works by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the peptidoglycan precursor and blocking cell-wall cross-linking. Vancomycin-resistant enterococci change that terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac, a structural change to the binding site itself (“altered target”), so the drug can no longer interfere with wall synthesis.

  • B: ESBL is enzymatic degradation of the drug, not a change in the wall target.
  • C: porin mutation restricts entry.
  • D: efflux pumps remove the drug.

B, C and D all lower the drug available at its target. Only A alters the target structure.

b4-w14-meds2024-q3-3.html:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines (Block 1). Both are non-live subunit vaccines. A polysaccharide vaccine uses capsular sugar alone and is not immunogenic in children under 2. A conjugate joins that polysaccharide to a protein, which gives a T-cell-dependent response, so it is more immunogenic and can be given at all ages (Prevnar 13, Hib, meningococcal). The lecture records no added danger: as non-live vaccines, both cannot replicate or cause disease.

  • A matches the lecture: more immunogenic, and just as safe.
  • B adds a safety penalty the lecture never states.
  • C is backwards: the conjugate contains the polysaccharide.
  • D: conjugates are non-live, not live attenuated.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys B (“more immunogenic but slightly more dangerous”). 09 - Introduction to Vaccines says conjugates are more immunogenic and usable at every age. It lists non-live vaccines as safe because they cannot replicate or cause disease, and says nothing about conjugates being riskier. The material supports A. Check the source key before relying on B.

b4-w14-meds2024-q31-31:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Endemic means the constant presence of a disease in a population, or its usual prevalence there. A TB rate that has stayed persistently high on reserves for years, driven by lasting structural conditions (overcrowding, poor ventilation, food insecurity), is an endemic pattern, however unacceptable the level is.

  • Sporadic: infrequent and irregular cases (e.g. SARS-CoV-1), each acted on rapidly.
  • Epidemic: a rise above what is expected (e.g. the influenza spike each winter). A chronic baseline is not a rise above itself.
  • Pandemic: an epidemic spread across countries or continents.
b4-w14-meds2024-q32-32:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Isolation separates sick people with a contagious disease from those who are not sick, and it lasts for the period of communicability. Quarantine restricts the movement of people who were exposed, to see whether they become sick, and it lasts for the incubation period. Taylor is a confirmed, symptomatic case, so she isolates. Drake is an asymptomatic close contact, so he quarantines. SARS-CoV-2 is communicable from 48 h before symptoms, and its incubation is 2-14 days.

  • A swaps the two terms.
  • C treats a confirmed case as merely exposed.
  • D treats an exposed contact as a case.
  • E is the distractor.

b4-w14-meds2024-q33-33.html:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Every option except propagated is a common-source outbreak, so the discriminator is how long exposure lasted. In a point source, exposure is brief and all cases fall within one incubation period, giving a sharp rise and fall. A continuous source exposes cases to the same source over an extended period, which flattens and widens the curve. An intermittent source produces repeated small spikes from on-off exposure (Legionella biofilms). A propagated outbreak spreads person to person, with no single source.

The stem says the hedgehogs could not be removed until enough data had been gathered, so exposure went on for as long as it took to implicate them. That describes a continuous common source, not a brief point exposure.
