flags.title: The epidemic curve is missing
flags.html: The stem says “the epidemic curve is shown below”, but the bank has no image. The question was meant to be answered from the curve's shape.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys A (point common-source). 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation defines a point source as exposure over a brief period, with cases within one incubation period. A source that stayed in place until epidemiologic data implicated it is ongoing exposure, which the lecture calls continuous common-source (B). The missing curve may have shown a single sharp peak, but the text as written supports B.

b4-w14-meds2024-q34-34:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Both measures exist to stop spread, and neither treats symptoms. Isolation separates sick people with a contagious disease from people who are not sick, for the period of communicability, so it is the measure for someone who has developed COVID-19. Quarantine restricts people who were exposed, for the incubation period, to see whether they become sick.

  • A: quarantine is for exposed people, not affected ones. The statement describes isolation.
  • B, D: neither measure is a treatment, and neither reduces symptoms.

b4-w14-meds2024-q35-35.html:
From 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation. Check each statement against the lecture's four curve patterns.

  • A false: a continuous common source means cases exposed to the same source over an extended period, a property of the exposure, not a verdict that control measures failed.
  • B true: a point source is a single brief exposure, like one contaminated meal, with all cases within one incubation period.
  • C true: a propagated outbreak spreads person to person. Each generation of cases arrives about one incubation period after the last, so the curve shows successive peaks. The lecture names the person-to-person mechanism, not the peak spacing.
  • D (keyed true): the lecture defines intermittent common source as intermittent spikes from intermittent exposures to one source (e.g. Legionella). A curve that mixes continuous and propagated transmission describes a mixed outbreak.

flags.title: The key looks wrong for D
flags.html: The bank keys B, C and D. 05 - Approach to Public Health and Outbreak Investigation describes an intermittent common-source outbreak as repeated small spikes from on-off exposure to a single source, with no propagated component. A curve that combines continuous-source and propagated transmission is a mixed outbreak, which the lecture does not call intermittent. On the lecture's definitions the supported answer is B, C.

b4-w14-meds2024-q36-36:
From 09 - Antivirals. CMV needs the ganciclovir family: ganciclovir and valganciclovir cover CMV, while acyclovir and valacyclovir cover only HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV. Ganciclovir is IV only. Valganciclovir is its oral prodrug (bioavailability 55%), so it is the answer for a patient who wants a tablet.

  • A acyclovir and B valacyclovir: both oral options exist, but neither covers CMV.
  • C ganciclovir: right spectrum, wrong route (IV).
b4-w14-meds2024-q37-37:
From 09 - Antivirals. Neuraminidase frees newly formed influenza particles from the cell surface as they bud off. Neuraminidase inhibitors, oseltamivir (oral) and zanamivir (inhaled), therefore prevent budding and release.

  • Acyclovir: a guanosine analogue that inhibits herpesvirus DNA polymerase. It has no influenza activity.
  • Baloxavir marboxil: an influenza drug, but it is a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor that blocks RNA replication, an earlier step.
  • Foscarnet: a pyrophosphate analogue that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, used for drug-resistant herpesviruses and CMV.
b4-w14-meds2024-q38-38:
From 09 - Antivirals. Spectrum is the dividing line. Ganciclovir covers CMV (plus HSV and VZV), while valacyclovir, like acyclovir, covers HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV and not CMV.

  • A: both need activation. The lecture says these guanosine analogues are prodrugs that must be triphosphorylated, starting with viral thymidine kinase. Valacyclovir is additionally an oral prodrug of acyclovir.
  • B: ganciclovir and its prodrug valganciclovir share the same virus-specific activation, so both are selective.
  • C: valacyclovir treats HSV-1 and HSV-2, and the lecture recommends acyclovir or valacyclovir for them.
  • E: foscarnet and acyclovir both inhibit viral DNA polymerase, by different chemistry.
b4-w14-meds2024-q39-39:
From 09 - Antivirals. Acyclovir must be triphosphorylated before it can act on viral DNA polymerase, and the first phosphorylation is done by viral thymidine kinase. That enzyme is absent from uninfected cells, which is why the drug is inactive in normal cells and selective for infected ones.

  • A: hemagglutinin mediates attachment. Blocking virion release is what the neuraminidase inhibitors do.
  • C: foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analogue that inhibits viral DNA polymerase, not envelope binding.
  • D is backwards: ganciclovir is IV only, and oral valganciclovir is the prodrug designed to give 55% bioavailability.
b4-w14-meds2024-q6-6:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines (Block 1). The lecture's PrEP table gives each disease's pre-exposure options.

  • Measles: IG is N/A, so the only pre-exposure option is vaccine, given 2 weeks before.
  • Varicella: IG is N/A, so the only option is vaccine, given 4-6 weeks before. The lecture stresses there is no chemo- or immuno-PrEP for varicella.
  • Hepatitis A: has both options. IG 2 weeks before suits immunocompromised people, infants under 6 months, chronic liver disease or age over 40, and vaccine suits travellers 6 months or older.

So only i and ii are vaccine-only, which is A. B, C and D each include hepatitis A.
b4-w14-module-q1-1:
From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents. This is the lecture's definition almost word for word. Colonization is the presence of microorganisms in or on a host, with growth and multiplication, but without tissue invasion or cellular injury. Infection differs by involving cellular and tissue changes, and it runs from asymptomatic to severe depending on the organism and the host.

This matches 07 - The Normal Healthy Microbiome: a coloniser is a microbe in an unusual habitat that is not causing disease, e.g. Pseudomonas in a chronic wound. The statement is true.
b4-w14-module-q10-10:
From 09 - Antivirals. Acyclovir is cleared in the urine and needs renal dose adjustment. Renal dysfunction is listed among its adverse reactions, and the high IV doses used for meningitis/encephalitis (10 mg/kg q8h) make it most likely here.

  • B: anaphylaxis is an allergic reaction, and the patient has tolerated acyclovir before.
  • C: tinnitus (ototoxicity) is not on acyclovir's adverse-effect list. It is the classic toxicity of other drugs, such as the aminoglycosides.
  • D: eosinophilic pneumonia is not among its listed reactions. Those are malaise, renal dysfunction, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and cytopenias.
b4-w14-module-q11-11:
From 09 - Antivirals. The two influenza drugs act at different steps. Zanamivir (inhaled), like oseltamivir, is a neuraminidase inhibitor: it stops new virions budding off and being released from the infected cell. Baloxavir marboxil is a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor that blocks viral RNA replication. It is oral, single-dose and not available in Canada.

They share only their modest benefit (about 1 day shorter symptoms), not their mechanism, so the statement is false.
b4-w14-module-q15-15:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture's unifying mechanism is that any organ can fail because of microcirculatory dysfunction in the arteriolar–capillary networks: inflammation clogs and damages capillaries so they can no longer perfuse tissue or clear waste, and cellular injury then produces multiple organ dysfunction (MODS).

  • A MHC class II describes antigen-presenting cells, not a site of septic injury.
  • B the damage is in arterioles and capillaries, not the large vessels; hypotension follows arteriolar vasodilation and capillary leak.
  • D ARDS is one downstream organ failure among many (heart, brain, kidney, liver, clotting), not the unifying site.
b4-w14-module-q16-16:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture's four basic principles of sepsis management are early recognition, early treatment (broad-spectrum antibiotics, about 8% more mortality per hour of delay), source control (surgery, drainage, removing an infected device) and life support for failing organs.

  • B admission and ICU are settings, not links; it also drops recognition and life support.
  • C CPR and defibrillation belong to the cardiac-arrest chain, not sepsis.
  • D withholding antibiotics for cultures is exactly what the lecture forbids: draw cultures first only if it will not delay antibiotics.
b4-w14-module-q5-5:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Vancomycin is a glycopeptide that covers most Gram-positives, including MRSA, and its listed uses include oral therapy for C. difficile. Both route-specific statements are therefore true.

  • A true: IV vancomycin is the drug for MRSA (the IV choice for MRSA-risk sepsis or deep infection).
  • B true: oral vancomycin treats C. difficile colitis.
  • C false: E. coli is a Gram-negative bacillus and vancomycin is a Gram-positive drug, so E (all of the above) fails too.
b4-w14-module-q7-7:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The adverse-effects list gives aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) two signature toxicities: nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, which are why levels and renal function are watched.

  • A hypoglycemia is not an aminoglycoside effect; the lecture attaches dysglycemia (hypo/hyperglycemia) to the fluoroquinolones.
  • D fails because it includes A.

So the answer is B and C together.

b4-w14-module-q9-9.html:
From 09 - Antivirals. The influenza drugs are oseltamivir (oral neuraminidase inhibitor), zanamivir (inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor) and baloxavir marboxil (oral, single dose, a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor that blocks viral RNA replication). All shorten symptoms by only about a day.

  • A acyclovir/valacyclovir are guanosine analogues for HSV-1, HSV-2 and VZV.
  • B penicillins are antibacterials with no antiviral activity.
  • D ganciclovir/valganciclovir are the CMV drugs.

flags.title: The key's rationale is half right
flags.html: The bank's key says both drugs target neuraminidase. 09 - Antivirals says that is true only of oseltamivir: baloxavir marboxil inhibits cap-dependent endonuclease and blocks RNA replication. The letter (C) stands; the reason does not.

b4-w14-new-q10-10.html:
From 06 - New Vaccine Platforms. Viral-vector vaccines (adenovirus, as in Janssen and AstraZeneca) carry a named disadvantage: patients can mount a strong immune reaction to the vector itself, especially if previously exposed, with lower efficacy. That is why repeated dosing may lose effect.

  • A lipid nanoparticles are how mRNA vaccines are delivered.
  • C the cold chain is the mRNA drawback; viral vectors are stable in regular storage.
  • B the bank assigns this to mRNA (rare myocarditis/pericarditis); see the note below.

flags.title: Option B is arguable
flags.html: 06 - New Vaccine Platforms lists a strong immune reaction to the vector as a viral-vector disadvantage, and VITT as its rare side effect, so “triggers unintended immune reactions” could describe adenoviral vectors too. D is the more specific match; the key's claim that B belongs only to mRNA is not in the note.

b4-w14-new-q18-18:
From 09 - Antivirals. Neuraminidase frees newly budded virions from the cell surface, so the neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir) stop viral particles leaving the host cell. The lecture also stresses that compared with placebo they shorten symptoms by only about 1 day, a modest effect.

  • A true (release step of the life cycle).
  • C true.
  • B false: oseltamivir is right, but “zyclovir” is not a drug (acyclovir, the look-alike, is a herpesvirus drug).
  • D fails because it includes B.

b4-w14-new-q2-2.html:
From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents. The lecture's examples by mode:

  • I C. difficile: direct contact, listed with MRSA as the most common mode.
  • II varicella zoster: airborne (particles under 5 microns, with TB and measles).
  • III Plasmodium falciparum: vector-borne (mosquito), like West Nile and dengue.
  • IV C. botulinum: common vehicle, the lecture's example being home-canned food.

So the four agents map to four different modes; none of them share a mode.

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
flags.html: The “C.” of C. difficile was read as option letter C, so the real option C is missing and item I's name is broken. The surviving options are A airborne, B vector, D direct contact.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives C for both I (C. difficile) and IV (C. botulinum). 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents puts C. difficile under direct contact and botulism under common vehicle, so the two cannot share a letter. Whatever the lost option C was, one of those two keyed pairs contradicts the lecture; on the surviving options I should be D (direct contact).

b4-w14-new-q20-20:
From 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance. Every statement is in the lecture:

  • A enzymatic inactivation by β-lactamase is called a major resistance mechanism for Gram-negative pathogens.
  • B β-lactamases destroy drugs containing the β-lactam ring (penicillins, cephalosporins).
  • C they can be plasmid-borne (ESBL is picked up on a plasmid, per Lecture 1) or chromosomal.
  • D the SPACE organisms (Serratia, Pseudomonas/Proteus, Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter) carry AmpC β-lactamases encoded on their chromosomes.

With all four true, E is the only complete answer.
b4-w14-new-q21-21:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. The lecture names qSOFA as the bedside score for recognising sepsis, reserving the full SOFA score for measuring organ failure in trials.

  • A septic shock is hypotension that does not respond to fluids, not one that responds half the time.
  • B sepsis follows infection by bacteria, viruses or fungi.
  • C cardiovascular dysfunction means low BP with a high heart rate and weak contraction, not a falling heart rate.
  • E source control is one of the four management principles: you must find and control the cause (drain, operate, remove the device).
b4-w14-new-q3-3:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture groups antibiotics by the bacterial process they hit:

  • I β-lactams → B: bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking (cell wall).
  • II macrolides → C: bind the 50S subunit (protein synthesis).
  • III quinolones → D: inhibit DNA gyrase, a type II topoisomerase (nucleic acid synthesis).
  • IV aminoglycosides → C: bind 30S and cause mRNA misreading (protein synthesis).
  • V carbapenems → B: they are β-lactams, the broadest-spectrum ones (cell wall).
  • VI sulfonamides → A: folate synthesis inhibitors (e.g. TMP-SMX).
b4-w14-new-q9-9:
From 16 - How Viruses Work. The lecture's table on SARS-CoV-2 and influenza as multisystem disease lists, for SARS-CoV-2:

  • A respiratory: respiratory failure (ARDS).
  • B VTE: PE and DVT, with stroke listed under CNS.
  • C cardiac: acute cardiac injury and arrhythmias.

It also adds GI upset, anosmia, headache and a Kawasaki-like cytokine storm. Because all three options appear, E (all of the above) beats D (A and B only), which leaves out the cardiac injury.

b4-w14-sa-q2-2.html:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. What separates severe sepsis from sepsis is organ dysfunction. The lecture's early-recognition physiology lists the kidney sign as oliguria, and acute kidney injury is one of the organ failures of MODS, so low urine output is evidence that an organ is failing.

  • A, C fever and tachycardia are signs of the systemic inflammatory response that sepsis already has; on their own they show no organ failure.
  • B recent surgery is a high-risk group for sepsis, not a feature of its severity.
  • E shortness of breath is a symptom; the lung dysfunction the lecture counts is hypoxia or ARDS, which the option does not establish.

flags.title: The case was not banked with this question
flags.html: “This patient” refers to a shared self-assessment case that is not in the stem, most likely the bowel perforation during colonoscopy in the preceding question (b4-w14-sa-q1-1). The reasoning here does not depend on its details.

b4-w14-sa-q3-3.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Cell wall agents are the β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) and the glycopeptides (vancomycin). Imipenem (carbapenem), cefazolin (1st-gen cephalosporin) and amoxicillin (aminopenicillin) are all β-lactams.

  • A ciprofloxacin inhibits DNA gyrase.
  • B clindamycin binds 50S and gentamicin binds 30S (protein synthesis).
  • D doxycycline (30S) and clarithromycin (50S) are protein synthesis inhibitors; only vancomycin fits.
  • E clindamycin is a lincosamide acting on 50S, although imipenem and amoxicillin-clavulanate are β-lactams.

b4-w14-sa-q6-6:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. Gram-positive cocci in clusters are staphylococci, so S. aureus bacteremia is the worry. Injection drug use is on the lecture list of MRSA risk factors (09 - Approach to a Patient with Fever), and a febrile bacteremic patient is in the sepsis/deep-seated column, where the IV choice with MRSA risk is vancomycin. Empirically you assume the worst until susceptibilities return.

  • A piperacillin-tazobactam is broad Gram-negative/anti-pseudomonal cover that the lecture does not use for MRSA.
  • B cefazolin treats MSSA but not MRSA; it is where you narrow to once the isolate proves susceptible.
  • C ciprofloxacin is weak against Gram-positives.
  • E clindamycin is a bacteriostatic oral option for stable MRSA-risk SSTI, not empiric bacteremia therapy.
b4-w15-meds2024-q27-27:
From 03 - Important Fungal Infections. The lecture makes the exception explicit: tinea versicolour is NOT a dermatophyte infection; it is caused by Malassezia furfur. The other “tinea” conditions (capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium) are dermatophyte infections.

  • A Candida causes mucocutaneous thrush, vulvovaginal and diaper candidiasis, not pigmented patches.
  • B Saccharomyces cerevisiae is baker's yeast and is not a pathogen in the lecture.
  • D Aspergillus is an invasive or allergic mould of the lungs and sinuses.
  • E tinea corporis is a disease name (a dermatophyte infection of the body), not an organism.
b4-w15-module-q1-1:
From 06 - Approach to Allergy. The Gell and Coombs table puts Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis under type IV, cell-mediated (delayed) hypersensitivity, together with blistering and morbilliform drug eruptions and allergic contact dermatitis. Onset days into therapy fits a delayed T-cell reaction.

  • A type I is IgE-mediated and immediate (urticaria, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis).
  • B type II is IgG/IgM cytotoxic (hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, interstitial nephritis).
  • C type III is immune-complex disease (serum sickness, drug fever, vasculitis).
  • E the lecture's classification has only four types.

A severe delayed reaction like SJS is a hard contraindication to ever re-challenging the drug.
b4-w15-module-q10-10:
From 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation. The lecture lists the cells of chronic inflammation as the mononuclear cells (macrophages, the dominant cell and the core of granulomas; lymphocytes, which sustain the response with cytokines; plasma cells, with clock-face nuclei, making antibody) plus eosinophils in allergy and parasitic infection. It adds a note that neutrophils are not typically involved in chronic inflammation unless an acute process is running at the same time.

Neutrophils are the first cells to arrive in acute inflammation, which is why they are the odd one out. A, B, C and E are all named chronic-inflammatory cells.
b4-w15-module-q2-2:
From 06 - Approach to Allergy. The venom-allergy section defines a large local reaction as swelling contiguous with the sting site, building over 1–2 days and larger than 10 cm. A hand-and-forearm swelling for 3 days with no other symptoms fits exactly.

  • A a “large irritant reaction” is not a category; a normal local reaction is pain, itch and redness lasting hours.
  • B systemic cutaneous reactions (flushing, urticaria, angioedema) appear on skin not contiguous with the sting.
  • D anaphylaxis is systemic extracutaneous: bronchospasm, airway edema, hypotension.
  • E venom reactions in sensitised people are IgE-mediated (type I), not immune-complex.

b4-w15-module-q9-9.html:
From 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation. The previous question's image is keyed as caseating, granulomatous inflammation. The lecture describes a granuloma as epithelioid macrophages ringed by T cells, and says the central cheese-like (caseating) necrosis is classically associated with tuberculosis.

  • A Crohn's disease forms granulomas, but they are non-caseating.
  • B Hodgkin lymphoma is a malignancy, not a granulomatous infection.
  • C, D Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus cause acute, purulent (neutrophil-rich) inflammation, not caseating granulomas.

flags.title: The presentation is in the previous question
flags.html: “The above presentation” is the histology image in b4-w15-module-q8-8 (keyed caseating and granulomatous). This explanation relies on that key; the image itself is not in this question.

b4-w15-new-q19-19.html:
From 03 - Important Fungal Infections. The lecture gives this exact description for mucormycosis: on calcofluor white stain of tissue or BAL, wide, irregular hyphae (6–15 μm) with few septations that twist like a ribbon and branch at 90°. Transplant recipients are a named risk group. So the stain points to C.

  • A, B Candida and Cryptococcus are yeasts; they bud rather than forming wide hyphae (Cryptococcus is diagnosed by CrAg).
  • D dermatophytes are superficial moulds of hair, skin and nails and do not cause pneumonia.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys D (dermatophytes). 03 - Important Fungal Infections describes wide, irregular hyphae with few septations on calcofluor white of BAL as the hallmark of mucormycosis (C), lists transplantation as a risk factor, and places dermatophytes among the superficial mycoses of hair, skin and nails. The lecture supports C.

b4-w15-new-q24-24.html:
From 04 - Antifungals. Azoles inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (a CYP450), so no ergosterol is made and the membrane's permeability is altered. That is the one correct pairing.

  • C echinocandins inhibit 1,3-β-D-glucan synthesis in the cell wall; they leave ergosterol alone.
  • D amphotericin B (a polyene) binds ergosterol and inserts into the membrane, forming pores; the glucan target belongs to the echinocandins. C and D have swapped mechanisms.
  • A the allylamines are not in the lecture; see the note below.

flags.title: Option A is not covered by the vault notes
flags.html: Neither 03 - Important Fungal Infections nor 04 - Antifungals covers allylamines (terbinafine). In general pharmacology they inhibit squalene epoxidase, an earlier step in ergosterol synthesis, so “disrupts the fungal cell membrane” is at best imprecise. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w15-new-q3-3.html:
From 05 - Approach to Immunodeficiency. Secondary immunodeficiency is the most common type in practice. The lecture's causes are malignancy (lymphoma, leukemia), immunosuppressive drugs, chronic infection such as HIV, asplenia, malnutrition, prematurity or older age, and environmental stress.

  • A and C are both named, so E (A, C) is the keyed answer.
  • B iron deficiency is not listed on its own; the nearest cause in the lecture is general malnutrition, and the question's author has excluded it.

Asplenia does not stop immune cells being made; it removes the spleen's filtering of encapsulated bacteria.

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
flags.html: The options run A, B, C, E: option D is missing, and the answer is a free-text sentence rather than a letter. The key's reason (“damage the body's ability to produce immune cells”) fits malignancy but not asplenia.

b4-w15-new-q5-5.html:
From 06 - Approach to Allergy. Of patients labelled penicillin-allergic, more than 90% are not allergic on skin testing, and the lecture lists why:

  • A the reaction was often an intolerance (diarrhea, nausea), not an allergy.
  • C labelled patients are more likely to get alternative broad-spectrum antibiotics, with more C. difficile, MRSA and surgical site infection from less perioperative cefazolin.
  • D the most common cause of a rash is the infection, not the drug.

Every statement is supported, which is what the bank's own rationale says (“all of the options describe a penicillin allergy”).

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys D, but its own rationale says all of the options are true, and 06 - Approach to Allergy supports A, C and D each in turn (intolerance, the switch to broad-spectrum alternatives, infection as the usual cause of rash). On the lecture the answer is E (all of the above).

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
flags.html: Option B is missing and option A starts with a stray “A”, so the list has lost a statement. The lecture's point that labels wane (80% not allergic after 10 years' avoidance) may have been it.

b4-w15-new-q6-6.html:
From 09 - Autoimmunity. Each option is one of the lecture's mechanisms for breaking tolerance:

  • A defective deletion: peripheral deletion kills self-reactive T cells through a Fas ligand death signal, so mutations in Fas, Fas ligand or their pathway let those cells survive (MS, RA, SLE).
  • B infection-driven superantigens link the TCR to MHC II regardless of antigen, giving polyclonal activation that can include self-reactive T cells (Kawasaki disease).
  • C tissue injury releases intracellular self-antigens to ignorant T cells, e.g. uveitis after eye surgery, usually transient.

All three are possible breakdowns in self-tolerance.

flags.title: An option was lost in transcription
flags.html: Only A-C survive and the key is a free-text sentence; an “all of the above” option D was most likely dropped.

b4-w15-ra-q1-1:
From 07 - Understanding Immunology Lab Test Results and 06 - Approach to Allergy. The allergic-rhinitis history asks whether symptoms are present all the time or intermittently, indoors or outdoors, and at what time of year. Daily congestion and sneezing for a whole year is perennial, which points to an indoor allergen that is always present, and the lecture's example is the dust mite (its feces are the allergen extract).

  • B, C tree and grass pollens are seasonal allergens, with spring or summer flares rather than year-round symptoms.
  • D an animal allergen needs regular exposure; a horse is not a daily household contact for a 7-year-old, whereas dust mites are in every home.

b4-w13-meds2024-q13-13.html:
From 04 - Adaptive Immunity and 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. IgM is the first antibody made, is secreted as a pentamer (10 antigen-binding sites) and is highly avid. It is described as a potent activator of complement via its Fc regions, the best of the classes.

  • B IgG also activates complement, but it is a monomer.
  • C IgE sits on mast cell Fcε receptors and does not fix complement.
  • D IgA is a monomer in blood and a dimer in secretions; its job is neutralisation.

b4-w13-meds2024-q14-14.html:
From 04 - Adaptive Immunity and 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. IgE circulates at low levels because it is bound to the high-affinity FcεRI on mast cells and basophils. When antigen cross-links the surface IgE, the cell degranulates and releases histamine. This is type I hypersensitivity (allergy, asthma, anaphylaxis), and IgE also rises in helminth infection.

  • A IgM is the pentameric complement activator of the primary response.
  • B IgG uses Fc receptors on phagocytes for opsonisation and ADCC, not mast cells.
  • D IgA neutralises at mucosal surfaces.

b4-w13-meds2024-q15-15.html:
From 04 - Adaptive Immunity. IgG is the class “found within the circulation and in the extracellular space”, and the lecture calls it a potent activator of opsonisation, ADCC, complement and neutralisation. The refresher adds that it is the most abundant antibody in blood and rapidly leaves the bloodstream into inflamed tissue.

  • A IgM is mainly in the blood, not the extracellular space, and its forte is complement.
  • C IgE is bound to mast cells.
  • D IgA acts on its own at mucosal barriers and does not engage the rest of the immune system.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys letter D, which is IgA, but its own key text says “(IgG)”, and 04 - Adaptive Immunity gives the circulation-plus-extracellular-space and ADCC description to IgG. On the lecture the answer is B. The letters of this question and the next (IgA) look swapped.

b4-w13-meds2024-q16-16.html:
From 04 - Adaptive Immunity and 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. IgA is secreted as a dimer across mucosal barriers (gut, lungs, nasal mucosa), carried through the epithelium by pIgR, and neutralises pathogens there. It is abundant in saliva, tears and breast milk, especially colostrum, which transfers maternal immunity to the infant.

  • A IgM is a pentamer found mainly in blood.
  • B IgG protects the newborn by crossing the placenta, not through milk, and is not the mucosal class.
  • C IgE is bound to mast cells.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank keys letter B, which is IgG, but its own key text says “(IgA)”, and both 04 - Adaptive Immunity and 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher place mucosal secretion and breast milk with IgA. On the lecture the answer is D. The letters of this question and the previous one (IgG) look swapped.

b4-w13-module-q1-1.html:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The specimen table follows one rule: sample the site of infection.

  • i UTI → A urine: suprapubic aspiration is the gold standard, then catheter or mid-stream. Never take it from a catheter bag.
  • ii infective arthritis → C synovial fluid: joints and other sterile sites need fluid or tissue.
  • iii wound infection → B tissue or deep wound swab: deep tissue beats a surface swab, which only grows colonisers. A biopsy of the advancing margin is best.
  • iv meningitis → D CSF: by lumbar puncture, 3–4 tubes.

b4-w13-module-q11-11.html:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The lecture's “organisms outside the Gram scheme” table lists Mycoplasma as the organism with no cell wall, and so no peptidoglycan. That is why it does not Gram stain and why cell-wall drugs do not touch it.

  • A Finegoldia is an anaerobic Gram-positive coccus with thick peptidoglycan.
  • C mycobacteria have a cell wall; it is the waxy wall that makes them acid-fast.
  • D Actinomyces and its relatives are Gram-positive bacilli.
  • E Borrelia is a spirochaete, grouped separately but not wall-less.

b4-w13-module-q12-12.html:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The acid-fast stain is used for mycobacteria (and corynebacteria). Red carbol fuchsin is held by the wall against an acid-alcohol decolouriser, so acid-fast organisms stay red on a methylene blue or malachite green background (Ziehl-Neelsen).

  • A the lecture gives no two-minute timing; the Gram stain is the rapid, presumptive stain.
  • B an indeterminate Gram stain is not the indication; suspicion of mycobacteria is.
  • C safranin and alcohol/acetone are the Gram stain's counterstain and decolouriser; acid-fast uses acid alcohol and methylene blue.
  • E organisms without peptidoglycan (Mycoplasma) have no wall to hold the stain.

b4-w13-module-q18-18.html:
From 07 - The Normal Healthy Microbiome. The lecture's site-by-site commensals:

  • A S. epidermidis → i skin: coagulase-negative staphylococci are skin flora, and losing them lets S. aureus drive eczema.
  • B viridans group streptococci → ii mouth: oral flora (streptococci, S. anginosus), whose compartment breach gives dental abscess.
  • C E. coli → iii colon: an aerobic Gram-negative of the gut, and the cause of peritonitis when the gut is breached.
  • D Lactobacillus → i, iv: listed on skin and as the key vaginal commensal; its loss is bacterial vaginosis.
  • E Candida → all four: listed as a commensal at every site.

b4-w13-module-q2-2.html:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The lecture lists the uses of microscopy as rapid preliminary or final organism detection, detecting several organisms in one specimen, and detecting organisms that are hard to culture. For some pathogens the appearance under the microscope is diagnostic in itself, for example acid-fast bacilli or the ribbon-like hyphae of mucormycosis on calcofluor white.

So the statement is true. Two caveats keep it from being universal: the Gram stain is only presumptive, and for most bacteria growth in culture is still needed for definitive identification and susceptibility testing.

b4-w13-module-q20-20.html:
From 06 - Interpreting Microbiologic Investigations. The lecture lists the bacterial causes of meningitis by age, and under one month they are S. agalactiae (GBS), E. coli and Listeria monocytogenes. The same trio is what empiric neonatal septic work-up covers (09 - Approach to a Patient with Fever).

  • A Pseudomonas and C S. aureus are not on any age band's meningitis list; they are hospital, wound and device pathogens.
  • D Cryptococcus is the lecture's fungal cause of meningitis, a disease of the immunocompromised, not of the newborn.

b4-w13-module-q21-21.html:
A specimen needs at least two independent patient identifiers (e.g., full name plus date of birth or health-card/chart number) so that it can be matched to one patient without ambiguity. 05 - Microbiology Lab says only to “label accurately — identifiers and clinical information” and that unlabelled, mislabelled or incompletely labelled specimens are rejected; the pathology-report table in 06 - Cancer Genetics likewise lists name, DOB and ID number together.

  • A (one) fails: a name alone cannot separate two patients with the same name, which is the error the rule exists to stop.
  • C and D overshoot the minimum; more identifiers are allowed, but two is the standard floor.

flags.title: The number two is not in the vault notes
flags.html: 05 - Microbiology Lab requires specimens to carry identifiers and rejects incompletely labelled ones, but no note states the minimum number. The two-identifier rule is general patient-safety practice; verify it before relying on it.

b4-w13-module-q22-22.html: From 06 - Interpreting Microbiologic Investigations. The statement is false. The lecture's rule for clinicians is “collect a specimen, not a swab”: a superficial swab picks up colonising skin flora, so what grows cannot be told apart from contamination. For skin and soft tissue infection, diagnosis is usually clinical, and when a specimen is needed the specimen of choice is a biopsy of the advancing margin or a deep wound swab (05 - Microbiology Lab: “deep tissue is better”). The lab is also told not to report everything that grows, which is exactly what a surface swab would produce.

b4-w13-module-q24-24.html:
From 14 - Pathology of Acute Inflammation. An abscess is purulent (suppurative) inflammation localised to a cavity, and purulent inflammation is most often caused by pus-producing pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus, which cause liquefactive necrosis. 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass puts it the same way: an abscess is a collection of pus, “usually bacterial”.

  • A allergy drives type I hypersensitivity and eosinophils, not a neutrophil-filled pus cavity.
  • C a foreign body is a classic trigger of a granuloma (chronic inflammation), not the usual cause of an abscess.
  • D fungi and E viruses can cause abscesses in unusual hosts, but they are not the common cause.

b4-w13-module-q25-25.html:
From 14 - Pathology of Acute Inflammation. An abscess is walled off from the surrounding tissue and has no blood vessels in its pus-filled necrotic centre, so antibiotics struggle to reach it. That is why skin abscesses are treated with incision and drainage and deep organ abscesses may need surgery.

  • A true: the wall (in S. aureus, a fibrin pseudocapsule; 08 - Some Important Gram-Positives) limits penetration.
  • B true: the avascular centre means the drug cannot be delivered by blood.
  • C false: most abscesses are caused by pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus, not resistant mycobacteria.
  • D false: most are infected, not sterile; drainage is needed because the drug cannot get in, not because there is nothing to kill.

b4-w13-module-q28-28.html:
From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The lecture's classification table sorts all six directly.

  • Gram-negative bacilli (I): Pseudomonas (A), E. coli (B), Proteus (D) and Klebsiella (E) all sit in the aerobic Gram-negative bacilli row — pink rods with an outer membrane and LPS.
  • Gram-positive cocci (II): Staphylococcus saprophyticus (C) is a staphylococcus (cocci in clusters) and Enterococcus (F) sits with the streptococci (cocci in pairs/chains) — purple, thick peptidoglycan.

All six are also uropathogens (the KEEPS list: Klebsiella, E. coli, Enterococcus, Proteus, S. saprophyticus), which is why a Gram stain matters in UTI: it splits them into two treatment groups.

b4-w13-module-q3-3.html: From 05 - Microbiology Lab. True. The KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation dissolves the protein material in skin, hair or nail and leaves the fungal elements, which are not affected by the strong alkali, easy to see; a dye such as phenol blue can raise the contrast. It is used to separate dermatophytes and Candida from skin disorders such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. 03 - Important Fungal Infections sends scrapings, nail clippings or hair for KOH smear and fungal culture for exactly this reason. Contrast calcofluor white, a fluorescent fungal stain that binds chitin.

b4-w13-new-q26-26.html:
From In-Class - Fever. The lecture classifies fever by onset: acute (< 7 days), subacute (1–2 weeks) and chronic/persistent (> 2 weeks).

  • Acute (I): UTI (A) and bacterial soft tissue infection (E) are listed with viral infection and pneumonia.
  • Subacute (II): intra-abdominal abscess (D) is the lecture's example.
  • Chronic (III): TB (B), HIV (C) and connective tissue disorders such as SLE (F) are listed with cancer.

The timing itself narrows the differential: a fever past two weeks shifts the search away from ordinary acute infections toward TB, HIV, malignancy and autoimmune disease.

b4-w13-sa-q1-1.html:
From 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. IL-4 is the Th2 cytokine: it induces Th2 differentiation and Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5 and IL-6, driving IgE, eosinophils and humoral immunity. IL-12 actively opposes IL-4's effect on APC-stimulated T cells.

  • A IFN-γ induces Th1 and is its signature product (macrophage activation).
  • C lymphotoxin is TNF-β, which the lecture lists among Th1 products.
  • D IL-2 is secreted by Th1 cells (and drives T cell proliferation).
  • E IL-12, from macrophages and dendritic cells, drives T cells down the Th1 pathway.

b4-w13-sa-q3-3.html:
All four statements are true, so E. The vault covers the group A strep half directly: 05 - Microbiology Lab and 08 - Some Important Gram-Positives list pharyngitis among S. pyogenes's non-invasive diseases and rheumatic fever among its post-infectious ones (anti-M-protein antibodies cross-reacting with cardiac tropomyosin). 02 - Classification of Different Microbes adds that GAS in the throat is “very common and you don't want to miss it, since there is treatment for it that prevents complications”.

  • A true: most pharyngitis is viral (07 - The Normal Healthy Microbiome lists adenovirus beside GAS), which is why antibiotics are not given by default.
  • B and C true: GAS causes rheumatic fever, and early antibiotic treatment of strep throat prevents it.
  • D true: throat culture is the reference standard for confirming GAS; clinical features alone cannot separate it from viral pharyngitis.

flags.title: Options A and D are only partly covered
flags.html: The vault supports B and C. That most pharyngitis is viral and that culture is the diagnostic standard for strep throat are not stated in any note; they are from general principles. Verify them before relying on them.

b4-w13-sa-q4-4.html:
Every clue points to Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a Gram-negative rod that is oxidase-positive and non-fermenting, makes the blue-green pigment pyocyanin, smells of grapes, and is highly antibiotic resistant. The vault supports the setting and the resistance: hospital-acquired pneumonia is driven by Gram-negative organisms (05 - Microbiology Lab), and Pseudomonas uses porin loss, efflux pumps and β-lactamases (“it can actually do all of these things”, 11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance).

  • A E. coli is oxidase-negative and a lactose fermenter (11 - Some Important Gram-Negatives).
  • B Yersinia pestis, C Salmonella Typhi and D Shigella are oxidase-negative, glucose-fermenting enteric organisms, and none makes a pigment.

flags.title: The pigment and odour clues are not in the vault notes
flags.html: The notes place Pseudomonas among the Gram-negative bacilli and describe its resistance, but pyocyanin, the grape odour and its oxidase-positive, non-fermenting identity are from general microbiology. Verify them before relying on them.

b4-w13-sa-q7-7.html:
From 03 - Innate Immunity Refresher. Pattern recognition receptors such as the TLRs recognise PAMPs: conserved structures shared across whole classes of microbes, such as bacterial LPS and CpG motifs. 05 - Microbiology Lab adds that lipoteichoic acid signals through TLR2 and LPS through TLR4. Pertussis toxin is a secreted protein exotoxin specific to one organism. It is not a conserved pattern, and the lecture handles toxins through antibody neutralisation (adaptive immunity), not PRRs.

  • A fungal mannans (cell-wall sugars), B LPS, C viral RNA and E peptidoglycan are all conserved microbial structures, and each is a PAMP that some PRR recognises.

flags.title: Mannans and viral RNA are not named in the vault notes
flags.html: The notes name LPS, CpG motifs and lipoteichoic acid as PRR ligands; that fungal mannans, viral RNA and peptidoglycan are also PAMPs is from general immunology. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w13-sa-q9-9.html:
From 08 - Some Important Gram-Positives. S. aureus is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive (coagulase binds and activates prothrombin), whereas S. epidermidis is the classic coagulase-negative staphylococcus, a skin commensal and blood-culture contaminant (06 - Interpreting Microbiologic Investigations). The test's job is to split staphylococci that already look alike: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, both catalase-positive.

  • A, D and E pair organisms that earlier steps already separate: Gram stain (Neisseria is a Gram-negative diplococcus) or catalase (staph positive, strep negative).
  • C S. pyogenes and Enterococcus are both catalase-negative and neither makes coagulase, so the test cannot tell them apart.

b4-w14-meds2024-q10-10.html:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. The lecture lists what is NOT routine in Canada: oral polio, yellow fever, shingles, Salmonella, Japanese encephalitis, hepatitis A, meningococcal B, pneumococcal polysaccharide and BCG. BCG is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine against TB, used only for selected high-risk groups.

  • B varicella is a live vaccine given routinely in childhood.
  • C influenza is offered to everyone every year under Ontario's universal program.
  • D pertussis is given routinely as the acellular component of DTaP/Tdap.

b4-w14-meds2024-q15-15.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture explains ESBL as a bacterium “hanging around a bunch of bad guys” that picks up a plasmid carrying the instructions for extended-spectrum β-lactamase. That is horizontal gene transfer, and it is the fast route to resistance: the lecture notes that bacteria “can transfer their antibiotic resistance to other bacteria”. ESBL E. coli and Klebsiella then destroy 3rd/4th-generation cephalosporins and pip-tazo.

  • A fails: a single cell does not “evolve”. Resistance arises from mutation and selection across a population, or from acquiring a gene.
  • B fails: ESBL is an enzyme each resistant cell makes from its own gene, not a cooperative product.
  • C fails: environmental signals cannot make a cell express a gene it does not carry.

b4-w14-meds2024-q17-17.html:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin with no anti-pseudomonal activity. The lecture's anti-pseudomonal penicillin is piperacillin/tazobactam, and Pseudomonas sits at the resistant outer edge of the spectrum chart (11 - Intro to Antimicrobial Resistance).

  • B carbapenems are the broadest-spectrum antibiotics (Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and anaerobes), reserved for serious or resistant infections.
  • C aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) cover aerobic Gram-negative bacilli.
  • D pip-tazo is the one the lecture explicitly names: in the peritonitis case it is “wider coverage than we need (since it also covers Pseudomonas)”.

b4-w14-meds2024-q18-18.html:
From 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 2. In the cellulitis case the lecture says penicillin covers group A strep (S. pyogenes) but is too narrow on its own because it lacks anti-staphylococcal activity. Penicillin is the lecture's example of a narrow-spectrum drug.

  • A E. coli: the Gram-negative outer membrane “makes it resistant to penicillin” (05 - Microbiology Lab).
  • C S. aureus: penicillins give no S. aureus coverage apart from the anti-staphylococcal agents such as cloxacillin, because most strains make penicillinase.
  • D MRSA carries mecA/PBP2a, which no β-lactam binds, so it needs vancomycin.

b4-w14-meds2024-q26-26.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Trimethoprim is a folate-synthesis inhibitor, the partner of sulfamethoxazole in TMP-SMX. The lecture notes that folate is “vital for DNA”. Blocking the folate pathway starves the cell of the building blocks for purine and thymidine bases, so it acts upstream on the nitrogenous bases rather than on the DNA strand itself.

  • A fluoroquinolones and E ciprofloxacin (one of them) inhibit DNA gyrase (type II topoisomerase), acting on DNA supercoiling, not on base synthesis.
  • C metronidazole is the lecture's anaerobe-only drug; it damages the DNA strand directly rather than blocking base synthesis.
  • D carbapenems are cell-wall β-lactams that bind PBPs.

flags.title: Base synthesis and metronidazole's mechanism are not in the vault notes
flags.html: The notes class trimethoprim as a folate-synthesis inhibitor and say folate is vital for DNA; that this blocks purine and thymidine synthesis, and that metronidazole damages DNA directly, is from general pharmacology. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w14-meds2024-q28-28.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture sorts antibiotics by the process they hit. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) bind the 50S ribosomal subunit and are bacteriostatic protein-synthesis inhibitors.

  • A β-lactams and B carbapenems (a β-lactam class) bind penicillin-binding proteins and block cell-wall cross-linking.
  • D fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase, so they target nucleic acid synthesis.

b4-w14-meds2024-q29-29.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem) are β-lactams, and every β-lactam works by binding penicillin-binding proteins, the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan. So D is right.

  • A fails: vancomycin binds the peptidoglycan precursor itself (D-Ala-D-Ala, which VRE alters to D-Ala-D-Lac), not the cross-linking enzymes. Targeting those enzymes is the β-lactam mechanism.
  • B fails: tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit; folate synthesis is the sulfonamide/trimethoprim target.
  • C fails: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase; the 30S binders are aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
  • E fails: clindamycin binds the 50S subunit; pore-forming membrane agents are the lipopeptides/polymyxins.

b4-w14-meds2024-q9-9.html:
From 11 - Herpes. Varicella zoster virus is a herpesvirus, and the defining feature of herpesviruses is lifelong latency. After primary chickenpox, VZV persists as a silent episome in the sensory ganglia, with no replication. It reactivates years later, typically as waning immunity or stress lets it through, causing shingles in a dermatomal distribution (08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation: about 33% lifetime risk).

  • A hepatitis A, B mumps and D measles cause acute infections that are cleared and leave lasting immunity. None establishes a latent reservoir that reactivates.

b4-w14-module-q2-2.html: From 01 - Transmission of Infectious Agents. False. The lecture opens by saying that not every exposure leads to infection: the probability depends on host susceptibility, the size of the exposure, the organism's viability and virulence, and how well control measures work. The susceptible host is also the last link in the chain of infection. The same exposure can colonise one person and cause severe disease in another, and vaccines lower the risk by raising the host's defences.

b4-w14-module-q3-3.html:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. The penicillin family has no S. aureus coverage apart from the anti-staphylococcal agents such as cloxacillin, because most S. aureus make a penicillinase. That is why the lecture calls penicillin “too narrow” for cellulitis.

  • B group A strep: the lecture states outright that penicillin covers GAS.
  • A syphilis (Treponema pallidum), D group B strep and E viridans streptococci remain penicillin-susceptible, and penicillin is a first-line treatment for each.

flags.title: Options A, D and E are only partly covered
flags.html: The vault supports B and C (penicillin covers GAS but not S. aureus). Penicillin's activity against T. pallidum, GBS and viridans streptococci is not stated in any note; it is from general pharmacology. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w14-module-q4-4.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Clindamycin is a lincosamide that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and is bacteriostatic. It covers aerobic Gram-positive cocci (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus) and anaerobes.

  • A 30S inhibition is the aminoglycoside and tetracycline mechanism.
  • C DNA gyrase inhibition is the fluoroquinolone mechanism.
  • D cell-wall inhibition is the β-lactam and vancomycin mechanism.

b4-w14-module-q6-6.html:
From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone. Fluoroquinolones inhibit the ligase activity of type II topoisomerases (DNA gyrase) and are bactericidal. Resistance correspondingly comes from gyrase/topoisomerase target-site mutations.

  • A 30S belongs to aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
  • B 50S belongs to macrolides, clindamycin and chloramphenicol.
  • D cell-wall synthesis belongs to β-lactams and glycopeptides.

b4-w14-module-q8-8.html:
From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. The spectrum chart runs from penicillin (narrowest) to carbapenems (broadest).

  • I. Penicillin → focused: the lecture's example of a narrow-spectrum drug, covering GAS but not even S. aureus.
  • II. Cefazolin → focused: a 1st-generation cephalosporin (Gram-positive cocci, limited Gram-negatives), chosen in the cellulitis case precisely because it targets staph and strep, where ceftriaxone is “too broad”.
  • III. Amoxicillin → focused: an aminopenicillin; the lecture lists it as broad only in combination with clavulanic acid.
  • IV. Meropenem → broad: carbapenems have the broadest spectrum of all and are reserved for serious or resistant infections.
  • V. Pip-tazo → broad: “wider coverage than we need”, since it reaches Gram-negatives, anaerobes and Pseudomonas.

b4-w14-new-q11-11.html:
From 08 - Vaccine Hesitancy. The lecture's comparison table splits the rare adverse effects by platform. The adenoviral-vector vaccines (AstraZeneca, J&J) carry clots/TTS (under 10 per million), capillary leak syndrome and Guillain-Barré syndrome. The mRNA vaccines carry myocarditis/pericarditis and Bell's palsy. So Bell's palsy is the exception. 07 - Vaccine Adverse Effects gives the same split, with VITT and GBS under adenoviral and myocarditis and Bell's palsy under mRNA.

  • A, B and D are all adenoviral-vector effects, so they are included.

flags.title: The bank's rationale has the platforms backwards
flags.html: The letter C is right, but the key line's reason (“A, B, and D are side effects of mRNA vaccines”) is wrong. 08 - Vaccine Hesitancy and 07 - Vaccine Adverse Effects both list TTS, capillary leak and Guillain-Barré under the adenoviral vaccines, and Bell's palsy under mRNA. That split is the whole reason C is the exception.

b4-w14-new-q22-22.html:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. Under early recognition, the lecture names the high-risk groups: recent surgery, recent chemotherapy, the immunosuppressed and the elderly. All three of A–C are on it. Each one either opens a portal for infection (surgery) or blunts the host response that should contain it (chemotherapy, immunosuppression).

  • D reduced mobility is not one of the lecture's sepsis risk groups; immobility is the classic risk factor for venous thromboembolism and pressure injury instead.

b4-w14-ra-q1-1.html:
From 04 - Adaptive Immunity. The one immune mechanism that can prevent infection outright is neutralisation: antibody binds the part of the virus that has to engage a host-cell receptor, a physical blockade. So pre-exposure prophylaxis targets the viral surface entry protein. 16 - How Viruses Work applies this to SARS-CoV-2, whose spike protein (binding ACE2) “is a vaccine target”, and lists the COVID and influenza vaccines as PrEP.

  • A a transcription factor acts only after the virus is already inside the cell.
  • B the host receptor is a host protein, not a viral component, and blocking it would interfere with the receptor's normal job.
  • D the cytokine is made by the host once it is already infected.

b4-w14-sa-q1-1.html:
From 10 - Introduction to Sepsis. Sepsis is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection, so the supporting work-up looks for the source and the organ failure. Troponin is a myocardial-injury marker. It is nonspecific here and does not identify infection, a source or the systemic response, so it adds least.

  • B ABG shows respiratory failure and hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion.
  • C CBC shows leukocytosis or leukopenia and the thrombocytopenia of sepsis-associated coagulopathy.
  • D blood and urine cultures identify the organism; the lecture draws them before antibiotics only if that will not delay treatment.
  • E CXR looks for pneumonia or ARDS and, after a perforation, free air under the diaphragm (03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 2).

b4-w14-sa-q4-4.html:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines and 10 - Vaccine Preventable Diseases in Canada. Hib is a vaccine-preventable disease. The Hib conjugate vaccine links the capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier, so infants, who respond poorly to plain polysaccharide, mount a T-cell-dependent response. Routine infant vaccination is what made invasive Hib disease (meningitis, epiglottitis) rare, and it is why Hib now appears only on the list of VPDs “still seen” occasionally in Canada.

  • A hygiene and D nutrition improved gradually and cannot explain a collapse that followed the vaccine's introduction.
  • B better diagnosis finds more cases, not fewer.
  • E the reason is known.

b4-w14-sa-q5-5.html:
From 09 - Introduction to Vaccines. Measles vaccine is live attenuated, in the lecture's list with OPV, rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever, BCG and oral typhoid. Live vaccines are contraindicated in the immunocompromised, in pregnancy and in neonates, because the attenuated strain can cause vaccine-strain disease in a host who cannot contain it. This is why exposed immunocompromised patients get measles immunoglobulin instead.

  • A Hib is a conjugate vaccine.
  • B pneumococcal 23 is a polysaccharide vaccine.
  • D hepatitis B is a protein subunit vaccine.
  • E hepatitis A is inactivated whole virus.

All four non-live vaccines are safe to give to the immunocompromised.

b4-w15-module-q8-8.html:
From 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation. The image shows a cavity filled with white, chalky, cheese-like material. That is the lecture's description of a granuloma with a necrotising/caseating centre, the necrosis coming from hypoxia and free-radical injury, classically in TB. Caseating (A) and granulomatous (E) are keyed.

  • B fibrinous inflammation is a fibrin exudate on serosal surfaces (pericardium, pleura), not a cheesy mass.
  • C purulent inflammation is liquid pus from neutrophils and pyogenic bacteria, which gives liquefactive necrosis, not caseous.
  • F chronic: see the flag below. The lecture defines the granuloma as a structure of chronic inflammation.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key is A and E, but 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation defines a granuloma as an aggregate of macrophages and T cells “formed in chronic inflammation”, and it lists TB, the textbook caseating granuloma, first among the causes of chronic inflammation. On the lecture, F (Chronic) is also correct for this image.

flags.title: Option D is missing
flags.html: The options run A, B, C, E, F with no D. This is likely extraction damage in the bank; the missing option could not be recovered.

b4-w15-new-q7-7.html: From 09 - Autoimmunity and 08 - Pathology of Chronic Inflammation. RA is a systemic autoimmune disease (mediated by both antibodies and T cells, linked to HLA-DRB1 and citrullination). The chronic-inflammation lecture lists it as a hypersensitivity cause of chronic inflammation, so A holds. B holds too: persistent synovitis produces joint erosions, which the Week 15 module case says “strongly predicts future damage and disability”. C fails: autoimmune diseases are chronic processes of unknown trigger, and treatment (DMARDs such as methotrexate, and biologics such as abatacept or rituximab; 10 - A Generalist's Approach to Autoimmunity) controls the disease but does not cure it. So D (A and B).

flags.title: Option B is only partly covered
flags.html: The vault supports A and C. That RA causes severe pain and disability rests on the module case's erosion-and-disability wording rather than on a lecture statement. Verify it before relying on it.

b4-w15-sa-q6-6.html:
This continues the previous question's infant with bare lymphocyte syndrome type II, which has no HLA class II and few T cells, while B cells and monocytes are present in normal numbers. Without MHC II, CD4+ T cells cannot develop or be activated. B cells need CD4+ T cell help to make antibody and to switch from IgM to IgG and IgA (05 - Approach to Immunodeficiency; class switching happens with T helpers in the germinal centre, 04 - Adaptive Immunity). That help is exactly what is missing, so IgG and IgA fall most.

  • A fails: nothing is intrinsically wrong with the plasma cells.
  • C fails: the CD40–CD40L defect is the hyper-IgM picture. Here the whole CD4 helper cell is absent, so B is the fuller, upstream explanation.
  • D fails: B cell numbers (CD19+CD20+) are normal, so marrow maturation is intact.
  • E fails: monocytes are normal, and phagocytosis does not set immunoglobulin levels.
